The brigade landed in Cuba in April of that year and was broken within days. The record does not say whether this document predates or follows the landing, and no subject is stated. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the CIA's declassified release.
cia-0000136962: Correct the distortions, this June 1954 cable urges about coverage of the uprising against the Guatemalan regime. Communist counter-propaganda outlets and an unwitting free press are distorting the revolt as patriotic defense against outside invasion, the cable says, citing heavy bombing and a land attack launched over borders. Reports received through agency channels, it claims, reveal no bombing nor large-scale invasion, though a small number of anti-communist patriots may have returned. Headquarters urgently desires correction through the best available means.
cia-0000139162: Cooperation with the National Resource Evaluation Center is arranged in this 1968 memo. The copy is badly garbled, though. Officials visited the center. A letter requested cooperation from it. A director told staff to keep talking but make no promises. No personnel or material resources were promised. A package of training materials was prepared with the emergency office. Its director and deputy were expected for a tour. The file records routine agency work of the imagery era. Its finer details are lost to a poor scan.
cia-0000139462: American hostages in Lebanon are located in this 1988 summary of information. It comes from the remote viewing reporting stream. Frank Herbert Reed will be released with the German Cordes, reporting persists. The captors show strong reluctance to release any Americans. Joseph Cicippio and Alann Steen are held at Ash Shuwayfat. The area sits southwest of barracks ringed by Syrian troops. One man is bound by the feet, face in the dirt. He is in extremely poor condition. Terry Waite and Terry Anderson are elsewhere.
cia-0000141162: Headquarters cabled the JMWAVE station in Miami in November 1961 with orders on the 933 aircraft issue. A two-man team had been sent to Managua, the capital of Nicaragua, to name the plane and its crew. The cable points the station to an earlier message that set out how the case should be handled, and says a copy is on its way.
cia-03020462: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1955/12/14, a CIA publication. A further December briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-06084662: THE SITUATION AND PROSPECTS IN CUBA, a CIA assessment. The Cuban outlook. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
cia-06766062: The tenth Vietnam situation report sits in this file. The agency tracked the war's progress. The Southeast Asia briefing. Its pages add to the record of the past. This file preserves that declassified assessment. Writers of history may cite it later.
doe-osti-3363541-product-defect-detectio: Defects got SYSM-5620-detected, and this DOE final covers the product system. The pages detail the project findings. The industry folks get their closeout. The project was final. The closeout was industry. The 5620 were SYSM. The final were project. The industry were closeout.
europmc-pmc10093562:
Isik and co-authors review how microglia drive inflammation in Parkinson's disease in a 2023 paper. Parkinson's is the second most common brain degeneration disease, marked by tremor, stiffness, and slow movement. It involves the loss of dopamine-making nerve cells in a deep brain region.

Microglia are the brain's own immune cells, and they can turn harmful when overactive. The review gathers evidence on how their inflammation may speed nerve cell loss. It also looks at drugs that aim to calm them. The paper weighs a hopeful but still unproven treatment path.
europmc-pmc10119362:
Söderberg and colleagues compare how three Alzheimer's antibody drugs bind to different forms of amyloid-beta, in a 2023 study. The drugs are lecanemab, aducanumab, and gantenerumab. Amyloid-beta comes in several forms, from single molecules to clumps and plaques, and the loose clumps seem most harmful to brain cells.

The team measured each drug's grip on each form of the protein. The binding patterns differ in ways that may explain why trial results and side effects differed too. The study helps clarify how these much-debated drugs actually work. It also informs the design of future trials.
europmc-pmc10258562:
Lotfollahi and a large team present a model that predicts how cells respond to complex mixes of drugs and gene changes, in a 2023 paper. Modern screens can test many single changes in single cells. Testing every combination is impossible, since the number of mixes explodes. A reliable prediction model would fill that gap.

Their model learns from past single-change experiments to forecast combined effects. They show it can predict responses to pairs it never saw in training. Such forecasts could guide the design of drug combinations and genetic studies alike.
europmc-pmc10287562:
Mummery and a large trial team report a phase 1b trial of a tau-lowering drug in mild Alzheimer's disease, in a 2023 study. Tau is a protein that tangles inside brain cells in Alzheimer's and helps drive the disease. The drug, MAPT Rx, is an antisense oligonucleotide, a short strand that blocks production of tau at its source.

Patients received the drug or a placebo in a randomized trial. The team measured tau levels in spinal fluid and tracked safety. Tau fell in treated patients. The results support larger trials of tau lowering as a treatment path.
europmc-pmc10396962:
Singhal and a large team tested in 2023 how much medical knowledge big language models hold. They built a test set, MultiMedQA, from six past sets of medical questions. It spans exam questions, research queries, and health searches by the public. Human raters also scored answers for truth, logic, harm, and bias.

Their tuned model, Flan-PaLM, set new top scores on each choice-based test. It scored 67.6% on US licensing exam style questions, over 17 points past the prior best. A further step, brief tuning with sample answers, gave Med-PaLM. Human raters still ranked doctors above it. Gains grew with model size and with the tuning step.
europmc-pmc10478462:
Cai, Li, Tan, Xu, and Li reviewed three next-wave immune targets for cancer in 2023. The targets are proteins on immune cells called LAG-3, TIM-3, and TIGIT. Each acts as a brake that can blunt an immune attack on a tumour. The first brake drugs, aimed at CTLA-4 and PD-1, helped many patients but far from all.

These three form a second wave of brake targets. Cai traces how each was found and how blocking it may free immune cells. Lab tests and patient trials give early proof of effect in solid tumours and in blood cancer. Pairs of brake drugs may beat single drugs. The review sums up trial results to guide the next steps.
europmc-pmc10589462:
The Global Cardiovascular Risk Consortium pooled health data in 2023 to weigh five changeable risks for heart disease. The risks are body weight, blood pressure, a cholesterol measure, smoking, and diabetes. Past counts lacked person-level data across regions. The pool joins 112 cohort studies from 34 nations.

In all, 1,518,028 people took part, with a median age of 54.4 years at entry. New heart disease struck 80,596 of them during follow-up. The five risks jointly explained 57.2 percent of new cases in women and 52.6 percent in men. For deaths from any cause, the shares were 22.2 percent in women and 19.1 percent in men. Rates and weights of each risk split by region and sex.
europmc-pmc10640762:
Henrich and co-authors reviewed faulty cell power units in Parkinson's disease in 2023. Parkinson's is a brain disease that erodes movement control over time. Broken mitochondria, the power units of cells, are a hallmark of the disease. Both the common form and rare gene forms show the fault.

Cells lose power as a key energy chain, complex 1, fails. Henrich lists added faults: stress from reactive oxygen, poor quality control, and low fuel output. Many drugs have tried to fix these faults, from antioxidants to iron binders. Each has failed to slow the disease in trials so far. The review asks why those efforts missed, to guide the next round.
europmc-pmc10767962:
Yurekten and co-authors described MetaboLights in 2024, a free store for metabolomics studies. Metabolomics reads the small chemicals in a sample, from blood to plant leaf. The bank holds raw data plus the notes that frame each study. It spans all species and all lab methods.

Leading journals and ELIXIR, the European life science network, name it their go-to store. Yurekten reports steady growth in the range of studies sent in. A new arm, MetaboLights Labs, runs standard workflows at bank scale through the Galaxy platform. Public data see wide reuse by other teams, the authors show. Access runs through the EMBL-EBI site under open terms.
europmc-pmc11058562:
Newman and Shadel review how DNA from mitochondria escapes and triggers immune alarms in this 2023 paper. Mitochondria are cell parts that make energy and carry their own small, circular DNA. That DNA can leak into the cell body, out of the cell, or into the blood. Escaped copies switch on immune sensors and inflammasomes, protein complexes that drive inflammation.

The review first covers the escape routes, including inducible pores in the mitochondrial wall and faulty clean-up of worn mitochondria. It then matches each form of escaped DNA to the sensor it activates. Free DNA in the blood is linked to body-wide inflammation, the authors note. The process is tied to human diseases, infections, cell ageing, and ageing itself. They frame the leak as a signal the immune system reads as danger.
europmc-pmc1413562:
Junker and co-authors presented a software tool called VANTED in 2006. Labs now gather huge sets of measures on genes, enzymes, and small molecules. Such data make little sense as bare tables. VANTED lets users lay the data onto network maps, such as the paths cells use to build and burn food.

Users load data through a spreadsheet form, then draw a map or import one from a public database. The tool can chart change over time and group items that move alike. Junker tested it on plant data sets. Some links it flagged between small molecules matched what past work had found.
europmc-pmc1819562:
Welch, Ravel and colleagues warned in 2007 that plague bacteria can pick up resistance to many drugs at once. Yersinia pestis causes plague, and resistance in it is rare but a serious public health and biodefense threat. A multidrug-resistant strain found in 1995 carried a self-spreading plasmid, a small DNA circle named pIP1202.

Sequencing showed that plasmid's backbone is nearly identical to resistance plasmids in Salmonella from food and in a fish pathogen. That match suggests the plasmids share a recent common ancestor and move between species. The same backbone turned up in resistant gut bacteria from retail beef, chicken, turkey, and pork sampled in the United States between 2002 and 2005. Samples came from nine states, so a ready resistance vehicle already circulates near the food supply.
europmc-pmc1904362:
Lesnick, Maraganore and co-authors tested in 2007 whether many weak gene variants in one pathway jointly drive Parkinson disease. Single variants tied to complex diseases usually carry tiny effects. The team bet that the axon guidance pathway, which wires growing nerve fibers, matters as a set.

They mined a genome-wide association dataset for variants inside axon guidance genes, then built combined models. The pathway model predicted who had Parkinson disease with an odds ratio above 90, and it predicted survival free of disease and age at onset with strong accuracy. Thousands of random variant sets, built the same way, predicted all three outcomes poorly. Mining a second dataset backed the approach. The contrast argues that pathway-level genetic load, not single genes, carries much of the risk.
europmc-pmc2124762: A medical paper on biliary cirrhosis in the rabbit. The rabbit's scarred liver. This article preserves that hepatology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
europmc-pmc2124962: A medical paper studying with the electrocardiograph the mode of death of the human heart. The failing beat. This article preserves that cardiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125362: A medical paper on the fate of typhoid bacilli injected intravenously into normal rabbits. The germs' journey. This article preserves that bacteriology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2125962: A medical paper on the morphological changes in rabbit tissues from reduced oxygen. The oxygen-starved flesh. This article preserves that pathology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2126262: A medical paper on renal function in experimental hydronephrosis. The swollen kidney's work. This article preserves that nephrology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
europmc-pmc2128062: A medical paper on reactions of the nasal cavity to chilling of the body surface. The cold nose. This article preserves that physiology. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128362: A medical paper on chemical changes in the dog's blood after intestinal obstruction. The blocked gut's blood. This article preserves that biochemistry. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2131162: A medical paper with a simple method for isolating pure cultures from single bacterial cells. The single-cell method. This article preserves that laboratory technique. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2131262: A medical paper with studies on pathogenic B. coli from bovine sources, normal and serological. The cattle E. coli. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2174962:
Khaw and co-workers quantified in 2008 how four healthy behaviours together affect death rates in British adults. The EPIC-Norfolk study followed 20,244 men and women aged 45 to 79, free of heart disease and cancer at entry. Follow-up averaged eleven years. Each person scored one point per behaviour: not smoking, being physically active, moderate alcohol intake, and blood vitamin C suggesting five daily fruit and vegetable servings.

There were 1,987 deaths during follow-up. Compared with scoring four, the adjusted death risk rose step by step as behaviours dropped. It reached 4.04 for those scoring zero, a four-fold difference, with confidence limits well above no effect for the whole gradient in this prospective population study. The trend held across sex, age, body mass and social class. Having all four behaviours matched being fourteen years younger in death risk.
europmc-pmc2211462:
Grønskov, Ek and Brondum-Nielsen reviewed oculocutaneous albinism in 2007, a group of inherited disorders of pigment production. Affected people make too little melanin in hair, skin and eyes. All forms together affect about one in 17,000 people, and roughly one in seventy carries a gene for it. Four types exist, caused by four genes including TYR and OCA2, all inherited recessively.

The severest type, OCA1A, gives a complete lifelong lack of melanin. Milder types gain some pigment over time. Eye signs include involuntary eye movement, light-sensitive pale irises, underdeveloped central retina and misrouted optic nerves, which reduce sharp and three-dimensional vision. Skin cancer risk may be raised. Diagnosis needs gene testing because types overlap clinically. Glasses, dark lenses, eye surgery and sunscreens help, and lifespan and intelligence are normal.
europmc-pmc2243162:
Bucher and Britten reviewed in 2008 a cancer strategy that disables the cell cycle's G2 checkpoint. Checkpoints are quality-control pauses letting cells repair DNA damage before dividing. Chemotherapy and radiation activate them. Most cancer cells have already lost some checkpoints through mutations. Blocking the remaining ones, especially after DNA damage, can force cancer cells to die instead of repairing themselves.

The review explains the cell cycle framework and the rationale for targeting checkpoint kinase-1, called Chk1. This enzyme transduces signals at both the S and G2 checkpoints. Cells lacking the first G1 checkpoint depend heavily on those later pauses. Preclinical concepts behind Chk1 inhibitors are laid out. Early Phase I and II trial results for efficacy and safety are summarised, giving clinicians a map of this emerging drug class.
europmc-pmc2359962:
Kamba and McDonald explained the side effects of anti-VEGF cancer drugs in 2007. VEGF is short for a growth factor that tells blood vessels to grow and survive. Blocking it starves tumors of blood, which is the point of these drugs.

The authors argued that side effects are not random accidents. Normal small blood vessels also depend on VEGF signals to maintain themselves. Shutting those signals down can disturb vessel control and even make fine vessels shrink back. Existing illness in an organ can make these changes worse. Most effects, they noted, stayed manageable and posed less risk than the tumors being treated. The review framed side effects as a window on how much tumor vessels and normal vessels share.
europmc-pmc2366062:
Becker and Palsson presented a method in 2008 for tailoring cell metabolism models to one situation. Computer models of metabolism usually include every reaction a genome allows. Yet many reactions stay off in a given cell type or condition, which makes the full model a poor guide.

Their method, called GIMME, takes gene activity data plus a stated goal for the cell, such as growth. It then keeps the model that fits the data best while still meeting that goal. GIMME also returns an inconsistency score, showing how badly the data and the goal clash. Tests matched real experiments in three settings: bacteria adapting over generations, engineered microbe strains designed on purpose, and human skeletal muscle cells. The authors offered it as a step toward models specific to the conditions measured.
europmc-pmc2394262:
Clark, Bradburn, Love, and Altman opened a four-part teaching series on survival analysis in 2003. Survival analysis handles time-to-event data, such as time from diagnosis to death or relapse. It needs special methods because follow-up usually ends with some patients still event-free, so their true times stay unknown.

This first part lays out the basic ideas. It shows how to build and read survival curves, which plot the share of patients still event-free over time. It also shows how to measure survival gaps and compare them across two or more patient groups. The authors cover the three tools most cancer papers use: Kaplan-Meier plots, logrank tests, and Cox regression. They also point to methods they say deserve wider use, and set up later parts on multi-factor analysis and advanced topics.
europmc-pmc2412862:
Henry and co-authors tested an antibiotic as a brain inflammation calmer in 2008. The drug is minocycline, long used against bacteria, but it also quiets microglia, the brain's own immune cells. Mice were given a bacterial toxin, LPS, that triggers sickness behaviour: appetite loss, weight loss, and social withdrawal.

In cell culture, minocycline blocked the toxin-driven release of inflammatory cytokines, the immune alarm signals. In adult mice, three days of the drug sped recovery from sickness and prevented anhedonia, the loss of pleasure measured by sweet-water preference. Brain alarm genes, including IL-1 beta and IL-6, fell in key regions such as the hippocampus. In aged mice, whose brains overreact to the toxin, the drug still cut those alarm genes markedly. The authors said it tempers both inflammation and the behaviour changes that follow it.
europmc-pmc2564862:
Toro and colleagues reported in 2008 on 50 new families with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition that predisposes people to skin bumps, lung cysts, collapsed lungs, and kidney tumours. The cause is faults in a gene called BHD, which makes a protein named folliculin. The team sequenced the gene across the families and compared its sequence across species to judge which changes matter.

They found the family mutation in 88 percent of families tested, cataloguing 23 different faults, 13 of them new. One was the first known missense change. It is a single-letter swap in a spot unchanged across evolution. It turned up in a patient with many kidney growths. A family history of kidney cancer or collapsed lung significantly raised a carrier's own risk of the same problem.
europmc-pmc2607262:
Lo Muzio reviewed in 2008 nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, also called Gorlin syndrome, an inherited condition that mixes developmental abnormalities with a strong tendency to tumours. Its prevalence is estimated between 1 in 57,000 and 1 in 256,000 people, affecting the sexes equally. The cause is mutations in the PTCH1 gene, inherited in a dominant pattern.

Hallmarks include many basal cell skin cancers, from a few lesions to several thousand, and recurrent cysts in the jaws, which occur in 90 percent of patients. Skeletal oddities, palm and sole pitting, skull calcifications, and facial differences are frequent, and 5 to 10 percent of patients develop the brain tumour medulloblastoma. Management demands a specialist team. Care includes surgery for cysts and skin lesions. It includes avoiding radiotherapy and excess sun. Families also need genetic counselling.
europmc-pmc2612662:
Willis-Shattuck and colleagues reviewed in 2008 what motivates health workers in developing countries to stay in their jobs. Losing clinical staff cripples fragile health systems and threatens global health goals, yet the evidence on incentives was scattered. The team searched four databases plus grey literature and kept twenty studies that used primary data from developing countries.

Seven themes emerged: pay, career development, and continuing education; the state of hospital facilities; having enough resources to work with; management quality; and simple recognition. Some evidence showed that motivation schemes improved staff retention. Financial incentives, career paths, and management quality formed the core factors, but money alone was not enough. Recognition strongly swayed motivation. Adequate resources and infrastructure lifted morale a lot. Effects differed by staff type. The evidence could not yet say why.
europmc-pmc2634662:
Rowlands and colleagues reported in 2008 on the virus behind an outbreak of African swine fever in Georgia, in the Caucasus. The disease causes a deadly bleeding fever in domestic pigs. It can spread fast, no vaccine exists, and control rests on quick diagnosis and culling.

The team studied DNA pieces taken from virus samples collected during the 2007 outbreak. They compared those pieces with known virus types from other regions. The Georgia virus matched genotype II, a group already known from Mozambique, Madagascar, and Zambia. That match pointed to an African source for the new outbreak. It also showed which lab tests would detect this strain correctly as it spread to nearby countries.
europmc-pmc2654662:
Tseng, Tyler, and Setubal surveyed in 2009 the machines bacteria use to pump proteins out of the cell, and the shared terms coined to describe them. Many bacteria live on or inside larger hosts, as partners, guests, or invaders. Sending proteins across their membranes lets them feed, hide, or attack, and some machines even inject proteins straight into host cells.

Gram-negative bacteria face a double wall, so they have evolved several distinct pump designs. The authors walk through each known system and what it delivers, from nutrients to toxins. A joint project, the Plant-Associated Microbe Gene Ontology Consortium, had built standard terms for these parts and jobs. Using one vocabulary, the paper argues, lets researchers compare systems across very different bacteria and spot what they share.
europmc-pmc2654962:
Cheng and colleagues worked out in 2009 how two plant hormones pass control of flower growth between them in Arabidopsis, a small weed used as a lab model. Male flower parts, the stamens, must grow long filaments to deliver pollen. Two hormones are each essential: without gibberellin or without jasmonate, the filaments stay short and the plant is male-sterile.

The team found the link runs one way. Gibberellin removes brake proteins called DELLAs. Freed from the brakes, the plant switches on DAD1, a key gene for making jasmonate. Jasmonate then turns on three growth genes, MYB21, MYB24, and MYB57, in the stamen. Plants missing all three genes grew short stamens and were sterile, just as hormone-starved plants were. Flower buds short on gibberellin held far less jasmonate than normal buds, confirming the chain.
europmc-pmc2663562:
Gendron and Petrucelli reviewed in 2009 how the protein tau turns harmful in a group of brain diseases called tauopathies, which include Alzheimer disease. Tau normally steadies the cell's inner tracks. In these diseases it piles into tangles inside nerve cells, and faults in its gene alone can cause dementia, proving tau can drive the damage.

The review weighs a puzzle: nerve cells can die even where no tangles form. Attention has shifted to tau changed in smaller ways, such as extra chemical tags or cut pieces, which may be the true poisons. Harm likely comes from both directions at once: toxic new behavior by the altered protein, plus loss of its normal track-steadying work. The authors map what is known about each route and flag the questions that still block treatments.
europmc-pmc2677662:
Engler and colleagues described in 2009 a one-pot method, Golden Gate shuffling, for stitching many DNA pieces together and remixing genes. The trick uses type IIs cutting enzymes, which snip DNA just outside their recognition site. That quirk lets many pieces be cut and glued in a single tube in a set order, leaving no scars.

Nine separate pieces plus a carrier ring went in together, and nine of ten resulting clones carried the exact intended build. The team then shuffled a digestive enzyme gene drawn from cows and humans, each split into nine modules. One round produced a library covering all 19,683 possible module combinations, on paper. Screening a slice of the library surfaced variants that made more active enzyme. The method needs no matching overlap between pieces, so it can mix parents that share nothing.
europmc-pmc2705362:
Francisco and co-authors presented in 2009 goeBURST, a computer method for tracing how bacterial strains are related. It builds on multilocus sequence typing, which codes each strain by gene variants to give a sequence type. The older eBURST tool grouped related types, but its links were not the best possible across the whole set.

The new method recasts the task as a graphic matroid problem, a math form where a greedy search finds the global best answer. Tests on public data for five bacterial species found links that differed from the older tool. A new display also shows how far tie-break rules had to go, so users can judge how firm each link is.
europmc-pmc2709662:
Shankavaram and co-authors launched CellMiner in 2009, a web database that joins molecular data on the NCI-60, a panel of sixty human cancer cell lines. The panel has screened drugs since 1990. Labs can now profile cells at DNA, RNA, protein, and drug-response levels. Those data used different labels, which made them hard to combine and search as one set.

CellMiner stores raw and cleaned data with notes on samples and methods in one linked system that users can query and download for free. A tool finds genes shared across data sets and pulls their values together. The package can also hold profiles from other cell or tissue sets beyond the NCI-60.
europmc-pmc2712762:
Milne and co-authors analyzed in 2009 which immune cells inside ovarian tumors predict survival, focusing on high-grade serous tumors, the most lethal form. Immune cells in tumors had been linked to better outcomes, but their state and role across tumor types stayed unclear. The team stained tissue arrays for many immune markers at once.

In tumors from patients with the most complete surgery, many T-cell and B-cell markers tracked with longer survival. Three markers stood out as new positive signs: CD20, FoxP3, and TIA-1, with FoxP3 being a surprise since it also marks cells that can damp immunity. Other tumor types had fewer immune cells and far fewer survival links.
europmc-pmc2744662:
Gabrysch and Campbell reviewed in 2009 the determinants of delivery service use. They asked why so many women across poorer and middle-income nations give birth without skilled help. Skilled attendance at birth cuts deaths of mothers and newborns, yet most maternal deaths occur where such care is unused. The classic framework focused on home births with complications, and they widen it to preventive facility birth for normal cases.

Across twenty determinants in four themes, higher maternal age, schooling, and household wealth raised facility use, as did lower parity and urban residence. Prior facility birth and antenatal care strongly predicted later facility use. Distance lowered use, and care quality mattered in qualitative work but is hard to measure in surveys, which limits many studies.
europmc-pmc2845662:
Németh and colleagues produced the first genome-wide map in 2010 of which DNA regions cling to the nucleolus. The nucleolus is the dense hub inside the cell nucleus where ribosomes, the protein factories, are built. Using sequencing and gene chips on DNA pulled from purified nucleoli of human cells, they charted these nucleolus-associated domains for the first time.

The domains cover about four percent of the genome and are built mainly from set gene families and repeated satellite DNA. Genes parked there lean toward smell perception, responses to other organisms, and tissue development. Microscope work showed the domains arranged in a set pattern around the nucleolus, shifting when gene activity was forced to change. The map links nucleolus position to how the genome is organized.
europmc-pmc2921362:
Bowen and a multinational panel updated in 2010 the consensus algorithm for hereditary angioedema, a genetic disease of sudden, dangerous swelling attacks. The disease stems from shortage or malfunction of C1 inhibitor, a blood protein that brakes several inflammation cascades. Without the brake, attacks swell the skin, gut, and airway, and throat attacks can suffocate. Earlier algorithms dated from 2003 and 2007.

The 2010 update refolds diagnosis, since blood complement patterns and genetic tests can separate the disease from allergic swelling that mimics it. Treatment advice now spans stopping attacks, preventing them long-term, and pre-procedure cover for surgery and dental work, incorporating newly available targeted drugs beside older androgen and antifibrinolytic options. A single international pathway aims to end the diagnostic odysseys these families report.
europmc-pmc2987762:
Hashimoto and colleagues ran a prospective Japanese study, called SINPHONI, of a treatable brain fluid disorder of older people in 2010. In idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, walking, thinking, and bladder control falter, yet a drainage operation can help.

Across twenty-six centres, a hundred patients aged sixty to eighty-five whose scans showed enlarged fluid spaces plus tightly packed folds near the top of the brain received a programmable shunt. A height and weight scheme set valve pressures. A year later the team scored disability and symptom grades to judge whether scan-based selection predicted who gained from surgery.
europmc-pmc3033362:
Varshney and coauthors rebuilt in 2011 the complete wiring diagram of the tiny roundworm nervous system at the level of single connections. Earlier published maps of this worm were incomplete and did not fully agree with each other. The team combined older records with fresh microscope images to assemble consistent networks for both chemical and electrical links.

They measured network features such as how many partners each nerve cell has and which small connection patterns repeat. Certain cells stood out as likely hubs for processing information. Computer models of activity spread predicted response patterns that match known worm behaviors. Many network features resemble those in mammal brains, hinting at shared design rules. The map offers a base for predicting what gene changes or cell damage should do.
europmc-pmc3040162:
Li and Zhou reported in 2011 how a protein that drives tumor cells to change shape also helps them act like stem cells. Forcing breast and cervical cancer cells to make extra Twist, a shape change driver, made the cells look and behave as if they had shifted state. Those shifted cells also gained traits linked to cancer stem cells, which resist drugs and restart tumors.

Shifted cells formed floating spheres more readily and raised two stem linked markers. Two inner signaling routes were switched on alongside the change. Turning down one route, or blocking the other with drugs, sharply cut a key stem marker. The authors conclude both routes are needed to keep the stem like state going. The finding ties tumor spread and tumor regrowth to the same switches, which drug makers could aim at together.
europmc-pmc3051362:
Khoury and coauthors studied in 2010 how childhood trauma, drug and alcohol dependence, and posttraumatic stress fit together in a low income urban clinic population. Nearly six hundred patients were recruited from medical and pregnancy clinic waiting rooms at a large Atlanta hospital. Interviews covered early abuse, lifetime substance dependence, and current stress symptoms in a group with heavy trauma exposure.

Dependence was common for alcohol, cocaine, marijuana, and, less often, heroin type drugs. Heavier substance use, above all cocaine, tracked closely with more severe childhood physical, sexual, and emotional abuse and with stronger current stress symptoms. The more types of childhood trauma a person had, the stronger the link between cocaine history and current symptoms became, even apart from adult trauma. The authors urge clinics serving poor, high trauma populations to screen for both problems together.
europmc-pmc3059462:
Rasoanaivo, Wright, Willcox, and Gilbert reviewed in 2011 why whole plant extracts often beat their single purified ingredients against malaria. Traditional healers use whole plants or mixtures, and crude extracts repeatedly outperform isolated compounds at the same dose in lab and animal tests. The review sorts the kinds of teamwork between plant chemicals that could explain the gap.

Some ingredient pairs attack the parasite together more strongly than either alone, a pattern shown for the bark alkaloids behind quinine. Other ingredients speed absorption, so a tea delivers its active drug faster than the pure drug alone. Some extracts also calm the immune side effects or block the parasite's drug resistance pumps. Ginger style additions are sometimes there just to ease nausea. The authors call for clinical trials of both purified combinations and traditional mixtures, especially for remote areas.
europmc-pmc3070162:
Wallden, Rivera-Calzada, and Waksman reviewed in 2010 the type IV secretion systems, machines that move proteins and DNA across bacterial cell walls. These large complexes span the whole cell wall and burn cell fuel to push cargo through a channel. Different bacteria put them to very different uses, which the review compares in detail.

Some disease causing bacteria use the machines as syringes, injecting attack proteins directly into human cells. Others use them to pass DNA between bacteria, the main route by which antibiotic resistance genes spread through hospitals and farms. Recent structures show how the channel is built and how its motors may drive cargo through. The authors stress the family's range, from fertility systems to toxin delivery. Blocking these machines could disarm pathogens without killing them, an idea gaining interest as resistance grows.
europmc-pmc3131562:
Shinichi Takaichi reviewed the coloured pigments of algae in a 2011 paper in Marine Drugs. These pigments, called carotenoids, sit beside green chlorophyll in every light-harvesting cell, guarding it and gathering extra light. Algae make an unusually wide range of them, and which pigments a species carries tracks its family line closely.

Certain pigments mark whole algal groups, found in brown algae, red algae, or green algae and their kin, which helps classify species. The review lays out likely building pathways from pigment structures, since the genes involved in algae remain mostly unknown. It also describes how pigments bind into the protein complexes of photosynthesis, including two water-soluble carrier proteins, and what jobs they do there.
europmc-pmc3149062:
Sidhartha Chaudhury and colleagues benchmarked a protein docking program in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The software predicts how two proteins fit together, a core task in drug and protein design. They ran the newest version and its predecessor against a standard set of more than a hundred known protein pairs of graded difficulty.

The new version found correct docking shapes slightly more often overall, with the best success on antibody and enzyme-inhibitor pairs and the weakest on loosely grouped others. Hard targets that force shape changes on binding caused most failures, which the authors traced in detail. A repeat-run analysis showed how reliable the random search results are. The paper sets a baseline for future interface modelling and adds docking with small helper molecules.
europmc-pmc3218662:
Simon Anders and Wolfgang Huber introduced a method for finding genes whose activity differs between samples, in this 2010 paper in Genome Biology. Modern sequencing assays such as RNA-Seq report results as counts of reads. Comparing counts fairly requires a proper error model, since count data vary in complicated ways across their range.

Their approach models the counts with a negative binomial distribution, linking each gene's average level to its variability through local regression fitted across genes. Good estimates of variability give the test its statistical power. The method is implemented as DESeq, a package in the R and Bioconductor ecosystem, ready for researchers to apply to RNA-Seq, ChIP-Seq, and similar counting experiments. The paper became a standard reference for this kind of analysis.
europmc-pmc3222162:
Liesje Donkin and colleagues reviewed how sticking with online therapy affects whether it works, in this 2011 systematic review in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. E-therapies often suffer high dropout, yet researchers measured adherence in ways that did not match. The team listed those measures and asked which ones actually predicted better outcomes across many different programs.

Sixty-nine studies reported some adherence measure, but fewer than half tested its link to outcomes. Log-ins were the commonest measure, followed by modules completed. Log-ins predicted outcomes most consistently in physical-health programs, while module completion mattered more in psychological programs. The authors suggest a combined measure, covering time online, activities finished, and active engagement, and call for a shared standard so studies can be compared.
europmc-pmc3224862:
Matthew Brookes and colleagues compared two ways of measuring functional connectivity in the resting brain, in this 2011 paper in NeuroImage. Connectivity between regions is central to how the brain processes information and may go wrong in disease. The popular MRI method is indirect, reading blood flow rather than neural activity, so the team cross-checked it against magnetoencephalography, which records the brain's magnetic fields.

They show that a beamforming technique can measure connectivity from the magnetic recordings at their source locations. Signal leakage between nearby points can fake connections, though. It must be handled carefully. The two methods agreed well in space, both detecting linked activity between the sensorimotor areas on the two sides, especially in one frequency band. Agreement strengthens confidence in each method.
europmc-pmc3322362:
Muppirala, Honavar, and Dobbs built computer tools that predict whether a given RNA and protein will bind, using only their sequences, in a 2011 paper. RNA protein partnerships run much of cell life, from gene control to defense against viruses. Lab methods for finding them are slow and costly, so a reliable shortcut would help map these networks.

Their system, called RPISeq, turns each partner's sequence into a summary of its short building block patterns and feeds those summaries to learning algorithms. Two versions, built on different algorithms, scored strongly on standard test sets built from a database of known partnerships. They also correctly flagged most known partnerships involving non coding RNAs across species from bacteria to humans. The tool runs free on the web, offering a cheap first pass at building interaction maps.
europmc-pmc3378562:
Cardona and co-authors presented TrakEM2 in 2012, software built to rebuild nerve circuits from huge image stacks. For model animals such as fruit flies and roundworms, taking the pictures is no longer the slow step. Turning deformed, tiled images into a wiring diagram is.

TrakEM2 stitches image volumes together, then lets users trace neuron branches and mark synapses by hand or with semi-automatic help. It also manages the large collections of images and notes that such projects produce. The finished circuit is written out in standard formats, ready for analysis. The tool made large connectome projects practical for ordinary labs.
europmc-pmc3407962:
Mallet and colleagues found in 2012 that a deep brain hub called the external globus pallidus splits into two opposing workforces. The hub belongs to the basal ganglia, circuits that shape movement, and the work used rats with a Parkinson-like condition. One workforce was expected; the second turned out to be a brand-new cell type.

The familiar cells fire out of step with the neighboring subthalamic nucleus and send their wires to many downstream hubs. The new arkypallidal cells fire in step with it, carry a distinct chemical signature, and wire only back to the striatum. They form the striatum's largest outside calming input, reaching both main neurons and interneurons. Movement control, it seems, is run by paired opposites.

free-masons-answer-jachin-boaz-1762:
Jachin and Boaz had barely appeared in 1762 when this Free-Mason's Answer struck back. The anonymous reply addresses the suspected author of the great exposé directly. It is the fraternity's contemporary rebuttal to its most damaging publication, written hot off the press in the same year.

The Answer is indignant, detailed, and determined to set the record straight. It disputes the exposé's accuracy while defending the Craft's right to its secrets. Together, exposé and answer preserve a complete quarrel of 1762.
frus-1861-d162:
Writing on 23 November 1861, William H. Seward worked to keep Paris calm in the Trent crisis. The letter is document 162 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By 23 November the Trent news had crossed the Atlantic and Paris was alive with it. France's stance in the crisis could sway Britain's. Seward's late November letter to Dayton belongs to the effort to keep Paris calm while London raged. Paris in the Trent weeks held back and watched, which served the Union well. Holding back, for Paris, was an act the Union had cause to thank it for.
frus-1861-d262:
In a letter dated 17 October 1861, William H. Seward gave James Shepherd Pike his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 262 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the autumn of the war's first year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d62:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 July 1861. The dispatch is document 62 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By the time Adams wrote, word of the Union defeat was on its way to London. His late July report faces the hard task of the season: keeping British respect after a public loss. His calm hand in that task is why his letters remain a classic of the craft. Adams's own father, John Quincy Adams, had held the same London post a generation before him. A famous name opened doors in London that a new man would have found shut.
frus-1862-d162:
Although it stands late in the printed sequence, Document 162 is dated 3 October 1862 and runs from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The Foreign Relations volume grouped papers by subject, not by strict date order.

Out-of-order printing is common in these volumes, since enclosures and late arrivals were filed where clerks thought they fit. The letter itself belongs to the first days of October, when Washington waited to see if Britain would act on the war. It rewards reading alongside the Adams reports of the same week. London's answer, when it came, would turn on battlefield news ten days old or more.
frus-1862-d262:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward directed a dispatch to William L. Dayton in Paris on 26 March 1862, printed as Document 262 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The same date carries a Dayton report home, so the letters crossed at sea.

Seward's mail to Paris had to serve two ends at once: warn France off the Confederacy and avoid a break over Mexico. That balance runs through the whole 1862 Paris file. This dispatch, written in the week France's solo course in Mexico grew plain, is one link in a chain of careful, firm letters. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d362:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, on 4 April 1862. In a letter printed as Document 362 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Early April 1862 was a charged moment in the Mercier channel. The French minister was preparing a controversial visit to Richmond, the Confederate capital, which he made later that month. Washington tolerated the trip while watching it closely. A Seward letter to Mercier in this window belongs to the delicate handling of an envoy whose errands could blur into recognition of the South. French citizens and ships caught by the war gave the legation a steady stream of case work.
frus-1862-d462:
John Lothrop Motley sent this report from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 October 1862. It appears as Document 462 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, among the autumn Austrian papers.

Motley wrote just after news of Antietam and the emancipation order began reaching Europe. From Vienna he could report how a conservative empire received word that the war now aimed at slavery's end. His October letter gave Seward one more reading of European opinion at a turning point. Set beside the instructions he was receiving, it completes the two-way picture of a working legation. Reports flowed home and orders flowed out. A war was being argued on paper across an ocean.
frus-1862-d562:
On 13 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to Henry Shelton Sanford. It is Document 562 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Three days after his last Brussels order, Seward returned to the same desk. The French mediation idea was then taking shape. Every post needed the Union's answer ready. Sanford, with his lines into the Belgian court and its British connections, was a useful man to keep exactly informed. The instruction belongs to the dense October run of the Belgian file. Together those letters show how a small legation, well run, could serve a great government's purposes far beyond its size.
frus-1862-d62:

The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d662:

Kept with its twin, the letter shows how the State Department broke one post's work into short, clear orders. A man could act on them half a world away.
frus-1863p1-d162:

Back-to-back letters from the secretary chased points that would not wait. For London in late April, the points were the ships still on the stocks and the law that might hold them. This letter keeps the press on in that work. It is a mid-run sheet, and its force comes from the run: day after day of clear, short orders to the war's key post.
frus-1863p1-d262:
Circular No. 39, dated 12 August 1863, is document 262 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. A circular was an instruction the State Department sent to many of its posts abroad at once, rather than to one envoy. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

General orders of this kind kept far-flung ministers speaking with one voice. In a war year, that voice had to explain the Union cause, defend the blockade, and warn against aiding the Confederacy. The circular's place in the British papers shows it formed part of the guidance behind the London mission's work. Such routine orders rarely make headlines, yet they set the frame inside which the famous letters were written.
frus-1863p1-d362:

After the Emancipation Proclamation in January 1863, Seward could frame the war as a fight against slavery. That put Britain, which had banned slavery at home, in an awkward spot when it aided the South. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d462:
Among the day's business on 15 April 1863 was a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d262:
Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 24 November 1943 record an evening session at half past nine. Ambassador Harriman briefed the chiefs on the Soviet attitude ahead of the Tehran meeting. General Marshall had asked him to speak to the proposals of the Joint Strategic Survey Committee.

Harriman expects no detailed Soviet strategy plan, since Moscow is wholly absorbed in its own fighting, and he warns against arriving with a cut-and-dried plan of their own. The Soviets hate being handed finished decisions, he says, but frank explanation has worked well, and Stalin has already told his people a second front is coming soon. Harriman also reports strong Soviet pressure to end the war fast, and a firm intent to join the war on Japan once Germany falls.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d362:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the dinner conversation at Tehran on 28 November 1943, beginning at half past eight in the evening. After talk of where the leaders might meet next, with Fairbanks in Alaska favored, Stalin opens the question of France's future.

Stalin argues at length that France's ruling class is rotten to the core. It delivered the country to Germany. It deserves neither gentle treatment nor her empire back, since no strategic points can safely be left in French hands. Roosevelt partly agrees, naming New Caledonia and Dakar as points needing trusteeship or firm control. Churchill answers that the four victorious nations must hold the world's strategic points. On Germany, Roosevelt wants the very word Reich struck out; Stalin replies that the Reich itself must be made impotent, and presses for stronger measures than either Western leader names.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d462: An editor's note, numbered 462, appears in the Cairo-Tehran volume. The Office of the Historian wrote notes like this for the published record. Decisions taken there guided the campaigns of 1944. The note marks a spot where the editors judged help necessary.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d562:

For readers, Matthews's paper shows a professional diplomat gathering impressions at the center of the war, weeks before D-Day changed every calculation.

frus-1944-quebec-d162:
The United States Chiefs of Staff answered the British Pacific proposals on September 8, 1944, in C.C.S. 452/25. The paper is only a few lines long, but it settles a large question. London's preferred option, a British fleet under American command in the main operations, was not the one Washington accepted here.

Instead the Americans accepted the alternative: a British Empire task force under a British commander, built from British, Australian, and New Zealand land, sea, and air forces. It would operate in the Southwest Pacific under General MacArthur's supreme command. The chiefs noted this would still place the British Fleet well to reinforce the American Pacific Fleet if later desired.
frus-1944-quebec-d262:
A secretaries' note, C.C.S. 417/9 of September 11, 1944, records the Combined Chiefs' informal acceptance of a new statement of the over-all objective against Japan. The restatement replaced the older formula in C.C.S. 417/2. It was accepted subject to the assurances the British had requested and the Americans had given in the preceding papers of the series.

The objective was to force Japan's unconditional surrender in two ways. First, lower her ability and will to resist by sea and air blockade, intensive bombardment, and destruction of her air and naval strength. Second, invade and seize objectives in her industrial heart. Marshall had explained the new wording was designed to allow for invasion of the home islands.
frus-1944-quebec-d62:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff prepared this memorandum on September 10, 1944, two days before the Quebec Conference opened. The British mission in Washington worked alongside the American chiefs year-round. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

A staff paper dated on the conference's eve usually fixes a delegation's final positions. The British chiefs' representatives in Washington coordinated with London and with the traveling British party at Quebec. For readers, the memorandum shows both staffs converging on Canada with their arguments in order, ready for the sessions that would settle the war's last campaigns.
frus-1945-50-intel-d162:
A memorandum from the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) reached the National Intelligence Authority on 13 August 1946. The State Department prints it as document 162 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d262:

The State Department prints it as document 262 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d362:
Dated 8 February 1949, this letter runs from Allen W. Dulles to Robert Blum of the Office of the Secretary of Defense. It is document 362 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

The text is one side of an exchange, set out in full under the writer's own name and title. Letters like this one let a reader follow a debate between two offices in their own words. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d62: A memorandum for the record, dated 27 December 1945, was written to fix an event or a talk in writing before memory faded. Officers wrote such notes to protect the file and themselves. This one falls in the last week of 1945. The long argument over a central intelligence system was nearly settled, and the January directive was being readied. Its bare title names no author and no reader, so it stands as a small act of record-keeping inside a famous negotiation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d162:
Churchill answered Roosevelt on Poland on 6 January 1945, in his message number 876. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He thanks the President for Stalin's reply and remarks drily on the new actor in the story, the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet.

Britain, Churchill reports, has made its stand plain, in parliament among other places: it continues to recognize the London Poles as the government of Poland. His own fresh note to Stalin calls the course of events distressing. Much the best thing, he told Stalin, is for the three leaders to meet and talk these matters through. The whole world picture, war and the passage to peace alike, should frame the talk. Meanwhile the British attitude stays unchanged.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d262:
General Leslie Groves reported the state of the atomic bomb to General Marshall on 30 December 1944. His top secret letter from the War Department, headed “Atomic Fission Bombs,” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Groves ran the Manhattan District project that built the weapon.

Planning, he writes, should rest on the gun-type bomb, expected to equal ten thousand tons of TNT. The first bomb should be ready about 1 August 1945, with no full-scale test thought necessary beforehand. A second should follow by the end of the year. Hopes for the implosion type by late spring have faded on scientific difficulties not yet solved. Material for a first implosion bomb should exist by late July, with a much smaller yield at first.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d362:
Caring for freed prisoners brought Eden to write to Molotov at Yalta on February 5, 1945. He recalled their Moscow talks of the past October on repatriation. Soviet citizens freed in the south and west, and British subjects freed in the east, all needed food, shelter, and a way home. Drafts had passed between the governments since then.

A Soviet redraft had reached the British Embassy on January 20. London had studied it, Eden wrote, and found it generally acceptable, with points stated below. A like draft had gone to Washington. Because the Allied commands were joined, Eden argued, the answer should be joined too.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d462: Oil slipped into the last Yalta lunch, and Bohlen's short note of February 11, 1945, preserves the moment. The three leaders, their foreign secretaries, ambassadors, and interpreters ate together, and talk stayed general and personal. Then Stalin made an obvious reference to Iran. Any nation, he said, which kept its oil in the ground and would not let it be used was in fact working against peace. The remark aimed at Persia's stalled concessions, and perhaps further. It reads like a preview of the oil politics ahead.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d62:
No reporters would cover the Big Three meeting if Churchill got his way. In a personal and top secret telegram of 21 January 1945, he put the idea to President Roosevelt. The message, numbered 891, is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences.

Churchill proposes barring the press from the conference, code-named Argonaut, entirely. Each leader could still bring three or four uniformed service photographers. Their still and motion pictures would be released only when the leaders chose. He also expects the usual agreed communiqué at the end. A matching telegram went to Stalin, and Roosevelt's agreement followed the next day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d162:
Secretary Stettinius suggested a council of foreign ministers in a telegram from San Francisco dated June 19, 1945. The extract is document 162 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It answers the President's June 9 request for ideas on how the European peace settlements should be worked out.

A full-dress peace conference should be avoided, Stettinius argues. The problems should instead be handled case by case by a council of foreign ministers. The idea could be sounded out with the British first, and the Russians told that Washington meant to raise it at the Big Three meeting. There the leaders would try to fix the new council's first meeting, its time and place, and some of its agenda. The proposal became the Council of Foreign Ministers created at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d262:
Naval aide George Elsey reported another blank in the files in an undated note printed as document 262 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Like its companion on the rivers, it was submitted to Admiral Leahy on July 1, 1945, and forwarded to the President.

There has been no reference, Elsey writes, to the free use of the Suez and Panama canals in either president's Map Room papers. The Kiel Canal is a different story. Churchill reported to Roosevelt after his Moscow talks of October 1944 that Stalin wanted the Kiel Canal internationalized, and that Churchill agreed with him. No details were given, the subject was not discussed at Yalta, and it has not been mentioned since. The note left Truman free to shape his own line on the canals.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d362: Pauley assured President Truman from Moscow on June 29, 1945, that a plan was coming. He was bending every effort, he wrote, to have a proposed reparations plan ready. It would go to Truman and to the heads of the British and Soviet governments at their forthcoming meeting. Only an extract of his top secret cable is printed here. Its substance stays in the fuller version printed elsewhere in the volume. The note went to the Secretary of State ad interim over Ambassador Harriman's signature.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d462:
Reuters comes under fire in an extract from Shantz's Belgrade telegram of July 11, 1945. The Yugoslav paper Borba sharply criticized the news agency for protectionism toward the Greeks in the Yugoslav-Greek dispute over the treatment of Macedonians in northern Greece. Its editorialist denied a Reuters charge that Yugoslavia wished to make territorial claims on Greece.

He pointed instead to the alleged expansionist ambitions of Greek chauvinist officials. He admitted that Yugoslavs, and all true democrats, stand against the Athens government. Yugoslavia, he said, hopes the question of Greek misrule in Macedonia will come before an international forum, if not the Big Three conference itself. The extract preserves Belgrade's case in its own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d562:
Marshal Stalin sent President Truman a personal and secret letter on June 21, 1945. It is document 562 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The letter, sent from Moscow in translation, protests Allied handling of the Trieste and Istria dispute.

Stalin says Yugoslavia had met the Allies halfway by taking their proposal. Yet talks in Trieste had hit a dead end, since Allied officers would not weigh even small Yugoslav points. He attacks Field Marshal Alexander's tone and his public words likening Tito to Hitler and Mussolini. He also calls the June 2 Anglo-U.S. note an ultimatum in tone. He closes by hoping that just Yugoslav claims will be met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d62:
Churchill gave the Potsdam Conference its code name in telegram number 89 to President Truman, sent from London on June 15, 1945. The one-line message is document 62 in the Foreign Relations papers on the conference. A code word let officials talk about the secret Berlin meeting without naming it in cables and files.

Churchill suggests the word Terminal for the coming conference and asks if Truman agrees. A note in the volume adds that he made the same proposal to Stalin the same day, and Stalin also said yes. The name fit the moment: Berlin was meant to be the last stop of the wartime alliance's grand strategy, the terminal point of the road through Tehran and Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d662:
Paris ambassador Caffery reported Moscow's Tangier note to the French on July 2, 1945. His secret wire is document 662 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The Russian note answered the notification delivered in Moscow on June 30.

The note expressed astonishment that the talks were called with so little notice to Moscow. It stated Russian interest in Tangier and asked that the opening be put off. Consultations should first arrange four-power discussions. A French official, Meyrier, told British colleagues the Russian move was inevitable. London and Washington wanted a temporary regime in place of Spain's, while France wanted the 1939 state of things restored. If the French plan were adopted, he said, the Russian request could be refused, since no change would be in train.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1062:
Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled Ambassador Caffery in Paris on July 20, 1945. He has written to Molotov that day, proposing Soviet participation in supervising the Greek elections. The letter follows the text Washington proposed on July 17.

Byrnes asks Caffery to make a like proposal to the French government at once. He adds one caution, suggested by the British delegation and accepted by him. No publicity should be given the proposal. Silence must hold until the French and Soviet replies arrive, and the Greek government can be properly informed. The exchange belongs to the Potsdam Conference record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1162:
A working group with a long name, the Subcommittee on Cooperation in Solving Immediate European Economic Problems, reported on 25 July 1945. Its charge was the crisis on the ground. While leaders debated grand plans, this group faced hunger, cold, and idle factories across a ruined continent.

The report urged the three powers to work jointly on relief and recovery. Food, coal, and transport could not wait for perfect politics. Findings of this kind fed the summit's choices on aid and trade. The paper is Potsdam at its most practical: policy aimed at empty stomachs and dark homes, written by staff who saw the need up close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1262:
General Somervell, who commanded the Army Service Forces, wrote to Leathers, Britain's Minister of War Transport, on 20 July 1945. Somervell's command fed, clothed, and moved the American army around the world. Leathers ran the British side of wartime transport.

A letter between the two supply chiefs joined the logistics of both nations at the top. Ports, ships, rail, and stores all had to serve one plan as the war shifted east. This message shows that joint supply world at work during the summit. The peace talks sat on a mountain of moved goods, and men like these moved it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1362:
The British Embassy in Washington delivered a note to the Department of State on 28 July 1945. Embassy notes are formal papers, worded with care and meant for the record. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A note from an embassy speaks for its government in full, unlike a chat or a cable between friends. Britain and the United States were close allies in 1945, but allies still put hard points in writing. This note reached the department while its leaders were at Potsdam, so it landed on the desks of the men holding the fort. It shows allied business being done in the capital even with the summit under way abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-162:
Benjamin Cohen took these notes on August 1, 1945, the final day of the Potsdam Conference. His notes stand in the second Potsdam volume beside the formal minutes. Cohen watched the legal shape of the closing acts. The day's work fixed texts that governments would cite for years.

Final-day notes by a lawyer have lasting use. Later arguments about Potsdam turned on commas and clauses. Cohen's record helps readers judge what was meant at the time. The notes also close his personal run of witness. Few staff papers in the volume combine nearness and care as his do.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-62:
A United States delegation memo sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 22, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Four heads of business are reported from the Sunday morning session.

On the Yalta declaration, the ministers agreed to report no agreement on election observation. That was paragraph 1 of the U.S. paper on liberated areas. The press and control commission paragraphs went to a subcommittee instead. It would study recent improvements in the commissions in Bulgaria, Rumania, and Hungary. It would also study Soviet complaints about the Allied body in Italy. On German economics, several paragraphs of the draft principles were approved, with more discussion to come. On Rumanian oil equipment, extended discussion produced no agreement at all on how British and U.S. gear there should be treated.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d762:
The Acting Secretary wrote to John Erhardt, political adviser for Austrian affairs, on July 21, 1945. Document 762 carries Washington's guidance to the man handling Austria. Austria, freed from German rule, awaited its own settlement. Erhardt worked where Allied occupation was taking shape. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

Guidance letters like this one turned summit talk into field action. Erhardt needed to know how far he could go. Readers see the chain from a Washington desk to an adviser among the occupying powers. The document shows Austria's quieter file moving beside the conference's louder ones. Small posts felt Potsdam's reach too.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d862:
Dated July 20, 1945, at Babelsberg, this United States delegation working paper offers draft wording for the Potsdam talks on Germany. It was prepared for the Economic Sub-Committee that morning. The paper gives one numbered clause, paragraph 17, on how the occupation should handle reparations and imports.

The clause says a main aim of occupation is reparation for harm done by German aggression. It calls on the Control Council to set a program of minimum imports for Germany as a whole. Supplies inside Germany should be shared fairly among the zones. Paying back money advanced for approved imports would come first from the proceeds of German exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d962: American delegates added this short clause to their reparations proposal on July 30, 1945. It answers a practical question: who decides how much factory equipment is surplus to a peace economy, and thus open to reparations? The answer given is the Reparation Commission, with France added to its membership. The commission would consult the Control Council as it worked. Even then, the zone commander of the zone losing the equipment keeps the final say. A file note credits the draft of this addition to Secretary Byrnes himself.
frus-1947v05-d62: Another 1947 FRUS document from the Near East and Africa volume. The Acting Secretary addressed regional affairs. This entry preserves that record. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
frus-1969-76v38p1-d62: A 1969-1976 FRUS document from the foundations of foreign policy volume, 1973-1976. The later Nixon and Ford years. This entry preserves that record. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gadbury-collectio-geniturarum-1662:
John Gadbury was a Restoration astrologer who feuded in print with rivals for decades. His Collectio Geniturarum, published in 1662, gathers a collection of one hundred and fifty nativities, birth charts of real people. The book is the great Restoration case-book of judicial astrology.

Each chart comes with the events of the life it maps: offices, marriages, illnesses, and deaths read against the planets. Gadbury meant the cases to prove the art by its hits, as a lawyer proves a rule by precedents. Students of the period still mine his collection for the lives it records in passing.
gao-gaoreports-b-295462: Lucent Technologies World Services brought its March 2005 dispute to GAO, and the ruling delivers the call. The telecom heavyweight's protest got the standard full review. Size buys no shortcuts at the referee's desk. The desk stayed neutral. The call was neutral.
gao-gaoreports-b-295562: Singleton Enterprises carried its February 2005 dispute to GAO, and the ruling renders the judgment. The firm's claims faced the referee squarely. The protest got its full hearing and more. The hearing was complete. The judgment was rendered. The dispute was settled.
gao-gaoreports-b-297262: Metro Home Medical Supply took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Medical suppliers get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298662: Advanced Federal Services took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298962: Palmetto GBA doubled its January 2007 protest — two case numbers, one health-services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299862: Charleston Marine Containers fought a 2007 award at GAO — and this ruling is the decision. The box-maker said the agency's pick was wrong; the call tests the claim and rules. In the unglamorous world of shipping-container contracts, fair-bidding law applies just the same.
gao-gaoreports-b-302962: NARA's records center fund got a fiscal ruling in this 2005 GAO call, which tests property damage recovery. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the recovery was legal. The law had the final word. The recovery had to be legal.
gao-gaoreports-b-308762: Homeland Security's internal money shuffling got a legal once-over from GAO in 2007 — were the shared-service deals inside its Preparedness wing kosher? The ruling reads the purse statutes against the department's bookkeeping. Even a young giant, GAO reminds, must color inside the budget lines.
gao-gaoreports-b-310762: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by PM Services Company. The February 4, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-262: The SEC's cyber locks were weak in 2005, and GAO's report says the commission had to address poor controls over financial and sensitive data. The review sounds the alarm. The market's secrets deserved the guard. The controls had to be addressed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-462: Perchlorate tracking needed a system in 2005, and GAO's report says a way to track sampling and cleanup results was required. The findings demand the tool. The report warns that the tainted water deserved monitoring. The system had to be built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-762: The federal student loan repayment program needed better administration in 2005, and GAO's report says OPM could build on efforts to help agencies. The findings demand the support. The report warns that the indebted workers deserved help. The efforts had to be built upon.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-162: China trade was rising but the U.S. share was falling in 2006, and GAO's report says exports and investment grew while the share declined. The findings do the math. The report warns that the dragon's market needed honest measuring. The trends had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-362: Hurt troops' disability calls needed better eyes in 2006, and GAO's report says the system wanted firmer watching for fair, fast results. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the wounded deserved fair and quick calls. The watching had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-62: Medicare's equipment payment formula got a GAO verdict in 2006, and the report says Class III devices did not warrant a distinct annual update. The findings do the math. The report warns that the device dollars deserved fair formulas. The update was not warranted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-762: America's Middle East broadcasts needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says the broadcasting services could be improved. The findings tune the dials. The report warns that the airwaves' message needed sharper delivery. The management had to improve. The signal had to be strong.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-962: Force planning needed better data in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon had to integrate data into its force identification process. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the troop requirements should not be guesswork. The data had to drive the decisions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1062: Inflation had quietly shrunk the sting of tax penalties by 2007 — GAO's report does the deflating math. Fines fixed in old dollars punished less with each passing year. The findings make a dry but pointed case: penalties that do not keep up with prices stop deterring.
