gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1162: Sticky notes on the fridge were not cutting it — GAO's 2007 report says Washington could teach homes far more about saving energy. From bulb labels to public drives, the report grades the government's consumer coaching. Smarter tips, GAO argues, would trim family bills and national demand in one stroke.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-462: The Senate's restaurants got an audit in 2007, and GAO's report grades the revolving fund's finances for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion for the record in full detail. The report proves the watchdog's reach extends from missiles to meatloaf.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-62: The government's big surveys needed a rethink in 2007, and GAO's report says the portfolio of major household surveys deserved reexamination. The findings demand the review. The report warns that the nation's questionnaires should not waste the nation's time. The surveys had to earn their keep.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-762: Hanford's glass-log gamble needed a second look in 2007 — GAO's report says the Energy Department should rethink the bulk vitrification demo for the tank waste. The findings question the tech bet. The report's caution: billion-dollar demos deserve proof before they get permits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1062: GAO published its findings on pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation: Need for Improved Oversight Persists in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-162: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at embassy Security: Upgrades Have Enhanced Security, but Site Conditions Prevent Full Adherence to Standards. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-262: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at natural Resource Management: Opportunities Exist to Enhance Federal Participation in Collaborative Efforts to Reduce Conflicts and Improve Natural Resource Cond. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-862: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at international Marriage Broker Regulation Act of 2005: Agencies Have Implemented Some, but Not All of the Act's Requirements. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Between 1954 and 1962 the United States built a nuclear presence across Western Europe, stationing American weapons with allied forces under shared-control arrangements. This briefing-book page is the first part of an Archive set on that deployment. The evidence here is the title alone, and the documents in this part are not described. Those years set the pattern that still governs American weapons in Europe: bombs stored on allied soil, owned by Washington, and surrounded by political arrangements every host government must defend.
heydon-holy-guide-1662:
John Heydon published The Holy Guide in London in 1662, subtitled as leading the way to the wonder of the world. The massive volume is a Rosicrucian compendium. Astrology, geomancy, and Rosie-Crucian physic fill its books, making it the most encyclopedic English Rosicrucian work of the seventeenth century.

Heydon compiles, adapts, and expands earlier writers with a free hand. Star lore and earth divination stand beside recipes for the Rosicrucian medicine. His ambition is total: one book for the whole art. Critics of his day charged him with borrowing without shame. Modern readers value the Guide as a warehouse of the period's occult knowledge, gathered by its most industrious English salesman.
homestead-act-1862:
Congress passed the Homestead Act in 1862, and Lincoln signed it into law. Any settler who farmed public land for five years could own it. One hundred sixty acres came free to those who proved the claim.

Millions of claims followed as families poured onto the plains. The family farm became national policy in the act's plain terms. Towns, schools, and whole states rose from its quarter-section grants. Native peoples paid the price as their lands passed to settlers. The law that settled a continent still shapes the West's map and memory. Its grid of farms can still be seen from any plane window.
huxley-on-fossil-remains-of-man-1862:
Thomas Henry Huxley, Darwin's most forceful defender, lectured on fossil human remains in 1862. He spoke at the Royal Institution with very little material to work from. The Engis and Neanderthal skulls formed nearly the whole evidence.

Huxley compares those skulls with modern human and ape skulls, bone by bone. He finds no barrier that separates fossil humans from living ones. The lecture builds a Darwinian reading of human antiquity from scant bones. Its confidence helped set the tone for his famous book on man's place in nature the next year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowy-jacob-ezek:
Jacob Ezekiel Löwy (1814–1864) was a German rabbi and author born at Hotzenplotz in Austrian Silesia, profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch. After study at several yeshivahs and a turn toward Hasidism at Lemberg and Brody, he gained secular learning at Berlin. He worked in business before taking rabbinic posts.

In 1846 Löwy became district rabbi of Wadowice, seated at Oswiecin, and in 1854 he was elected rabbi of Beuthen, where he stayed until his death. The article names his one book, a critical Talmudic lexicon printed at Vienna in 1863. It held 150 articles meant as the start of a full Talmudic encyclopedia, but only the first volume appeared. The entry preserves both a rabbi’s winding path to office and an ambitious reference project left unfinished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-samuel-10:
Samuel Meyer, born in Hanover on February 26, 1819, was a German rabbi whose career is summarized in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling. He studied Talmud in Hanover and Frankfurt and attended the University of Bonn. In 1845 he succeeded Nathan Adler as district rabbi of Hanover and Lüneburg.

Two years later Meyer carried out Adler's plan to found a teachers' seminary in Hanover, a lasting mark on Jewish education there. His own writings were modest: a few sermons, an 1862 history of the synagogue community's charitable society, and an edition of poems by Abraham ibn Ezra that he had discovered in manuscript. He died in Hanover in 1882.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o: This volume of Saint-Simon covers the long years of war. The cold-eyed duke watches ministers and generals with deep suspicion. Idle court gossip mixes with great affairs of state. History observed from the antechamber.
mommsen-history-rome-vol-1-1862:
Theodor Mommsen's History of Rome appears here in William P. Dickson's translation of 1862. Volume 1 covers Rome from its legendary founding to the eve of the Punic Wars. Mommsen rebuilds the early Republic: its laws, tribes, wars, and constitution. His learning drew on inscriptions and coins as well as texts.

Mommsen writes with the confidence of a liberal who knew modern politics too. His Rome feels alive, partisan, and legally precise. The work later won him the Nobel Prize in Literature. No reconstruction of the Republic has replaced his in scope. Volume 1 is the gateway to a monumental history. Dickson's version served English readers for generations.
nasa-tm-19650009357-sweden-operations-19: Sweden got 1962-operated, and this 1965 NASA memo covers operations reports. The pages detail the Sweden findings. The engineers get their memo. The operations were 1962. The memo was engineer. The 1962 were report. The operations were Sweden. The 1965 were memo. The report were operations.
openalex-w2033075062: Severe leptospirosis kills — knowing the risk factors saves lives. This work titled 'Risk Factors and Predictors of Severe Leptospirosis in…' hunted the warning signs of severe leptospirosis. The catalog record is truncated and thin, so the setting is hidden; the study likely flagged who deteriorates fastest.
openalex-w2120599762: Alpine plants help each other survive — climate change tests that. Anthelme and colleagues' 2014 paper covers facilitation among plants in alpine environments facing climate change. The catalog record is thin, but the paper documents plant-plant help under warming.
openalex-w2169861662: Leptospirosis is a bacterial disease spread through water contaminated by animal urine — and in the Peruvian Amazon, the severe form struck only in cities. This 2006 PLoS Medicine study tested environmental surface waters for pathogenic Leptospira using molecular methods, asking why urban and rural areas with similar infection rates saw such different outcomes. The water testing points to which strains lurk where people get sick.
openalex-w2346770762: Rhabdomyolysis — the rapid breakdown of skeletal muscle flooding the bloodstream with its contents — can shut down kidneys, yet the literature on it is a mess of conflicting definitions and treatments. This 2016 Critical Care systematic review cuts through the heterogeneity to give clinicians practical guidance on recognizing and managing the syndrome.
openalex-w2463100762: Before hunting for new physics, physicists must understand the ordinary: how many charged particles fly out of a proton-proton collision, and how fast. This 2010 Physical Review Letters paper measures transverse-momentum and pseudorapidity distributions at 7 TeV with CMS's inner tracker. The baseline counts anchor every search that followed at the LHC's early energies.
openalex-w2555900862: Kids need a mix of activity, limited sitting, and enough sleep — Canada's 24-hour movement guidelines say so, but do children worldwide meet them? This 2016 study across 12 countries measures adherence to the guidelines' three recommendations and links them to body fat. The results show how far the world's children are from the daily mix their health needs.
openalex-w2895074862: Modern sugarcane is a polyploid hybrid — sweet from Saccharum officinarum, tough from Saccharum spontaneum. This 2018 Nature Genetics paper assembles the allele-defined genome of the wild parent, sequencing the haploid AP85-441 into 32 chromosome assemblies. The genome unlocks breeding for a crop that sweetens the world.
openalex-w4386220262: Classifying antiphospholipid syndrome needed international consensus. This 2023 Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases paper — by Barbhaiya, Zuily, Naden and colleagues — presents the 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria. The standard sharpens diagnosis of a clotting disorder.
openalex-w4386833262: Digital tools are reshaping healthcare — but professionals do not always adopt them. This 2023 npj Digital Medicine paper consolidates systematic-review evidence on barriers and facilitators to digital health technologies among healthcare professionals. The synthesis shows what helps and what hinders.
openalex-w4390175962: Generative AI raised fears of unfair academic use — and a rush to detect it. This 2023 International Journal for Educational Integrity paper tests detection tools for AI-generated text. The evaluation asks whether the detectors actually work.
openalex-w7152395362: Safety checklists only work if nurses actually follow them. This study translated the Compliance with Standard Precautions Scale into Japanese and validated it among Japanese nurses. The authors ran a two-phase adaptation. A nursing-research study of measuring safety culture across languages.
openalex-w7204261862: When a woman is murdered, her children become orphans of femicide, and the state owes them care. This paper studies whether Brazil's support networks actually reach these indirect victims. The authors measure the gap between legal promises of full protection and what families receive. A somber legal study of children left behind by gender violence.
openalex-w7204263062: The Red Pill ideology, an online worldview hostile to women, is spreading in Brazil. This study maps the country's academic research on the movement and its ties to gender violence. The authors survey the literature to chart what scholars know so far. A timely mapping of a digital subculture with real-world harms.
openalex-w7204271762: Heavy bleeding after birth remains a top killer of mothers worldwide. This narrative review covers how to recognize postpartum hemorrhage fast, manage it with a team, and improve outcomes. The authors synthesize current best practice for obstetric emergencies. A clinical review where the message is clear: readiness saves mothers.
openalex-w7213537262: Big blasts send pressure waves circling the globe. This paper modeled eruption-born wave types in a layered air model, testing how winds bend them. The team figured loudness and travel times. An air-physics study of the planet ringing like a bell.
openalex-w7213596462: ICU scores and patient suffering do not always agree. This study compared clinical risk scores like qSOFA and NEWS2 against how septic shock patients themselves rated their symptoms. The authors probed the gap. A critical-care study of numbers versus lived experience.
plos-pbio-0020162:
Tadashi Imanishi, Takeshi Itoh, Yutaka Suzuki, and a huge team reported a human gene catalog effort in PLOS Biology in 2004. They checked 21,037 human genes using full-length cDNA clones, which are complete copies of gene messages. Each clone proves a gene is real and shows its full shape.

Before this work, many listed human genes were mere predictions from the genome sequence. Clones in hand let the team confirm exons, starts, and ends for each gene. That cleanup matters for every later study that uses the gene list. Databases, disease hunts, and drug work all lean on knowing exactly where genes begin and end and what they encode.
plos-pbio-0020362:
Shoshana Shendelman, Alan Jonason, Cecile Martinat, and their team studied the DJ-1 protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. Faulty DJ-1 causes a rare early form of Parkinson's disease. The team found DJ-1 works as a chaperone, a helper that keeps other proteins from clumping, and that its action depends on redox state.

In particular, DJ-1 slows the clumping of α-synuclein, the protein whose clumps mark Parkinson's in the brain. A protector that fights the disease's hallmark clumps is a strong lead. The work also shows the helper switches on under oxidative stress, exactly when cells need it most. That timing makes DJ-1 a smart guard, not a constant one.
plos-pone-0000062:
Michael Schillaci asked in 2006 whether the contest for mates helped grow the primate brain. Brain size varies widely among primates, from tiny monkeys to apes and humans. Natural selection for survival skills is the usual explanation. Sexual selection, the pressure of competing for mates, is the rival Schillaci tested.

Comparing brain size across primate species against the strength of mating competition in each, he weighed whether the two rise together. A link would mean the social and sexual arena, not just food and tools, drove brain evolution. That possibility matters for the biggest version of the question: how humans ended up with brains so costly and so large.
plos-pone-0000162:
Christopher S. Raymond and Philippe Soriano published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents a high-efficiency way to use two site-specific recombination systems, FLP and PhiC31, in mammalian cells. These enzyme systems cut and paste DNA at exact target spots, letting researchers insert or remove chosen genes.

Genetic engineers rely on such tools to build cell lines and mouse models with precision. The authors show the two systems working efficiently side by side in mammalian cells. A reliable toolkit of this kind speeds up experiments in which genes are switched on, switched off, or swapped to test their roles.
plos-pone-0000262:
Guoyan Zhao, Kuan Y. Chang, Katherine Varley, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inverted repeats are DNA sequences that read the same way on opposite strands, forming structures genomes must maintain or remove. Using a comparative approach across genomes, the authors present evidence that these structures are actively maintained.

Active maintenance means selection keeps the repeats in place, rather than their surviving by chance. That would imply the structures do useful work, in gene control or chromosome stability. The paper challenges the view of inverted repeats as mere genomic clutter.
plos-pone-0000362:
Sharon E. Cox and colleagues published a genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2007 on haptoglobin, a blood protein long debated as a possible shield against malaria. Earlier studies had disagreed about whether haptoglobin protects people, and the team asked whether the answer lies in how two gene variants act together.

The study looks at the combined pattern, called a haplotype, formed by the Hp2 variant and a promoter variant known as A-61C. Looking at the pair together, rather than each variant alone, may explain why past work reached such different results. The paper speaks to the wider search for gene variants that change a person's risk from malaria.
plos-pone-0000462:
Wing-Sze Lo and colleagues looked for the fingerprints of natural selection in a gene tied to schizophrenia, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene makes the β2 subunit of the GABA A receptor, a receiver for the brain's main calming signal. The team reported evidence of positive selection acting within this schizophrenia-associated gene.

Positive selection means a variant spread because it helped survival or reproduction, which is puzzling for a gene linked to mental illness. Such evidence feeds the debate over why risk variants for schizophrenia persist in populations. Genetic studies of this kind cannot settle the question alone, but they show the gene's history is not one of simple decay.
plos-pone-0000562:
Arun Krishnan, Alessandro Giuliani, and Masaru Tomita examined a fundamental limit on reading gene networks backward, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Reverse engineering tries to infer a gene regulatory network from measurements of gene activity. The authors analyze the indeterminacy of that task, which they call the curse of gene elasticity.

Indeterminacy means many different networks can explain the same data, so the one a computer returns may not be the real one. Naming the curse warns the field against over-trusting reconstructed networks. Honest limits are useful: they push researchers toward experiments that break the tie between rival explanations.
plos-pone-0000662:
Markus M. Heimesaat, André Fischer, Britta Siegmund and co-authors tracked gut bacteria during acute colitis in mice for PLOS ONE in 2007. Gut bacteria can trigger colitis in animal models and are suspected of worsening inflammatory bowel diseases in people. The team had earlier reported Escherichia coli building up in ileitis, inflammation of the small intestine, and making it worse.

Their title states the next step: a shift toward pro-inflammatory intestinal bacteria aggravates acute colitis. The route runs through Toll-like receptors 2 and 4, sensors that detect bacterial parts. Blocking or calming that sensing could be a treatment angle for bowel inflammation, which is why the pathway matters.
plos-pone-0000762:
Jorge Ponseti, Hartwig R. Siebner, Stefan Klöppel and colleagues asked whether sexual orientation is associated with structural differences in the brain. For their 2007 PLOS ONE study, 80 homosexual and heterosexual men and women underwent structural MRI scanning. The group included 16 homosexual men and 15 homosexual women, with the rest heterosexual. Voxel-based morphometry, a method comparing grey matter volume across the brain, tested for differences.

Their title states one finding: homosexual women had less grey matter in the perirhinal cortex than heterosexual women. The perirhinal cortex sits near memory and recognition areas. A localized difference raises as many questions as it answers, which the authors' careful design reflects.
plos-pone-0000862:
Wenhui Wang, Xinyu Liu, Danielle Gelinas and their co-authors described a fully automated robotic system for injecting zebrafish embryos, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Injecting material such as DNA, RNA or protein into single cells is a basic tool in genetics and drug work. Doing it by hand is slow and hard to repeat.

The authors present a machine built to handle the microinjection step on its own. Zebrafish embryos are a common test subject because they are clear, fast growing and easy to raise in large numbers. A working automated system points toward faster, more even experiments in genetics, breeding work and early drug screening.
plos-pone-0000962:
Clement Kent, Reza Azanchi, Ben Smith and colleagues modeled the wax compounds on male fruit flies hour by hour, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cuticular hydrocarbons coat a fly's body and shape courtship, mating, grouping and egg laying. They also protect against drying out.

The team measured twenty-four of these compounds in single males across different light and dark conditions. A model based analysis turns those measures into patterns over time. Chemical signals that change by the hour could carry more news than a fixed scent. The work connects body chemistry to behavior with unusual time detail.
plos-pone-0001062:
Lam Tran-Hung, Ny Tran-Thi, Gerard Aboudharam and colleagues presented a new way to extract DNA from dental pulp, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dental pulp, the soft core of a tooth, is used to detect DNA from the host and from blood borne germs. Standard recovery needs dental expertise, and exposed samples pick up laboratory contamination.

Their method aims for simpler, cleaner extraction, paired with universal detection of bacteria. Teeth survive when other tissues do not, so pulp DNA is precious in forensics and in tracing past infections. A method that more labs can run widens who can use that record. The paper is a practical bench advance.
plos-pone-0001162:
Vaccines work when helper T cells work with B cells to produce lasting, neutralizing antibodies. Karl Lang and colleagues tried an unusual strategy in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. On purpose, they made one set of helper T cells tolerant, a tactic they call negative vaccination. With viruses that persist, long replication often goes with weak antibody responses.

The team reports that making certain CD4 T cells tolerant boosted virus-specific protective antibody responses. The idea runs against instinct, since helper cells are usually seen as allies of vaccination. Their result suggests that some helper responses get in the way, and removing them frees the antibody system to do better.
plos-pone-0001262:
Genome-wide association studies scan the genome for variants tied to disease, using chips that read hundreds of thousands of markers at once. Changzheng Dong and colleagues compared the two main ways those chips choose their markers, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The two approaches are direct, gene-focused selection and indirect selection spread across the genome.

The authors describe gene-centric characteristics of genome-wide association studies, weighing what each chip design can and cannot detect. Design choices decide which diseases and variants a study can find. Their analysis is a guide for researchers planning association studies in the chip era.
plos-pone-0001362:
Noncompaction of the ventricular myocardium is a rare heart disease. The heart muscle fails to compress properly during development, leaving a spongy inner layer. Birgit Budde and colleagues report a family case with a genetic cause, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The disease is of heterogeneous origin and has been traced to single point mutations in various genes.

The authors show that noncompaction in this case is associated with a de novo mutation in the beta-myosin heavy chain gene. De novo means new in the patient, not inherited. Identifying the gene helps diagnosis and family screening for a poorly understood cardiomyopathy.
plos-pone-0001462:
Stefan Amisten and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a platelet gene and heart attacks. Platelets help blood clot, and a receptor on them had been tied to artery disease. A variant near that receptor had raised doubts, since it sits close to a second receptor gene. The team asked which gene truly drives the risk.

They tested a variant in the second gene, which is in strong linkage with the first locus. They report it was not tied to heart attack in their groups. Null results like this prune false leads. They keep drug work aimed at the receptor that truly shapes clot risk.
plos-pone-0001562:
Xue-wen Chen, Mei Liu, and Robert Ward published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on guessing protein jobs. After genome reads, the rush is to assign jobs to vast lists of new proteins. Clues from one species can help read kin in another. The team built a method that mines protein links across species for that aim.

Their method pools link data to call jobs for proteins with no known role. Cross species pooling beats single species hunts when data are thin. The tool should speed the long task of filling the protein job map. That map underpins drug and crop gene work alike.
plos-pone-0001662:
Sandra L. Spurgeon, Robert C. Jones, and Ramesh Ramakrishnan described a chip that runs thousands of gene tests at once in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Their platform uses microfluidic dynamic arrays, chips with tiny channels that mix samples and reagents in thousands of small chambers. In one chip, the system runs 2,304 real-time PCR measurements, each tracking a gene's amount as the reaction proceeds.

The authors note the setup takes less pipetting than a standard 96-well plate, though it runs far more tests. The full text gives the chip design, the accuracy checks, and examples of gene measurements. High-throughput gene measurement at this scale helps labs screen drug effects, compare tissues, and track disease genes without weeks of manual bench work.
plos-pone-0001762:
Oliver Friedrich, Frederic von Wegner, Jeffrey S. Chamberlain, and their co-authors linked a missing muscle protein to faulty calcium channels in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In dystrophic mdx muscle, a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, calcium balance is off and fibers degenerate. Absent dystrophin had been connected to altered ion channel properties, including impaired L-type calcium currents.

Working in regenerating mdx muscle, the team tied L-type calcium channel function to dystrophin expression. The full text gives the fiber measurements and how currents recovered as dystrophin returned. Channel faults may be part of why dystrophin-free fibers die, which adds channel drugs to the list of candidate supports for this disease.
plos-pone-0001862:
Susannah G. Tringe, Tao Zhang, Xuguo Liu, and their co-authors sequenced the microbes floating in indoor air in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The indoor atmosphere is an ecological unit that impacts public health, yet its organisms were little known. The team applied culture-independent approaches to microbes harvested from the air of two densely populated urban buildings, analyzing 80 million base pairs of sequence.

Their airborne metagenome catalogues the bacteria, viruses, and other organisms sharing indoor air. The full text gives the organism list and the building comparison. People spend most time indoors, so a census of airborne microbes is baseline data for building design, ventilation, and disease transmission studies.
plos-pone-0001962:
Maxim Volgushev and co-authors measured how fast nerve spikes start, in rat and snail neurons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The action potential, a brief electric spike, is how nerve cells signal each other. In mammal brain neurons, spikes start with striking speed, far faster than the slow, gradual start seen in many other cells.

The team set out to quantify that gap, using rat neocortex neurons and identified neurons from snails. A hard number for spike onset shapes models of how brain circuits fire in sync. It also feeds the debate on where in the cell the spike truly begins.
plos-pone-0002062:
Doron Behar and co-authors counted the female founders of the Jewish diaspora, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. That diaspora began with Assyrian and Babylonian conquests in the Levant, followed by complex movements of people over thousands of years. Those layers make the genetic patterns of Jewish populations hard to unravel.

The team asked how many founding mothers lie behind today's groups, using DNA passed down the female line. If few founders account for most lineages, later growth came from small seeds. Maternal counts give a sharper view of how scattered communities stayed alike, or drifted apart, over time.
plos-pone-0002162:
Young Kwang Chae and co-authors linked a water channel protein to the spread of lung cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Aquaporins are channels that move water across cell membranes. Interest had been growing in whether they also play a part in how cancers grow and invade.

Using stained tissue samples, the team found the channel AQP5 present in non-small cell lung cancer, the most common form of lung cancer. They report that AQP5 boosts the ability of tumor cells to invade nearby tissue. A protein tied to invasion is a possible marker for sorting patients and a possible target for new drugs.
plos-pone-0002262:
Carles Rentero and co-authors asked why the T cell surface tightens up where it meets its target, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When a T lymphocyte switches on, its outer membrane condenses at the contact site. Whether that tightening is a side effect or does real work was not known.

The team blocked membrane condensation by feeding the cells certain lipids, then watched activation. Their experiments show the condensation has functional weight in T cell activation. The result adds the physical state of the membrane to the list of things an immune cell must get right to respond.
plos-pone-0002362:
James McCaw, James Wood, Christopher McCaw, and co-authors modeled how drug resistance could undermine flu control, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Wide use of antiviral drugs during an influenza pandemic is likely to breed drug-resistant strains, which could wreck containment plans. Planners needed to know which factors push resistance hardest.

Using a dynamic infection model, the team explored how subclinical infection, cases too mild to notice, affects resistance spread. They also weighed strategies for a stockpile holding one drug versus two. The results advise governments on how to spend a finite drug stockpile without breeding a virus that ignores it.
plos-pone-0002462:
Work from Derivery and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Emmanuel Derivery, Jenny Fink, Davy Martin, and others. Its subject is free Brick1 Is a Trimeric Precursor in the Assembly of a Functional Wave Complex. The Wave complex activates the Arp2/3 complex, inducing actin polymerization in lamellipodia and membrane ruffles.

The Wave complex is composed of five subunits, the smallest of which, Brick1/Hspc300 (Brk1), is the least characterized. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002562:
In 2008, Jun and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Sunny H. Jun, Bokyung Choi, Lora Shahine, and others. Its subject is defining Human Embryo Phenotypes by Cohort-Specific Prognostic Factors. Hundreds of thousands of human embryos are cultured yearly at in vitro fertilization (IVF) centers worldwide.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002662:
Jing Ai led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a triad of lys12, lys41, arg78 spatial domain, a novel identified heparin binding site on tat protein, facilitates Tat-Driven cell adhesion. The catalog record names Jing Ai first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Tat protein, released by HIV-infected cells, has a battery of important biological effects leading to distinct AIDS-associated pathologies. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002762:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Moritz J. Rossner and colleagues addresses disturbed clockwork resetting in sharp-1 and sharp-2 single and double mutant mice. Authorship is credited in the record to Moritz J. Rossner and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The circadian system provides the basis to anticipate and cope with daily recurrent challenges to maintain the organisms' homeostasis. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002862:
Yann Coello led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was perceiving what is reachable depends on motor representations: evidence from a transcranial magnetic stimulation study. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Yann Coello, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Visually determining what is reachable in peripersonal space requires information about the egocentric location of objects but also information about the possibilities of action. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002962:
Robert Wallis, Stephan Collins, Pamela Kaisaki and co-authors profiled a rat model of cardio-metabolic syndrome in 2008. The syndrome bundles heart, vessel, and metabolic problems with complex causes in people and animals alike. A good animal model lets those parts be studied together under control.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team built extensive profiles of body measures, genetics, and genome-wide gene activity in a specially bred rat strain. They set out its disease features at several levels at once. Researchers choosing a model for diabetes and heart risk get a detailed map of this one.
plos-pone-0003062:
Ranjan Chrisanthar, Stian Knappskog, Erik Løkkevik and co-authors linked CHEK2 and TP53 faults to epirubicin resistance in breast cancer in 2008. Chemoresistance is the main obstacle to cure in most cancers. Anthracyclines such as epirubicin are main drugs for breast cancer and many other cancers, yet predictors of resistance had failed.

Mutations reducing CHEK2 kinase activity, together with TP53 mutations, indicate a functional pathway tied to resistance, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, the pair points to a DNA-damage response route that could be tested before choosing therapy. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003162:
Stuart G. Turville, Meropi Aravantinou, Todd Miller and colleagues test Carraguard-based microbicides against HIV in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Anti-HIV microbicides were in clinical trials, and knowing how a promising approach works in the body, alongside proof that it works in vivo, is central to better next generation products. The team evaluated Carraguard and a new Carraguard-based formulation.

The title reports efficacy in vivo despite variable activity in vitro, in lab tests. Readers see why lab results alone can mislead for prevention gels. The study stresses testing protection in living systems before judging a microbicide a success or failure.
plos-pone-0003262:
Eric Jeziorski, Brigitte Senechal, Thierry Jo Molina and colleagues test herpesvirus links to a rare childhood disease in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a rare disease that affects mainly young children. It features granulomas with Langerhans-type dendritic cells. The role of several human herpesviruses in its pathogenesis was suggested by many reports but remained unproven.

The team use a case-controlled sero-epidemiological study and in situ tests to check infection in patients. Readers get two kinds of evidence, blood tests and tissue tests, on one question. Rare diseases need such combined checks because single reports can mislead for years.
plos-pone-0003362:
Ching Ouyang, David D. Smith and Theodore G. Krontiris study regulatory haplotypes in humans in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Variation in gene expression may give rise to a significant fraction of inter-individual phenotypic variation. Studies searching for underlying genetic controls for such variation had been conducted in model organisms and humans in recent years, including the team's previous effort.

The authors report evolutionary signatures of common human cis-regulatory haplotypes, blocks of control variants inherited together. Readers see selection leave its mark on gene control DNA. Regulatory variation is now known to drive much human diversity, and this study is an early map of it.
plos-pone-0003462:
Xiu-Feng Wan and co-authors traced bird flu change in Vietnam for this 2008 paper. Highly pathogenic H5N1 viruses caused heavy losses in the poultry industry. By June 2008, Vietnam held nearly a third of confirmed human cases worldwide. The team compared virus samples gathered between 2001 and 2007.

Reading the family tree of those samples showed how the virus evolved. Lineages rose, spread, and replaced each other over the years. Such maps warn which virus lines may threaten birds and people next. The work supports flu watch programs across the region. Vietnam's mix of farms and wild birds makes such tracking hard but vital.
plos-pone-0003562:
Lisa J. Ma and co-authors studied cell transfer through breastfeeding in mice in this 2008 paper. Nursing shapes the young immune system well beyond simple antibody cover. Immune cells from milk can cross the pup's gut lining. The team examined what that transfer does once pups grow up.

Non-transgenic pups were fostered to test the transfer cleanly. As adults, recipients showed altered delayed-type hypersensitivity responses. The effect also differed by the recipient's gender. Milk thus passes living immune education from mother to young. Nursing effects like these may reach well into adult health and disease risk.
plos-pone-0003662:
Karen M. J. van Loo, Tim Dejaegere, Martine van Zweeden, and colleagues published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Atherosclerosis, the clogging of arteries, comes from genes and environment acting together. Based on rat work, the team suspected a role for the gamma-secretase complex.

They tested a variant in that complex for links to early coronary disease. The variant tracked with premature clogged heart arteries in men, but not in women. A male-only link like this adds a sex-specific piece to the puzzle of why heart disease strikes some people young.
plos-pone-0003762:
Walter S. Leal and Yuko Ishida published this fire ant study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The red imported fire ant is an invasive pest with painful, sometimes dangerous stings. Its colonies come in two social forms, with one queen or many. Proteins called GP-9s were suspected of steering that social order by smell.

The authors found GP-9 proteins are in fact everywhere in the ant, not tied to smell organs. That makes them unlikely to run the social organization through scent. The negative result sends the search for the colony's chemical code in a new direction.
plos-pone-0003862:
Chao Tian, Roman Kosoy, Annette Lee, and colleagues published this population genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hidden ancestry differences within a study population can create false hits in disease gene hunts. As such hunts expand to new continental groups, their internal substructure must be mapped first. East Asia was the focus here.

Using genome-wide SNP arrays, the team charted genetic substructure across East Asian populations. The map shows how groups within the region relate and differ. Gene hunters can use it to avoid type 1 errors caused by ancestry rather than disease.
plos-pone-0003962:
Harald Staiger, Fausto Machicao, Silke A. Schäfer, and co-authors studied a new diabetes risk gene region in 2008. The region, MTNR1B, had just been tied to type 2 diabetes. It was also reported to affect fasting blood sugar levels. The gene makes a receptor for the hormone melatonin.

Their PLOS ONE article used a well-studied group at raised diabetes risk. They tested whether variants in MTNR1B track with insulin cell function. Pancreatic beta cells make insulin, and their failure drives diabetes. A gene that tunes those cells links sleep hormones to blood sugar control. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004062:
Kim Zarse and Michael Ristow tested antidepressant claims in worms in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Certain serotonin-blocking antidepressants had been said to extend worm lifespan. Mianserin and methiothepin were reported to mimic calorie restriction in C. elegans. Longer life in worms often excites aging researchers.

Zarse and Ristow report the opposite for the adult worms they tested. The drugs increased body fat and shortened lifespan in their hands. Conflicting results demand care before calling a drug anti-aging. The study shows how conditions can flip a lifespan claim. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004162:
Pan-Young Jeong and colleagues published this worm study in PLOS ONE in 2009. When the tiny worm C. elegans senses a pheromone that signals crowding and poor food, it can enter dauer. Dauer is a tough state built for long survival. The molecular path into dauer had stayed unclear.

The team tracked the full time course of molecular change as worms enter dauer, watching genes and metabolism shift step by step. Their data lay out the metabolic basis of the switch, showing what a worm burns and stores in this state. The map helps explain how animals remodel themselves to outlast hard times.
plos-pone-0004262:
Takuya Tamura and colleagues published this neurogenetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In several neurodegenerative disorders, glial cells, the brain's support cells, are suspected of harming neurons. Whether this non-cell-autonomous harm is general, and whether it differs by disease, had not been established.

Working in fruit flies, the team expressed mutant ataxin-1 and huntingtin, the proteins behind two inherited brain diseases, only in glia. They report that this alone induces both developmental and late-onset neuronal pathologies. Damage that starts in support cells reframes how these diseases might be treated. The fly work isolates glia as a source of harm.
plos-pone-0004362:
Camelia Kuhnen and Joan Chiao published this behavioural genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Individuals vary in their willingness to take financial risks. The authors show that variants of two genes are major factors in that variation. The genes regulate dopamine and serotonin neurotransmission. Both were previously linked to emotional behaviour, anxiety, and addiction.

The genes are tagged by the variants 5-HTTLPR and DRD4. Linking them to financial risk connects money choices to brain chemistry. The study is an early example of genoeconomics, the attempt to find DNA roots of economic choices.
plos-pone-0004462:
Tropical plants planted in Hawai'i sometimes wait quietly before they start to spread, and Curtis Daehler measured those waiting times in PLOS ONE in 2009. The delay between arrival and spread is called the lag time of an invasion. Most earlier estimates were indirect or based on stories, and they suggested lags are often long.

Daehler used records from experimental plantings, where the planting dates are known. That gives rare, direct evidence on how soon planted species turned invasive. He found short lag times for the invasive tropical plants in the plantings. Short lags are a warning: a new plant that looks harmless for a few years may simply not have started yet. Managers who judge risk by early calm may be fooled.
plos-pone-0004562:
Tomato extract calmed one kind of gut inflammation signal but made another kind of colitis worse, report Young-Eun Joo, Thomas Karrasch, Marcus Muhlbauer, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The extract is rich in lycopene, the red pigment of tomatoes, often praised as a health compound. Its impact on intestinal inflammation was unknown.

Mice were fed diets with two levels of tomato lycopene extract. The extract prevented a bacterial signal, LPS, from activating the inflammatory switch NF-kappaB. Yet in a chemical model of colitis using dextran sulfate sodium, the extract worsened the disease. Mixed results like these are a useful warning: a natural compound can help on one measure and harm on another.
plos-pone-0004662:
A transplant drug may cause diabetes by disabling two liver gene switches, propose Jurgen Borlak and Monika Niehof in PLOS ONE in 2009. Posttransplantation diabetes mellitus is a frequent complication of immunosuppressive therapy. Patients need those drugs to keep a transplanted organ, so the side effect cannot simply be avoided by stopping treatment.

The team investigated the effect of cyclosporine on the expression and activity of hepatic nuclear factors HNF1alpha and HNF4alpha. These switches control many liver and pancreas genes, including ones for glucose handling. Their dysfunction offers a molecular rationale for cyclosporine-induced diabetes, as the title states. A mechanism in hand suggests ways to protect transplant patients, such as monitoring or pairing drugs that spare the switches.
plos-pone-0004762:
Daniel Little and Lu Chen identified protein spots that evolve together, with focus on structure and catalysis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. A protein form and job depend on contacts among its building blocks. Pressure on one spot should thus depend on what sits at contacting spots nearby in the folded chain.

Past work used shared information scores to spot such linked pairs. The team refined that hunt and stressed bond formation and active site teamwork. Linked spot maps can predict which changes will break a protein. They also guide design of new proteins. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004862:
Richard Mushlin and colleagues presented the CHAMBER clique finding algorithm for heterogeneity in biomarker epidemiology, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Common disease etiology may involve complex combinations of genes and exposures resulting in etiologic heterogeneity. The computational algorithm employs clique finding for heterogeneity and multidimensionality in biomedical and epidemiological research to discover subgroups sharing causal patterns.

Cliques reveal patient subsets hidden in averages. Precision medicine needs such stratification tools. Algorithms can guide targeted prevention trials. Heterogeneity explains many failed replications. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004962:
Huntington's disease is an inherited disorder that destroys brain function. Patients also lose weight, which hints at hormone trouble. Nadine Saleh and colleagues looked for that trouble in PLOS ONE in 2009. They set out to detect neuroendocrine disturbances in patients. Neuroendocrine signals link the brain to the body's hormone systems.

Their measurements covered hormone and brain-chemical pathways in patients. The results revealed clear disturbances alongside the neurological decline. The disease's reach extends beyond movement and thought. It reaches the body's control systems for metabolism and stress. The findings widen the picture of Huntington's. They may also suggest new symptoms to monitor and manage.
plos-pone-0005062:
Chasing rewards means balancing two urges. One is exploiting known rewards. The other is exploring for new ones. Aaron Gruber, Rifat Hussain and Patricio O'Donnell studied the brain hub for that balance. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The hub is the nucleus accumbens. Prefrontal and basal ganglia circuits frame the problem.

They cast the accumbens as a switchboard for goal-directed behavior. It routes signals between motivation and action circuits. The region helps decide when to stick and when to stray. The hippocampus feeds it information about places and contexts. The work maps a key decision point in the brain. Disorders of motivation, from addiction to apathy, involve exactly this switchboard.
plos-pone-0005162:
Every ribosome needs a delivery protein. EF-1 alpha brings building blocks for protein synthesis. It was thought to be universal among eukaryotes. Gillian Gile and colleagues found the story richer in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some organisms use a stand-in called EFL instead. They traced both proteins across the Euglenozoa, a diverse microbial group.

The pattern suggests ancestors carried both proteins. Descendants then lost one or the other, lineage by lineage. Differential loss, not separate origins, explains today's patchwork. The finding rewrites a supposedly universal rule. Even essential machinery can be swapped in evolution. The study shows how to read that history from modern distributions. Phylogeny turns presence and absence into a narrative.
plos-pone-0005262:
Cartilage in joints lives under repeated squeezing, and the right amount of force keeps it healthy. Too much or too little force can spark inflammation and start cartilage breakdown. Nam and colleagues studied that force threshold in PLOS ONE in 2009, mixing experiments with modeling.

The team examined how compressive force switches on the NF-kB pathway, a master control of inflammation. Their results map biomechanical thresholds that separate safe loading from harmful loading. That map matters for joint injury care and for designing exercise after cartilage damage. Joint care rests on load: too much at the wrong time harms, too little weakens, and this map helps set the dose much like a drug dose.
plos-pone-0005362:
Echinococcosis is a parasitic disease of people and livestock, spread through contact with dogs and foxes that host the adult tapeworm. A vaccine antigen called EG95 protects livestock well. Haag and colleagues analyzed that antigen's evolution in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The EG95 antigen contains amino acids under positive selection, meaning evolution favored changes there. Those selected sites may influence which hosts the parasite can infect and how well the vaccine works. Watching selection on a vaccine target warns where protection might weaken. A vaccine that guards sheep and goats guards people too, since each case stopped in stock is a case that can never reach the men. Women who tend and eat that stock.
plos-pone-0005462:
Piyali Mukherjee and co-authors studied the timing of DNA copying in mammal cells for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Before a cell can copy its DNA, it must build a starter complex on the DNA in the right order. The team wanted to know how that building lines up with other cell cycle events.

They found that key starter parts load onto DNA late in one phase, at the same time as a known switch protein changes form. After that point, control of entry into DNA copying shifts to a new mode. Fine timing like this helps explain how cells avoid copying DNA twice.
plos-pone-0005562:
Kiran Yanamandra and co-authors studied protein clumping in the aging prostate in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many diseases of aging involve proteins folding into stiff clumps called amyloid. Alzheimer's disease and type 2 diabetes are among the best known.

The team linked amyloid formation to two inflammation proteins, S100A8 and S100A9, in prostate tissue. Those proteins are raised where there is inflammation, which is common in the aging prostate. The finding adds the prostate to the list of organs where inflammation and amyloid may feed each other. Amyloid in the prostate has been noted for years, but its causes and effects were largely ignored until work like this.
plos-pone-0005662:
Hanneke Korsten and co-authors studied the first steps of prostate cancer in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A mouse model lacking the tumour brake PTEN in the prostate passes through clear stages, from overgrowth to cancer. The earliest stage is where prevention could work best.

Staining tissue showed that the overgrowing cells pile up in the surface layer and carry markers of progenitor cells. The authors argue these piled-up cells are the ones that later start tumours. Finding the true starting cells focuses prevention research. Prostate cancer is common and often slow, and finding its true starting cells could spare men needless treatment.
plos-pone-0005762:
Jacob Minor and co-authors sequenced a hearing gene across patients and controls in 2009. The gene SLC26A5 makes prestin, a motor protein in the ear's outer hair cells. Prestin lets those cells change length with sound, sharpening hearing; mice without it are severely impaired.

Whether prestin variants cause human hearing loss was less clear. The team catalogued fourteen new DNA variations in the gene from their cohort. Each variant is a candidate for follow-up tests in deafness clinics. The catalogue also helps labs tell harmless variation from changes that truly damage hearing.
plos-pone-0005862:
Popchai Ngamskulrungroj and co-authors charted in 2009 the genetic variety within the Cryptococcus fungus group. The group holds two sibling species that cause serious disease in people and animals. Typing methods had split them into major molecular types.

The team's diversity analysis suggested one species, Cryptococcus gattii, is varied enough to deserve formal varieties. Names matter in medicine: finer labels help track which strains spread where and how sick they make patients. The study supports splitting the group more finely. It draws on samples and markers from across the complex.
plos-pone-0005962:
Where two kinds of fish meet and breed, their young carry a blend of traits. Nicolas Stolzenberg, Bénédicte Nguyen The, Marie Dominique Salducci and colleagues studied such a hybrid zone in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper asks how much of a fish's growth, shape and breeding comes from its surroundings, and how much from its mitochondria, the cell parts passed down by the mother.

Sorting those two forces helps explain how hybrid zones form and hold together over time. The fish offer a living test of nature and nurture side by side. The study shows that a mother's line can leave marks on traits that the local water alone cannot explain, a clue for anyone who manages mixed fish stocks.
plos-pone-0006062:
A weakened Salmonella can carry a DNA vaccine into the body by mouth. Michelle Gahan, Diane Webster, Steven Wesselingh and colleagues found a catch in that design in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tests Salmonella-delivered DNA vaccines in animal models, a route that builds on the success of oral Salmonella vaccines themselves.

The key, stated in the title, is that the bacterium must also make the vaccine's antigen itself. Delivery alone is not enough to raise a strong immune answer. That rule simplifies some designs and rules out others, and it guides the next round of needle-free vaccines that aim to protect through the gut.
plos-pone-0006162:
Every gene activity study leans on reference genes assumed to hold steady. Mi Jeong Kwon, Ensel Oh, Seungmook Lee and colleagues challenged that assumption in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses multiplatform expression data to find new reference genes, and validates them for quantitative gene expression analysis across tissues.

The classics, GAPDH and ACTB, vary more between tissues than their reputation admits, which can tilt every result normalized to them. New, checked standards make thousands of studies more honest at once. Reference work is unglamorous and foundational: when the ruler is wrong, every measurement made with it is wrong too.
plos-pone-0006262:
Corals depend on tenant algae that live inside their tissues and share food. Daniel Thornhill and colleagues studied those symbionts in two dominant Caribbean corals in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Little genetic data existed on how symbiont populations are structured across reefs.

The team examined reef loyalty, host specificity, and stability of the partnerships over time. Which algae a coral keeps shapes how the pair handles heat and light. Stable, local partnerships may respond to climate change differently than flexible ones. The data help predict reef futures under warming seas.
plos-pone-0006362:
Adaptive radiation in Mediterranean plants is poorly understood, despite the region's rich flora. Beatriz Guzman, Maria Dolores Lledo, and Pablo Vargas studied the white-flowered Cistus lineage in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The group holds twelve species spread mainly through Mediterranean habitats.

A total evidence analysis combined nuclear and chloroplast DNA data to trace the radiation. Combining data types gives a fuller family tree than either alone. The tree shows how one lineage diversified across the basin. Such histories explain how Mediterranean biodiversity was built. The tree also helps explain how the group spread as the sea basin changed over time.
plos-pone-0006462:
Lance Price and colleagues profiled the bacteria living in chronic wounds for PLOS ONE in 2009. Bacteria that colonize wounds are thought to help keep them from healing. The team characterized wound bacteria from a group of chronic wound patients. They used gene-based pyrosequencing, a fast DNA reading method, aimed at a marker gene found in all bacteria.

They also assessed how diabetes and antibiotic use shape the wound microbiota. Both factors could shift which germs thrive in a wound. Knowing the mix may explain why some wounds stall. It could also guide smarter use of antibiotics in wound care.
plos-pone-0006562:
Binzhi Qian, Yan Deng, Jae Hong Im, and colleagues identified a macrophage population in breast cancer spread in PLOS ONE in 2009. The stromal microenvironment, and particularly macrophages in primary tumors, influence malignant potential. However, at the metastatic site the role of macrophages was less clear. The team studied metastatic breast cancer cell extravasation, exit from blood vessels, and establishment.

Their title reports that a distinct macrophage population mediates extravasation, establishment, and growth. Helper immune cells thus escort cancer cells into new tissue. Blocking that escort could slow metastasis. The study shifts focus from the primary tumor to the landing site.
plos-pone-0006662:
Annebel De Vleeschauwer and co-authors compared influenza viruses in pigs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pigs are considered intermediate hosts for transmission of avian influenza viruses to humans. The basic organ pathogenesis of avian viruses in pigs had been barely studied. The team ran a comparative pathogenesis study of an avian H5N2 and a swine H1N1 influenza virus in pigs.

Comparing which organs each virus damages shows how host adaptation changes disease. An avian virus that behaves mildly in pigs differs from one that replicates widely. Such knowledge underpins pandemic risk assessment. Pigs remain a key species in influenza ecology.
plos-pone-0006762:
David J. Bacon and his team linked gene changes in malaria parasites to drug failure in PLOS ONE in 2009. A drug pair, sulfadoxine with pyrimethamine, once led the fight against falciparum malaria. It failed more and more as parasites grew resistant. Many lands switched to new drug pairs. Resistance comes from small changes in two parasite genes.

The team checked how each change shaped patient outcomes. They also tested the drugs on parasites in the lab. Gene checks can warn clinics which failures to expect. That sharpens the watch for resistance in each land. It helps health programs know when a drug is spent and must be dropped.
plos-pone-0006862:
Ronaldo Ichiyama and colleagues combined radiation therapy with treadmill training after spinal injury in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Training alone can restore weight-bearing stepping after complete cord transection. That stepping needs no reconnection to the brain. After contusion injuries, repair of tissue and circuits is the harder goal. Radiation therapy was tested as a repair aid.

Contused rats received radiation followed by training. Motor function improved beyond training comparisons, as the title reports enhancement. Combining a tissue treatment with rehabilitation is a promising pattern. Each part may do what the other cannot. The study supports pairing biological repair with physical retraining.
plos-pone-0006962:
Stephanie Ortigue, James Thompson, Raja Parasuraman, and colleagues studied how brains read intentions in PLOS ONE in 2009. Guessing others' intentions from their actions uses two brain networks. One observes action in fronto-parietal areas. The other, a social network, includes the posterior superior temporal sulcus. How these networks interact over time was unclear.

The team combined EEG and fMRI in one design. They used a repetition suppression method to follow signals in the temporo-parietal cortex. Their work charts when intention reading happens, not just where. That timing detail helps separate action watching from true social understanding.
plos-pone-0007062:
Michelle Spaulding, Maureen O'Leary, and John Gatesy revisited whale family ties in PLOS ONE in 2009. Whales and dolphins sit inside the even-toed mammals, the artiodactyls. Placing key fossils correctly is crucial for tracing the move from land to water. The team combined molecular data with fossil evidence.

Adding more species changed some accepted relationships. Interpretations of important fossils and trait changes shifted with the wider sample. Their result is a warning and a tool. Sparse sampling can mislead even careful family trees, and whale origins remain a test case.
plos-pone-0007162:
Peter McGarvey, Hongzhan Huang, Raja Mazumder, and others merged biodefense data in PLOS ONE in 2009. A national program sought drug and vaccine targets against germs of bioterror concern. Those germs span bacteria, parasites, and viruses. Data poured in from many omics tools at once, in forms that did not match.

The team built systems to merge those data streams. Merged data let them study how germs act inside their hosts. Shared targets stand out once data are pooled. Such groundwork speeds the hunt for cures and tests when a threat appears.
plos-pone-0007262:
Björn Kröger, Thomas Servais, and Yunbai Zhang traced the early rise of open-ocean cephalopods in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The Ordovician period saw a dramatic global rise in diversity. Families, genera, and species multiplied, partly as nutrients and phytoplankton became more available in open waters around the world.

Cephalopods, the group including squids and octopuses, became top ocean predators. The authors examine the origin and initial rise of pelagic cephalopods, those living in open water. Their fossil analysis helps explain how marine food webs gained powerful predators so early.
plos-pone-0007362:
Zeb Kurth-Nelson and A. David Redish examined a learning algorithm used to model the brain in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Temporal-difference algorithms have been proposed as models of reinforcement learning. In reinforcement learning, agents learn from rewards and prediction errors, much as animals learn from outcomes in daily behavior.

The authors examine distributed representations in these algorithms. They study distributed representations of belief and distributed discounting of future rewards. Their analysis refines how temporal-difference models map onto neural systems. Psychologists and computer scientists can use the refinement to build more realistic learning models.
plos-pone-0007462:
Han-Yu Yang and Carton Chen published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Streptomyces, soil bacteria known for making antibiotics. Many species carry enzymes called polyphenol oxidases that react with phenolic compounds from plants. One version works outside the cell, while a related version works inside it. The team compared what the two versions do to the bacterium's sensitivity.

The two enzymes pushed sensitivity in opposite directions. The outside enzyme protected the bacteria from phenolics, while the inside one made them more sensitive. The authors describe the arrangement as a double-edged sword. The same chemistry can shield or harm depending on where it happens. The study shows how location alone can flip an enzyme's effect on survival.
plos-pone-0007562:
R. Doug Hardy and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a toxin made by the pneumonia bacterium Mycoplasma pneumoniae. The toxin, called CARDS, damages cells and is tied to community-acquired respiratory distress. It had already proved toxic to cells and organ cultures. The team tested the purified toxin in mice and baboons. They measured lung inflammation and breathing function after exposure.

The toxin alone reproduced key features of the disease in both animals. Lungs became inflamed, and function suffered. Showing that one molecule can drive the illness strengthens its case as a major virulence factor. A named cause is a target for vaccines and treatments. The baboon data matter because primate lungs resemble ours closely. The study moves CARDS toxin from suspect to demonstrated culprit.
plos-pone-0007662:
Xiang Ming Xu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how plants build iron-sulfur clusters. These clusters are simple in structure yet serve as helpers in proteins for respiration, photosynthesis, and other core processes. Assembly and insertion of the clusters into proteins is a careful construction job. The team studied a protein called AtHscB in the model plant Arabidopsis. They asked where in the cell it works.

AtHscB turned out to be dual localized, working in two compartments at once. Both postings serve iron-sulfur protein biogenesis. A construction crew stationed in two workshops explains how distant proteins all get their clusters. Fundamental jobs like this are easy to overlook until they fail. The study maps one helper's double duty in a plant. It adds to the basic account of how cells equip their most ancient proteins.
plos-pone-0007762:
Heraldo Vasconcelos and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tracks insects and other small creatures in leaf litter after a fire. The site was a woodland savanna in the tropics. Fire is a major force in such savannas.

Litter creatures drive nutrient cycling and other key soil processes. Yet few studies had followed their response to fire. The team charted how the litter fauna changed over time after burning. Their dynamics show which groups return fast and which lag. That knowledge helps land managers judge how fire shapes savanna ecosystems.
plos-pone-0007862:
Hans Binder and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains quirks in the signals from SNP microarrays, a standard genetics tool. These arrays genotype DNA by binding fragments to probes fixed on a surface. Each probe is a short stretch of DNA with a known sequence.

Two effects distort the signal: mismatches and stacked G letters. The authors analyze how probe signals vary with these features. Their model helps users correct the distortions. Better correction means more accurate genotypes and copy number estimates. That accuracy feeds thousands of studies that rely on SNP arrays.
plos-pone-0007962:
Muh-Yong Yen and colleagues told how Taipei beat back a fast-spreading eye illness in PLOS ONE in 2009. In the fall of 2007, acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, a harsh pinkeye, jumped from Keelung into the capital. Spread surged on weekends, when clinics and habits changed.

The city answered with a wide risk message plan across many channels at once. Cases turned and fell fast once word got out on how the illness spreads and how to block it. The authors offer the episode as a working model for cities facing the next fast-moving outbreak.
plos-pone-0008062:
Georgios Kalantzis and Harel Shouval modeled how a synapse's past changes its future in PLOS ONE in 2009. Synapses, the links between brain cells, strengthen or weaken with use, which is how the brain learns. That very ability to change itself shifts with past use, a trait called metaplasticity.

Their model ties the shift to changes in the synapse's physical build. A link lately rebuilt answers the next signal in a new way. The idea helps explain how the brain tunes its own learning rate, keeping memory flexible without letting it run wild.
plos-pone-0008162:
Craig April and colleagues coaxed full gene readings from old preserved tissue in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hospitals store samples fixed in formalin and set in wax, a method that wrecks the RNA that gene readings need. Those archives hold decades of cases with known outcomes, a treasure if they could be read.

Their assay read genome-wide activity from such degraded samples with sensitivity close to fresh tissue. The archive is thus open. Studies can now link gene patterns to outcomes across thousands of stored cases, instead of waiting years for new ones to mature.
plos-pone-0008262:
Norihiko Sasaki and colleagues studied mouse embryonic stem cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Embryonic stem cells can grow into many cell types. Keeping them in their early state requires the right chemical signals. The team focused on two transporters, PAPST1 and PAPST2. These move a sulfate-carrying molecule called PAPS into the Golgi apparatus.

Work in flies had already shown these transporters matter for development. The mouse study tested their role in stem cell maintenance and differentiation. Sulfation shapes how cells signal and stick together. The findings connect a small transport step to big decisions in early development.
plos-pone-0008362:
Anna Aronovich and colleagues implanted pig tissue in mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Very little is known about what sets organ size differences between species. The team used embryonic pig tissue implanted into mice as their model. They defined the role of host Factor VIII in controlling implant size. Factor VIII is best known as a blood clotting factor.

Enhancing the implants revealed a novel role for the coagulation cascade. Blood clotting proteins thus help govern how large an organ grows. That surprise connects two distant fields of biology. It may matter for growing replacement organs in the future.
plos-pone-0008462:
Yonggang Wang and co-authors catalog SUMO proteases in frogs in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. SUMO proteins are small tags that attach to other proteins. All SUMOs start as longer pro-proteins. Enzymes must trim them before they can be attached. After trimming, they link to targets by a path like that of ubiquitin. The team work with the frog Xenopus laevis.

They identify the frog proteases that trim SUMO. They also track when each one is active as the frog develops. That timing shows which protease serves which stage. The catalog is a base for work on how SUMO tags shape growth.
plos-pone-0008562:
Gerardo Ceballos and co-authors document a grassland collapse in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Grasslands worldwide are imperiled by land conversion and desertification. Native populations and species are being lost with them. The Janos region of northwestern Mexico holds one of the largest remaining grasslands. It supports prairie dogs and many other native species. The team survey the region and track recent change. Their data show a rapid decline of the whole grassland system.

Losses include key species and the ecological processes they sustain. Prairie dog colonies that engineer the habitat have shrunk sharply. The authors draw ecological and conservation implications from the decline. Protecting Janos is urgent if this grassland is to survive.
plos-pone-0008662:
Armand Paauw, Maurine A. Leverstein-van Hall, Jan Verhoef, and colleagues published an evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It follows Enterobacteriaceae, a large family of gut bacteria. Mild residents of the gut can turn harmful after picking up foreign DNA carrying attack traits. Swapping genes sideways, between cells, drives much of that change.

The team traced the high pathogenicity island, a gene module shortened to HPI, plus several other modules. They found these blocks had moved between bacteria in varied combinations, again and again. Change therefore arrived in sudden leaps, not slow single steps. Readers see how new disease-causing strains can be assembled quickly from shared parts.
plos-pone-0008762:
Francisco Pan-Montojo, Oleg Anichtchik, Yanina Dening, and colleagues replayed Parkinson disease starting in the gut. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. In patients, Parkinson damage follows a telling route. It appears in gut nerves and the lower brainstem before reaching movement centers. A pesticide called rotenone is linked to Parkinson risk. Feeding it to mice tested the gut-first idea directly.

Mice given rotenone by stomach tube developed damage in that same order. Gut nerves showed changes first, then relay stations, then the substantia nigra. A working gut-first model lets researchers test ways to halt the march early.
plos-pone-0008862:
Carine Marinach-Patrice, Arnaud Fekkar, Ralitsa Atanasova, and colleagues sped up naming of invasive yeast infections. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Invasive candidiasis can kill quickly, especially in frail patients. Naming the exact Candida species guides drug choice. Classic culture methods are slow, often taking days. A laser-based mass method, MALDI-TOF, identifies microbes from their protein fingerprints in hours.

The team validated the method for rapid species diagnosis in these infections. Faster naming means faster, better-targeted antifungal treatment. Severe infections are exactly where speed pays most. The study supports wider clinical use of mass spectrometry for fungi.
plos-pone-0008962:
Francesca Gilli and co-authors read gene activity in blood cells of pregnant women with multiple sclerosis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Multiple sclerosis often goes quiet during pregnancy, then flares after birth. Nobody fully knows why carrying a child calms the disease. The team looked for clues in genes linked to inflammation.

They ran a genome-wide scan of blood cells from patients during pregnancy. Genes that drive inflammation changed their activity as pregnancy progressed. The pattern offers a natural model of how to switch the disease off. Drugs that copy pregnancy's effect could help patients who are not pregnant.
plos-pone-0009062:
Masako Osada and co-authors watched a mouse thymus wither when one signal was blocked, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The thymus trains T cells, the immune system's targeted fighters against germs. Its epithelial cells recruit young precursors from the marrow and coach them to maturity. Wnt signals help keep those epithelial support cells alive and working.

The team used DKK1, a protein that blocks Wnt signalling in tissues. In young mice the blockade drained the epithelial progenitor pool quickly. The thymus then degenerated ahead of its normal ageing schedule. Premature thymus shrinkage weakens immunity, so its triggers deserve close attention.
plos-pone-0009162:
Kim Lonergan and co-authors read gene activity at two waypoints of lung cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Non-small cell lung cancer advances through recognisable stages over time. Lesions progress from precancer to carcinoma-in-situ, then to invasive spread. Pathways marking each stage could guide treatment given far earlier.

The team used SAGE, a counting method, to profile the genes switched on. Carcinoma-in-situ, cancer still confined in place, was compared with invasive tumours. Different sets of genes lit up at the two stages of disease. Stage-specific genes may one day flag cancers that are about to turn invasive.
plos-pone-0009262:
Chang-Jin Park and co-authors published this rice immunity study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plants, like animals, detect germs by their surface patterns and fight back. A rice receptor called XA21 is one such detector. How receptors like XA21 get shipped to the right place in the cell was not clear.

The team studied BiP3, a helper protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's shipping department. Making extra BiP3 changed how XA21-mediated immunity worked in rice. The result ties the shipping machinery to the plant's front-line defense. Better understanding of that link could help breeders build rice that resists disease.
plos-pone-0009362:
Ilona Croy and co-authors published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Childhood maltreatment can reshape the brain for life. Smell is a telling sense to test, because its brain areas overlap regions often harmed by early trauma. The team used smells that had nothing to do with trauma.

Women with a history of childhood maltreatment underwent fMRI scans while smelling neutral odors. Their association areas of the brain activated more strongly than in other women. Even harmless smells were processed differently by these brains. The finding shows early harm leaves marks on everyday senses, not only on responses to threats.
plos-pone-0009462:
Sotoodeh Abhary and colleagues studied blood levels of a compound in people with type 2 diabetes in PLOS ONE in 2010. The compound is called ADMA. It blocks the making of nitric oxide, a gas that helps blood vessels relax. Two enzymes, DDAH1 and DDAH2, break ADMA down. The team looked for gene changes in those enzymes.

Changes in both genes added up to predict how much ADMA a person carried. Each change on its own had a small effect. Together they explained a large share of the spread between patients. The result points to the clearing enzymes as a place to help protect blood vessels in diabetes.
plos-pone-0009562:
Ioannis Karakasiliotis and co-authors studied a host protein and a cat virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. Feline calicivirus infects cats and relies on proteins of the host cell. One such protein, called PTB, binds RNA. Viruses often use it to boost their own protein making. The team tested what PTB does to this virus's translation, the step that builds proteins from RNA.

PTB turned out to hold the virus back, acting as a negative regulator. That is the opposite of the helping role it plays for some other viruses. The finding shows a two sided relation between a virus and its host. It may help in designing drugs against this common cat pathogen.
plos-pone-0009662:
Casper Roed and co-authors followed meningococcal disease survivors across Denmark in PLOS ONE in 2010. Meningococcal infection can kill fast, and survivors often face lasting effects. What was less clear is whether their risk of death stays high for years. The team used nationwide Danish records. They compared long term death rates of past patients with those of the wider public.
