Survivors carried a higher risk of death long after the illness ended. The excess risk lasted well beyond the hospital stay. Nationwide data make that shadow hard to dismiss. The findings argue for long term follow up of survivors, not just care during the acute illness.
plos-pone-0009762:
Much of the human genome is copied into RNA, including stretches nobody had cataloged. Daniel Klevebring and colleagues took an in-depth look at those copies in human cell lines. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A transcriptome is the full set of RNA copies a cell makes.

The team found novel TARs, short transcribed regions outside known genes. They also found prevalent antisense transcription, RNA copied from the opposite strand of DNA. Both findings widen the map of what human cells transcribe. A fuller map helps scientists interpret gene studies and disease data.
plos-pone-0009862:
Predicting how immune molecules bind used to take costly lab experiments. Nicolas Rapin and colleagues reviewed how prediction tools now let computers simulate the immune system. Their overview appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The immune system is too complex to model by hand alone.

The meeting point of computational immunology and bioinformatics is software that models immunity. Prediction tools estimate molecular binding, which molecules will grip which targets. Simulations built on those estimates can test vaccine ideas before bench work begins. The authors map where the field stands and where it heads.
plos-pone-0009962:
The gonorrhea bacterium passes DNA packages between cells, a trick that can spread drug resistance. Emilia Pachulec and Chris van der Does reviewed those packages in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Their review appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Conjugative plasmids are rings of DNA that copy themselves into a neighbor cell. Conjugation is the direct cell-to-cell transfer of that DNA. Plasmids live apart from the main chromosome. In gonorrhea, plasmids can carry traits that matter for treatment. Knowing the plasmid set helps track how resistance moves. Gonorrhea is a common disease passed through sex.
plos-pone-0010062:
The authors were Iveta Bottova, Ursula Sauder, Vesna Olivieri, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered Toxoplasma gondii, a widespread parasite. They focused on P-glycoprotein, a membrane pump that pushes substances out of cells. More of that pump is linked to drug resistance in many disease organisms, parasites included.

The team tested a pump blocker called GF120918 in the parasite. They watched its effects on calcium-dependent processes and on lipid handling. Learning what the pump does in normal parasite life, not just drug resistance, may reveal new weak points for treatment.
plos-pone-0010162:
The authors were Eric Bonnet, Marianthi Tatari, Anagha Joshi, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used cancer gene data to find control modules. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that recognize and regulate target genes. Evidence ties them to key jobs in development and disease, cancer included, though their place in gene networks stayed hard to define.

From a cancer expression dataset, the team inferred modules, groups of genes working together. Some modules appeared to be regulated by microRNAs. Mapping those modules can reveal which control points go wrong in a tumor.
plos-pone-0010262:
The authors were Anders Malmendal, Jarl Underhaug, Daniel Otzen, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper presented a fast way to map protein folding states. To understand what a protein does, scientists must explore the shapes it can take. The team combined NMR spectroscopy, a shape-sensitive method, with multivariate analysis of the resulting data.

They call the method GPS for proteins, since it locates a folding state quickly. A fast global map saves the slow work of solving each shape separately. That speed can help screen proteins whose folding goes wrong in disease.
plos-pone-0010362:
Bernat Vila, Frankie Jackson, Josep Fortuny and others rebuilt dinosaur egg clutches in 3-D for PLOS ONE in 2010. The huge fossil eggs called megaloolithids are linked to sauropods, the giant long-necked dinosaurs. Fossils of these eggs are found worldwide, yet experts disagreed on clutch shape and how eggs were incubated. A rich site in Spain, in rock from the late Cretaceous, gave fresh material.

The team scanned and modeled the clutches in three dimensions. The models preserved the exact layout of eggs as they were buried. That layout carries clues about how nests were built and covered. It can also hint at how parents behaved around the nest. Digital rebuilding lets those clues be tested without breaking fossils.
plos-pone-0010462:
Véronique Bertrand-Vallery and colleagues profiled skin cells driven into an unusual state by sunlight in PLOS ONE in 2010. Repeated UVB exposure can push skin cells that lack a certain guard protein toward a different way of maturing. Instead of aging out, these cells take an alternative path. The team used a protein-wide comparison method to catalog what changes in that state. One protein stood out from the profile.

That protein, called TRIM29, appeared to help the altered cells survive. A survival factor in sun-damaged skin deserves attention, since such skin can turn cancerous. The profile also gives other researchers a parts list for this odd state. Understanding alternative fates may explain how some damaged cells refuse to die.
plos-pone-0010562:
Becky Proskocil and colleagues showed farm pesticides weaken a protective receptor in airway nerves of guinea pigs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Population studies link these organophosphorus pesticides to asthma. The group had shown three such pesticides make airways overreact within a day of one injection. Overreaction involves nerves in the airway wall. A receptor there, M2, normally brakes nerve signaling; the team asked how pesticides disable it.

The pesticides reduced M2 function through indirect routes, not by blocking it head-on. Indirect mechanisms can be missed by simple safety screens. That gap matters for setting exposure limits for farm workers. Guinea pig airways mirror human responses closely in this system. The study gives regulators a mechanism to test for.
plos-pone-0010662:
Tommi Aho and colleagues rebuilt and checked a model of the yeast interaction network, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inside a cell, thousands of proteins touch, carry, and regulate each other. Network models gather those contacts into one map that computers can analyze.

Their model, called RefRec, merged data from many experiments on yeast. The authors then validated the merged map against independent evidence. A checked map is far more useful than a pile of raw contacts. Other researchers can build on RefRec to predict what happens when a protein fails, without redoing the assembly work.
plos-pone-0010762:
Zoi Kapoula and colleagues measured eye movements around a session of EMDR therapy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. EMDR uses guided side-to-side eye movements while a person recalls a worry. It is used for trauma care, yet its workings are debated. The team wanted an objective measure, not self-reports.

Seven healthy volunteers had their smooth pursuit eye movements tested before and after one session. The session targeted personal worries of moderate strength. Pursuit quality changed measurably after the session. Eye tracking cannot prove a therapy heals, but it gives researchers a hard number to pair with what patients say they feel.
plos-pone-0010862:
P J Hastings, Megan Hersh, P C Thornton and co-authors published this bacterial genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When E. coli bacteria are stressed, they sometimes copy DNA with a sloppy enzyme called Pol IV, and the copying errors raise mutation rates. Other, more careful copying enzymes exist in the same cell, and the authors asked whether they crowd into the same repair sites.

Using strains with several mutations, they gathered in-cell evidence that polymerases I, II, and III compete with Pol IV during stress-driven mutation. That means the careful enzymes are present where the sloppy one works, yet errors still get through. Hastings and colleagues clarify a tug-of-war inside stressed cells. The balance between faithful and error-prone copying helps explain how bacteria evolve resistance under pressure.
plos-pone-0010962:
Sara Becerril, Amaia Rodríguez, Victoria Catalán and co-authors published this obesity study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Brown fat burns energy to make heat, and both the hormone leptin and nitric oxide help control that furnace. The authors bred mice lacking leptin, which makes them severely obese, that also lacked an enzyme producing nitric oxide under stress.

At twelve weeks, the double-deficient mice weighed less, carried smaller fat pads, gained less weight per bite of food, and ran warmer than mice lacking leptin alone. Their blood sugar and fat chemistry also improved, and brown fat tissue showed a healthier profile of control molecules. Becerril and colleagues reveal that a stress enzyme quietly suppresses the body's heat-burning tissue. Blocking it might one day help treat obesity, though mouse results need care in translation.
plos-pone-0011062:
Narumi Ogonuki, Manami Mori, Akie Shinmen and co-authors published this reproduction study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Intracytoplasmic sperm injection, injecting a single male cell directly into an egg, rescues male infertility and powers much fertilization research, yet its success factors had never been systematically mapped. The authors ran a large mouse experiment crossing every combination of the likely factors.

Five mouse strains, three kinds of male germ cell from mature sperm to round immature spermatids, and fresh versus frozen-thawed cells were combined in a full factorial design. The type of male cell used affected every measured step, from egg survival after injection through cleavage and implantation. Ogonuki and colleagues deliver the reference table embryology labs lacked, showing which choices in the injection room carry the most weight.
plos-pone-0011162:
Martinez-Seara, Rog, Karttunen and colleagues modeled cell membranes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cholesterol is a major part of the fatty skins that wrap cells. Using computer models, the team asked how cholesterol arranges the other molecules around it inside a membrane.

They found cholesterol imposes a clear spatial and directional order on its neighbors. That order affects how stiff or fluid a membrane is, and how proteins sit in it. Such fine detail underlies ideas about ordered patches in cell membranes. The work helps cell biology by grounding membrane behavior in measurable physical rules.
plos-pone-0011262:
Traggiai, Casati, Frascoli and colleagues tracked B cells during chronic inflammation in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Lasting inflammation changes the mix of immune cells in bone marrow. The team followed two B cell groups: mature cells that recirculate through the body, and marginal zone cells with a guard role.

Chronic inflammation preserved the recirculating mature cells but not the marginal zone group. That selective loss reshapes defense, since each group fights different threats. The remodeling may explain why long inflammation weakens some responses while others stay strong. The finding aids work on autoimmunity and chronic disease.
plos-pone-0011362:
Steeve Comeau and co-authors tested in 2010 how an Arctic sea snail may fare in the future ocean. The snail, Limacina helicina, drifts in cold northern waters and builds a thin shell, and it is a key food for fish and seabirds. Oceans are warming and taking up more carbon, which makes the water more acidic and shells harder to build.

The team raised the snails under conditions projected for coming decades and watched their shells and survival. The snails struggled as the water grew more acidic, with shell building under strain. Because so many Arctic animals eat these snails, harm to them can ripple up the food web. The study gives climate planners a concrete early warning from one small but central polar species.
plos-pone-0011462:
Arun Balakumaran and co-authors checked in 2010 whether tagging stem cells with magnetic particles changes what the cells are. Bone marrow stromal cells, also called mesenchymal stem cells, are followed inside the body after transplant by loading them with superparamagnetic iron oxide particles that show up on scans. If the tag altered the cells, years of tracking studies would rest on a flaw.

After labeling, the cells kept their stemness, their ability to stay unspecialized and to form several tissue types. The tag therefore watches the cells without rewriting their identity. That reassurance matters for regenerative medicine, where knowing where transplanted cells go is essential for judging whether a therapy works. Researchers can now track cells with more confidence that the tracker is not the story.
plos-pone-0011562:
Marjan Wassenberg and co-authors priced hospital infection control in 2010 against the harm it prevents. MRSA, the drug-resistant staph germ, spreads between hospital patients, and hospitals deploy screening, isolation, and cleaning programs that cost real money. Managers asked to fund them need to know which measures pay for themselves in infections averted and which cost more than the damage they stop.

Their analysis quantified the cost-effectiveness of controlling nosocomial, or hospital-acquired, spread of resistant bacteria, using MRSA as the case. Putting numbers on both sides turns an argument about caution into an argument about value. Infection control often wins such comparisons once outbreak costs are counted honestly. The study gives hospital boards the arithmetic to defend budgets that look like pure cost until the infections that did not happen are priced in.
plos-pone-0011662:
Bin Shan and colleagues studied a surface protein that calms inflammation in mouse fibroblasts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fibroblasts vary in whether they display Thy-1, and that variation shapes inflammation, injury and repair. In the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis, marked by chronic inflammation, fibroblasts notably lack Thy-1.

The team showed Thy-1 dampens genes switched on by TNF-alpha, a major inflammation alarm, working through Src family kinases. Losing Thy-1 may therefore let inflammation run hotter in scarred lungs. The finding identifies a built-in brake whose absence could be part of why fibrosis persists.
plos-pone-0011762:
Melinda Suchard and co-authors tracked a regulatory T cell marker as HIV infection progresses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Which T cell responses protect against HIV, and which accompany decline, is critical for vaccine design. Whether changes in regulatory T cells help drive progression was unclear.

The team found expression of FOXP3, the master switch of regulatory T cells, is upregulated in CD4 T cells in progressive infection. Higher levels marked more severe disease. The climbing signal reads like immune exhaustion and may help clinicians gauge how far infection has advanced.
plos-pone-0011862:
Pasquale Scopelliti and co-workers measured in 2010 how the tiniest surface textures change which proteins stick to a material. Protein coating is the first event when a material meets living tissue, and it shapes later steps such as cell attachment and inflammation. The bumps and dips involved are measured in nanometres, far below what an eye can see.

By varying that nanoscale shape and measuring protein adsorption, the team linked surface form to the amount and kind of protein that settles. Designers of implants and sensors can use such links on purpose, choosing textures that invite a helpful coating or resist a harmful one. The findings turn a surface detail once left to chance into a design choice.
plos-pone-0011962:
Claire Jackson, Heidi Welch, and Tomas Bellamy worked out in 2010 how a form of learning in the cerebellum is controlled. The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, and its parallel fibre to Purkinje cell synapses can strengthen, a change called long-term potentiation. This potentiation was recently described and its induction rules poorly understood.

The team showed that P-Rex family exchange factors, together with the enzyme PI3-kinase, control whether this strengthening occurs. Those molecules link incoming signals to the cell's internal scaffolding. Pinning down the control set turns a vaguely known plasticity into a defined circuit that other labs can test, block, or boost in studies of motor learning.
plos-pone-0012062:
James Catterson and co-workers asked in 2010 what fruit flies can teach about the two-way street between food and sleep. Diet and sleep influence each other strongly in people, with real health stakes, yet the relationship is poorly characterized. Drosophila is a standard model for both metabolism and behavior, making it a natural test bed.

The team studied how dietary changes modulate the flies' sleep-wake behavior. If specific nutrients move sleep in a small fly with known genetics, the responsible circuits can be hunted gene by gene. That is the model's promise: a messy human complaint, poor sleep on a poor diet, reduced to parts that experiments can name.
plos-pone-0012162:
Cinzia Scambi, Valentina La Verde, Lucia De Franceschi, and co-authors compared blood proteins in two similar diseases for PLOS ONE in 2010. Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that scars skin and organs for reasons still unclear. A look-alike condition can follow bone marrow transplant, when donor cells attack the patient's body, and comparing the two may reveal shared machinery.

Their protein survey found signs that a guard protein of the immune system works poorly in these patients. That guard normally stops the immune system from chewing up the body's own tissue. A shared defect could explain part of both diseases and suggest one treatment angle worth testing for each.
plos-pone-0012262:
Regina Berretta and Pablo Moscato proposed tracking cancer through disorder itself, in PLOS ONE in 2010. It is widely accepted that cancer cells rewrite their gene activity as the disease advances toward its malignant forms. High-throughput tools can now follow thousands of genes at once, and the authors argue the pattern to watch is entropy, a measure of how disordered that activity becomes.

A tumor whose gene use grows more chaotic may be a tumor on the move, whatever its type. An entropy-based hallmark could therefore stage cancers and flag dangerous ones from a single measurement approach. The idea reframes cancer detection: instead of hunting one marker per cancer, measure the breakdown of order itself.
plos-pone-0012362:
Jiri Zavadil, Huihui Ye, Zhaojian Liu and colleagues profiled small regulatory RNAs in uterine fibroids in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Fibroids, called leiomyomas, are common benign tumors of the womb that can cause pain and heavy bleeding. They involve wide changes in gene activity, including changes in microRNAs, tiny RNAs that tune how much protein each gene makes.

By matching microRNA levels with the levels of their target genes in the same tumors, the team found pairs that move in opposite directions, as true targets should. The list of linked pairs points to pathways that drive fibroid growth. Those pathways may offer drug targets for a condition now treated mainly by surgery.
plos-pone-0012462:
Ryan Traylor, Damien Bruno, Trent Burgess and colleagues characterized a rare chromosome deletion by starting from the gene scan, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Deletions near the tip of chromosome 20's long arm had been described only about eleven times. Such microdeletions can cause developmental problems, but with so few cases the pattern of effects was fuzzy.

Using a genotype-first approach — grouping patients by the shared deletion, then comparing their traits — the team sharpened the clinical picture of the 20q13.33 deletion. Doctors can now counsel families with clearer expectations. The approach itself is a model for defining other rare deletion syndromes.
plos-pone-0012562:
Gwendolyn Gilbert, Michelle Cretikos, Linda Hueston and colleagues surveyed flu antibodies in New South Wales after the 2009 pandemic's first wave, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Pandemic H1N1 reached Australia in May 2009 and filled hospitals during the southern winter. Knowing how many residents carried antibodies shows how far the virus truly spread, beyond counted cases.

The survey measured H1N1 2009 antibodies across the population after that winter wave. Serology reveals the silent infections that case counts miss, and the immunity wall the next wave would meet. Australian data were prized worldwide that year, since the southern season previewed the northern winter.
plos-pone-0012662:
Philip, Yu, Donnell and co-authors studied serosorting, a practice in which men choose partners or acts by HIV status. The strategy grew up among gay and bisexual men, but solid data on whether it works were scarce. Their 2010 paper draws on the large EXPLORE study group.

They found serosorting was linked with a lower chance of becoming HIV positive. That does not make the practice risk free, yet it shows community-born strategies can cut risk. Honest numbers help health workers give advice that fits how people actually behave.
plos-pone-0012762:
Yang, Zhang, Liu and co-authors published the complete chloroplast genome of the date palm. The date palm ranks among the world's most valuable woody palms, beside oil palm and coconut. Its chloroplasts, the green cell parts that catch sunlight, carry their own small genome, which the team read in full in 2010.

A complete sequence gives breeders and scientists markers for sorting palm varieties and tracing their history. It also allows clean comparison with the chloroplasts of other palms. Such references support the crop that feeds and employs millions in dry regions.
plos-pone-0012862:
Hendrickson, Lautenberger, Chinn and co-authors found that variants in the cell's energy genes shape how AIDS advances. Human mitochondria carry only thirteen protein genes of their own. The nucleus supplies almost all the rest of the proteins that build and run mitochondria, handling shape, defence and energy.

Their 2010 study tested variants in those nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes across HIV patients. Some variants tracked with faster or slower AIDS progression. Energy genes joining the list of AIDS factors widens the hunt for why patients differ so much.  Their cohort sizes gave the tests solid statistical footing.
plos-pone-0330962:
Sarahrose Jonik and co-authors surveyed health workers and trainees in 2026 about what nicotine does and does not do. Many clinicians wrongly blame nicotine itself for most smoking diseases, a mix-up that can colour advice about e-cigarettes.

Nearly six hundred respondents at one academic medical centre rated nicotine's role in addiction, cancer, and heart disease, and judged vaping against smoking. Beliefs about nicotine tracked strongly with views on e-cigarette harm. Those who saw vaping as less harmful answered differently on several nicotine items. Correcting one core misconception, the authors argue, may shift counselling on the whole product range.
plos-pone-0333162:
Hiroshi Hoshijima and colleagues use in 2026 machine learning on hospital records to predict sickness and vomiting after surgery under spinal anaesthesia in Japan. Records covered thousands of adults over more than a decade, then matched patients with and without the problem for fair comparison. Five learning methods were combined into one predictor, and factor rankings were extracted.

Use of a strong pain drug after surgery ranked as the top contributor, followed by surgery length, body size, urine output, and anaesthesia length. Female sex, lower body size, shorter procedures, and caesarean birth also raised risk in their list. The model was accurate enough to guide prevention, the authors report.
plos-pone-0337662:
GloriaSalome Shirima and colleagues modeled what adding larviciding, killing mosquito larvae in their water habitats, would do for malaria control in rural southeastern Tanzania, beyond mosquito nets alone. National programs increasingly favor the combination, but most models use generic settings. Theirs was adapted to one district's real seasons and mosquito data, collected before and after an actual larviciding program.

Simulations varied how completely breeding sites were treated and tracked outcomes for the main malaria mosquito. Bayesian methods estimated mosquito death rates from the field data to anchor the model. District-level modeling matters because a strategy that sings in one ecology can flop in another; this study shows how local programs can test coverage choices before spending scarce control budgets.
plos-pone-0338562:
Mete Ucdal and co-workers compare simple blood-based scores for predicting bad outcomes in palliative care patients. Twelve combined indices, built from fats, sugar, swelling, and nutrition markers, were tested head to head. Their 2026 study reviews just over three hundred patients and asks which score best foresees infection, need for a breathing machine, and death within a month.

One index, blending a sugar-fat measure with body size, won on all three outcomes. Its edge grew even larger among patients with diabetes, while rival scores barely improved there. A single cheap calculation from routine labs could help care teams judge risk and plan support for very ill patients more honestly.
plos-pone-0342962:
Chunya Liu and colleagues built a maths model of seasonal flu spread across Chinese provinces that joins weather and news driven public awareness. Cold, dry spells help flu spread, while search and media attention can warn people into safer habits. Province case counts, search indexes, and weather records were used to tune the model and track how easily flu spread over time.

Low temperature and low rainfall both eased spread. Strong media attention cut spread risk, and when attention faded, modelled peaks grew taller. Provinces differed sharply: coastal and central provinces reacted strongly to media, while some western areas barely reacted. Flu plans should pair weather forecasts with timely public messaging, tuned by region.
plos-pone-0346062:
Adriana Armas, Diego Polanco Taipe, and David Soriano-Moreno studied diet and mood in medical students in Lima, Peru. Two hundred sixty-four students at a private university took part. They rated their eating on a healthy eating index. They rated anxiety and depression on two standard symptom scales. Medical training is a known pressure cooker. Diet is one lever students control for themselves.

Barely one percent ate what the index calls healthy. About a third reported anxiety symptoms, and nearly half reported depressive ones. Each extra point of diet quality came with a small, steady drop in both. A one-time survey cannot prove which side drives the other. The smooth gradient still argues for treating the cafeteria as part of mental health policy.
plos-pone-0347262:
Note on status: this is a protocol, a plan for a review not yet carried out, by Aeri Jang and Yun-Hee Kim, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The planned project asks which digital teaching methods best build clinical reasoning, the step-by-step thinking nursing students use to reach care decisions.

Following standard review guidelines, the team will search five major databases for randomized trials of digital education in undergraduate nursing, through the end of 2025. A network meta-analysis will then compare methods both directly and indirectly, rank them, and grade how certain the evidence is. The finished ranking is meant to help nursing schools choose digital tools with proof behind them rather than fashion.
plos-pone-0347662:
Alisa V Zubova and colleagues present what they argue is the oldest known dentistry, performed by Neanderthals roughly fifty-nine thousand years ago. A molar from Chagyrskaya Cave in Siberia carries a large hollow ground into its chewing surface during the owner's lifetime. The team studied the marks under magnification and tomography, then reproduced tool actions experimentally to test how the hollow was made.

The wear matched drilling or rotating with a stone perforator, and two further kinds of working with different tools were also found, requiring careful finger control. A cavity sits at the centre of the story: someone located the source of pain, judged it could be removed, and chose the technique most likely to work. The authors place deliberate dental treatment, not instinctive self-care, within Neanderthal capability.
plos-pone-0347862:
Li Ma and Ying Gu used the OECD's international TALIS teacher survey to test whether sharing leadership in schools makes teachers happier in their jobs. Distributed leadership gives teachers real say in decisions rather than concentrating power in the principal's office. Their 2026 analysis also asked whether collaboration among teachers carries part of the effect.

Schools with more distributed leadership did have more satisfied teachers, and the link was partly explained by collaboration: shared leadership encouraged teachers to work together, and that teamwork itself raised satisfaction. Both direct and indirect paths mattered. The authors advise school systems to spread leadership deliberately and to protect time for teachers to plan and solve problems jointly.
plos-pone-0348062:
Jiankun Wang and his team tried a cheap balm to ease a gut scope done wide awake. One hundred twenty-two young patients took the test. Half had a numb gel, with lidocaine, smeared at the anus. Half had plain salt water. No one knew who got what. All rated pain at the anus and in the belly, in and post test.

The gel cut pain at the anus, in and post test. It cut belly pain post test too, though not in the test. The scope reached its end mark more fast with the gel. More growths were found as well. Young doctors gained the most. The team calls the balm a sound, cheap aid.
plos-pone-0348162:
Surakshya Ghimire and three colleagues published this 2026 research article on traditional rice varieties grown in Nepal. Farmers there have kept local landraces for generations, and many carry traits that newer varieties have lost. Ghimire's team grew sixty-three of these landraces and scored them on visible plant traits and measured yield traits.

Two landraces, Vhadasar and Ratin, stood out for heavy grain harvests and strong harvest index scores. Sorting the plants by their traits placed them into eight groups of closer and more distant relatives. Grain yield rose alongside panicle number, filled grains, and grain size. Documenting this range gives breeders concrete local material for raising yields while keeping diversity alive.
plos-pone-0348262:
Lindsay Wilson and colleagues describe a large research cohort of mothers who used substances during pregnancy in British Columbia, Canada, and their children. Built from linked health records, the cohort covers everyone in the province who gave birth between 2000 and 2022 and had a recorded sign of substance use around pregnancy. Data come from ten linked databases.

The records follow mothers and children over time, covering care, prescriptions, housing, and health outcomes. Three planned studies will use the cohort to test specialized hospital care for pregnant patients, compare medicines for opioid use disorder, and track how maternal substance use relates to child health. The profile explains the resource so other researchers can use it well.
plos-pone-0348362:
Adamu Takele Jemere and colleagues surveyed four hundred twenty-three health workers in northwest Ethiopia about a government phone app that classifies diseases using standard codes. Correct classification underpins planning and records, but nobody knew whether front-line staff had even heard of the tool. Their 2026 study also hunted for what separates aware workers from unaware ones.

Only about a third knew the app existed. Workers with social media accounts, digital skills, or prior training on the paper coding booklet were far more likely to know it. Having used a phone for medical purposes before also helped. The authors recommend deliberate awareness campaigns, pairing the app rollout with training rather than assuming adoption.
plos-pone-0348762:
Tianxin Jiang and co-workers test a compound from a traditional medicinal root against scarring of the belly lining caused by dialysis fluid. Long-term dialysis can stiffen that lining until the treatment fails. Their 2026 study treats both rats with kidney failure and human lining cells bathed in sugary fluid, then tracks scarring signals and tissue change.

The compound eased scarring in both settings, lowering fiber buildup and restoring a marker of healthy lining cells. A chain of signals that drives cells to switch into scar-forming mode quieted as well. Cells tolerated the treatment without harm. The compound and its target pathway offer a lead for protecting dialysis patients' remaining treatment time.
plos-pone-0348862:
Aqbara Ibrahim Chande, Novatus A. Tesha, and Bruno Sunguya look for what drives uncontrolled HIV levels in treated patients in Tanga, Tanzania. A high viral load means therapy is failing and transmission risk climbs. Their 2026 study interviews more than two hundred patients on treatment at the city clinic and joins their answers with clinic records.

About a third of patients carried a high viral load. Severe household food insecurity stood out as the strongest single link, raising the odds many times over. Drinking alcohol and being in one's early twenties also raised the odds, as did certain service and sales jobs. Food support and drinking counseling, the authors suggest, belong inside HIV care, not beside it.
plos-pone-0349562:
Christopher Mai, Ricardo Buettner, and co-authors built a vision system to classify obstacles on railway tracks, where trains cannot swerve and need long distances to stop. Finding objects is well studied, but naming them reliably across types is harder. Their 2026 system blends two network designs, one strong on local detail and one on global context, plus an attention module that highlights the features that matter most.

Trained on about two thousand track images across six classes, from boulders and branches to people and barrels, the system reached balanced accuracy above ninety-nine percent in repeated cross-checks. The authors say such classification could power automatic track surveillance, preventing accidents and modernizing rail safety. They frame it as a benchmark for a task where a wrong call carries heavy consequences.
plos-pone-0349662:
Meng Wang and colleagues built in 2026 a combined measure of healthy lifestyle and tested its link with suicidal behavior among young people in China. Their school based survey covered young people aged ten to twenty-four in Zhejiang Province. Rather than judging habits one at a time, the team combined several lifestyle factors into a single composite score.

They then examined how that score relates to suicidal thoughts and behaviors reported by the students. Composite measures reflect how habits actually cluster in a life: sleep, activity, diet, and screen time move together. If healthier combined patterns track with lower risk, schools and families gain a broader, more practical target for prevention than any single habit offers.
plos-pone-0349762:
Alejandra Espinosa Andrade and Wilson Vásquez-Castillo studied guayusa, a caffeinated Amazonian leaf, among Kichwa families in Napo province, Ecuador, in 2026 work. The leaf is both a daily energising drink and a ceremonial one, and a growing export market is changing how it is grown and used.

Interviews and observation traced planting, harvest, brewing, and beliefs today. Families keep much ancestral know-how and value the leaf for easing sleepiness, aches, and hunger. Yet drinking has moved beyond home and ceremony, and old customs like dream reading over the dawn drink are fading. The study records a living tradition mid change.
plos-pone-0349862:
Christina Kranzinger and co-authors in Austria worked in 2026 on a stubborn craft problem: picking the right ski boot for each racer. Fit choices have rested on a few experts' feel, which keeps knowledge private and hard to pass on inside a company.

Using rounds of expert input, the team built a data sheet listing what truly decides a good match for a skier. Early trials with the sheet showed which facts matter and where judgment still rules. Turning private know-how into a shared model could make boot fitting faster, fairer across athletes, and easier to teach to new staff.
plos-pone-0350162:
A vaccine against human papillomavirus prevents cervical cancer, but uptake stays low in Pakistan for cultural as much as logistical reasons. Khola Noreen and colleagues adapted a World Health Organization framework on vaccination drivers to local language and customs, in this 2026 PLOS One study across Punjab districts.

Girls, parents, health workers, teachers, school leaders, and religious scholars all took part during 2025. Sorting their answers against the global framework mostly worked, but one new theme emerged that the original lacked: cultural integration, covering how vaccination fits community values and daily life. The adapted tool should help health teams ask the right questions before campaigns begin.
plos-pone-0350262:
Baluchi sheep graze both sides of the Iran and Afghanistan border, and Sadegh Taheri and colleagues compared the genes of the two herds. Their 2026 PLOS One study read tens of thousands of DNA markers in about eighty-six Iranian sheep and fifteen Afghan sheep.

Both herds held moderate genetic variety. The Iranian herd showed the least variety yet better recent population size, and its DNA markers stayed linked over longer stretches. A clustering analysis favored two ancestral groups. The authors warn the small Afghan sample and the standard test chip may skew results. They also searched the DNA for marks left by past breeding choices.
plos-pone-0350562:
Camilo Ramírez-Giraldo and a Bogotá task force set out how they will build a world guide for gallbladder surgery. The operation is done by keyhole cuts and is one of the most common on Earth. Past safety drives focus on one feared injury, to the bile duct. They say too little about the craft of the operation itself. This 2026 paper is a plan, not a set of results.

An expert group will frame key questions and search past studies in a set way. They will grade the proof for each claim. Then they will vote in rounds till they agree on each point. The end goal is one clear guide. It should make surgery safer and help train new surgeons in all kinds of health systems.
plos-pone-0350662:
Kerry A Ryan and colleagues interviewed patients and doctors about joint decisions in care for a chronic throat condition where the food pipe narrows from immune attack. Drug and diet options both work, with hard trade offs and no single best pick. Thirty five adult patients and sixteen gut and allergy doctors took part in one to one talks across Michigan.

Patients often held gaps or wrong ideas about the illness and its treatments, and they differed in where they wanted facts to come from. Doctors backed joint decisions, yet patients differed in how much say they wanted. Knowing a patients preferred role early, the team argues, makes shared choices real rather than routine.
plos-pone-0350762:
Companies publish glossy sustainability reports, but do the green topics they stress match real results? Ivan Savin, Mateo López Carel, and Eva Schlindwein read nearly fifteen hundred such reports from large European firms with text-mining tools, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The software found thirty-four themes, six of them environmental. Stress on renewable energy and greener supply chains went with genuine gains in environmental measures. Stress on emissions or electric vehicles showed no such link. Grouping firms by theme showed sectors talk differently, too. The authors argue judging reports theme by theme beats trusting a single overall score.
plos-pone-0351062:
Correction: this notice fixes tables in an earlier study, and readers should use these versions. Liana R Andronescu and co-authors' study linked past COVID infection with self reported brain and mood symptoms over the half year after infection in a large military health cohort.

Four tables, two main and two supplementary, were uploaded wrongly in the original article and are replaced here in full. The corrected tables set out depression, anxiety, fatigue, and thinking scores by infection status for more than two thousand participants. The notice changes no conclusions; it repairs the record so others can check and reuse the numbers safely.
plos-pone-0351162:
Shuqiong Wang and Zhao Zhang survey Chinese military veterans about what would draw them into village and neighbourhood governance, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Veterans are seen as a disciplined resource for grassroots administration. Five hundred and twenty-five veterans in Guizhou Province answered the questionnaire, and statistical grouping sorted them into three motivational types.

Just over half were mainly practical, responding best to subsidies. Roughly a quarter ran on honour and recognition, and another quarter on career development and promotion. One blunt policy cannot move all three. The authors propose diagnosing each group's expectations first, then matching the incentive — money, honours, or advancement — accordingly.
plos-pone-0351562:
Zareen Fatima and colleagues compared lung wash samples from patients with weak immune systems who had pneumonia against samples from healthy volunteers. Gene based lung tests can find many germs at once, but telling true culprits from background germs is hard. Samples came from fifty two patients and twenty healthy people, read with a portable gene reader.

Patient samples held fewer germs overall and less variety, yet differed more from person to person. Healthy lungs looked alike, led by a steady set of mouth like germs that live without air. A known healthy baseline helps doctors judge when a patient result truly stands out, rather than chasing normal background noise.
plos-pone-0351662:
Viruses such as coronaviruses wear surface proteins that change shape to fuse with human cells, and each shape offers different targets for antibodies. Sevilay Gülesen and colleagues tested whether the AlphaFold2 prediction program can draw both the before-fusion and after-fusion shapes, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Left to itself, the program rarely produced the after-fusion shape. The team adjusted the procedure to coax out both forms, since vaccine designers need each as a template. Their work matters because many viral surface proteins still lack any measured structure. Reliable predicted shapes in both states could speed the design of vaccines and blocking drugs.
plos-pone-0351762:
Reading chest X-rays takes training that many clinics lack. Juiria Humayan and colleagues built a small computer program to help. It sorts scans into nine lung conditions. Healthy scans are one class. Pneumonia and tuberculosis are among the others. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026. It targets places where heavy software cannot run.

The program is far smaller than standard rival models. It trained in about five minutes on ordinary hardware. Across repeated tests, it scored about ninety-six percent accuracy. It learned from nearly seven thousand images from one Brazilian center. Display tools highlight the image regions behind each call. Scores fell on outside data, though. Wider testing must come before clinic use.
plos-pone-0351862:
Shun Nakahara and colleagues pooled the randomized trials of inhaled nitric oxide for people with fibrotic lung disease, a scarring condition that raises pressure in the lung's arteries and steals exercise capacity. The gas relaxes those arteries when breathed, so it was a plausible help. Four trials with two hundred seventy-four patients, some crossing over between gas and placebo, were combined, with walking distance in six minutes as the main yardstick.

The pooled result was a near-perfect shrug: walking distance barely differed from placebo, everyday activity levels did not clearly improve, and side effects were no worse. The authors conclude the evidence does not support routine use in this population. Negative meta-analyses save real money and hope: clinics can stop spending on a treatment whose trials, gathered honestly, do not deliver.
plos-pone-0351962:
Yannick Epée and colleagues interviewed two hundred eleven people who gather giant African land snails along Cameroon's Atlantic coast, where the snails are both dinner and income. Farm pesticides are spreading through the same land, and harvesters are the first to notice what changes. The survey, across six localities, asked what they believe pesticides do to the snails they collect and how their harvests have shifted.

A majority believed pesticides shrink the snails they find, while a similar majority saw no effect on how many they gather. Night collecting in October remained the peak, matching the snails' own seasons. Despite worrying about chemicals, nearly two thirds had no interest in farming snails instead, preferring the wild harvest. Perceptions are not measurements, the authors stress, but they map where awareness campaigns and safer practices must start.
plos-pone-0352162:
Zirong Li led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of blood sugar in critically ill patients with high blood pressure. They used a large American intensive care database and a ratio that compares stress-driven sugar spikes with a patient's usual sugar level. They then split patients into four bands and tracked deaths over a year.

Higher ratio bands faced higher death rates at every checkpoint, from one month to one year. The pattern held across many patient subgroups. Li proposes the ratio as a simple warning gauge for intensive care teams judging how sick a hypertensive patient really is.
plos-pone-0352262:
Nicolette Stogios and colleagues lay out a planned brain imaging study on how antipsychotic drugs interfere with insulin's action in the brain, published as a protocol in 2026. Antipsychotics can trigger weight gain and diabetes, and women are hit harder than men. The study focuses on fifteen healthy women and on how the menstrual cycle changes the picture.

Each volunteer will visit in two cycle phases, receiving the antipsychotic olanzapine or a placebo pill, then insulin sprayed into the nose or a placebo spray, followed by brain scans. Nasal insulin normally quiets the liver's glucose output and shifts brain activity, giving a measurable stand-in for brain insulin sensitivity. The results should clarify why these drugs carry metabolic risk for women.
plos-pone-0352662:
Nurul Ibrahim and three colleagues link cultural wealth to health literacy in urban Malaysia. Their 2026 survey covers three hundred twenty-five adults in Ipoh, Perak. Health literacy is usually framed as personal reading skill. This study widens the lens. Cultural capital comes in three forms: habits carried in the person, objects like books, and formal credentials. A validated eighteen-item tool measured whether people can access, understand, judge, and apply health information.

Every form of cultural capital tracked with every literacy area. The links were strong and firm. Formal credentials, the institutionalised form, predicted access to health information best of all. Regression models confirmed each form contributed independently. The lesson reaches beyond tutoring individuals. Communities rich in education and cultural resources find health information easier to reach and use. Programmes that ignore that social backdrop will keep misreading low literacy as a personal failure.
plos-pone-0352762:
Wondimnew Desalegn Addis and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One survey of fever patients in Ethiopia's Dera District who treat themselves with antimalarial drugs instead of seeking confirmed diagnosis. Nearly six hundred patients at public facilities in June 2025 described their habits and knowledge. National policy calls for tested, confirmed treatment, so self-medication threatens both recovery and malaria elimination.

Over two in five patients had self-medicated with antimalarials. The practice was more likely among higher earners, people with poor malaria knowledge, those who saw little risk in self-treating, and those living near private drug sellers. Belonging to community health insurance cut the odds substantially. The authors recommend public education on the risks and wider insurance enrollment to pull patients toward proper diagnosis.
plos-pone-0352862:
Praveen Kumar and G. D. Goutham Simha present this 2026 PLOS One antenna study designing a compact dual-band millimeter-wave antenna for satellite and next-generation mobile networks. The tiny structure, built from concentric arc shapes, resonates in two high-frequency bands and offers useful signal gain at both. Because millimeter waves fade quickly in cluttered cities, the authors also modeled how the signal weakens with distance.

They tested the design's behavior under direct line-of-sight and blocked conditions using two standard urban path-loss models that account for shadowing and weather. The work pairs the hardware design with propagation estimates so network planners can judge where such antennas would hold a link. The authors pitch the device for dense urban deployments where compact size and two operating bands are both valuable.
plos-pone-0352962:
Eliyas and colleagues measured antibiotic use on Bangladeshi chicken and dairy farms in a 2026 study. Farm drug use drives resistance that later harms people, yet amounts were poorly counted. Thirty-six farms in two districts were followed across summer and winter, with use weighed against animal numbers.

Layer farms used the most antibiotics per animal unit, then broiler farms, with dairy farms far lower. Use fell in winter for chickens but rose for dairy cattle. Much use involved drugs classed as critically important for human medicine. The authors call for tighter rules and a national farm-level tracking system, using this pilot as the baseline.
plos-pone-0353062:
Bin Chen and six colleagues rebuild a DNA vaccine against gum disease so it switches on only in gut tissue, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Vaccines for periodontitis exist in the laboratory, but their usual genetic switch fires everywhere in the body, raising safety worries. The team swapped in a switch borrowed from a mucus gene that is active mainly in intestinal cells, and tagged the vaccine with a glowing marker to watch where it fired.

The glow appeared only in gut-type cells, as hoped. Fluid from a common probiotic bacterium then boosted the switch further, apparently through a growth-signal pathway, since blocking that pathway blunted the boost. Tissue-targeted vaccines of this kind could make oral immunisation safer.
plos-pone-0353162:
Jeffrey Casely-Hayford led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of university staff in Sweden moving from full remote work to a hybrid mix. Nearly seven hundred and fifty professional staff answered surveys across a year of transition, and the team modeled how work climate, health, and satisfaction shifted, by gender and household type.

Support from colleagues grew over time, but stress and exhaustion rose too, while satisfaction held steady. Women rated their work situation less favorably than men, and staff living alone fared differently from those with partners. Casely-Hayford urges universities to pair hybrid plans with equality and family support.
plos-pone-0353262:
Arman Latifi and four colleagues survey students in Maragheh, Iran. They ask what keeps students socially well. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Four hundred and sixty students answered questionnaires. One covered social capital: the trust and networks around them. Another covered psychological capital: hope, confidence, and resilience. A third covered social well-being itself.

The three measures rose together. Married students reported stronger social capital. So did students living away from the family home. So did those with better-educated fathers. A statistical model explained about a fifth of the variation. The authors argue universities build social health in a direct way. They should strengthen students' inner reserves, not just their friendship circles.
plos-pone-0353362:
Brandon Theurer led a team of six authors on this 2026 dinosaur anatomy study from Alberta, Canada. Horned ceratopsid dinosaurs are famous for their skulls, but their lower hind legs were poorly understood. A nearly complete leg, dug up over a century ago from the Dinosaur Park Formation and never described, was CT scanned and rebuilt digitally to settle how its bones fit together.

The reconstruction clarifies toe bone arrangement, ankle pieces, and how the shin bones met, with variation visible across related species. Theurer's work gives future studies of dinosaur walking a firmer anatomical base.
plos-pone-0353462:
Li, Kong, and Wang surveyed college students on hardship, stress, and mental health in a 2026 study. Students face study and life pressures, and early childhood hardship can echo into adult well-being. The online survey measured kindness toward oneself, felt stress, past hardship, bounce-back strength, and mental health in one combined model.

The model tests whether bounce-back strength carries part of the effect of the other factors onto mental health. Kindness toward oneself may protect students partly by building that strength, while hardship and stress may wear it down. If the pathways hold, campuses could teach self-kindness and resilience skills together rather than treating distress only after it deepens.
plos-pone-0353562:
Si Chen and co-authors evaluated in 2026 lightweight ways of adding a newer sequence model, called Mamba, to the task of outlining polyps in colonoscopy images. Polyp segmentation, drawing the exact boundary of a growth in the colon, helps doctors find and remove growths before they can turn cancerous. The software must run in real time during the procedure, on hardware a clinic can afford, which is why light weight matters in their tests.

Their empirical evaluation compares several strategies for integrating the model and measures the trade off between accuracy and speed. Endoscopy is one of the clearest cases where artificial intelligence can earn its place beside the doctor, and studies like this decide which designs are practical enough to try.
plos-pone-0353662:
Jańczak and colleagues studied adults in Poland hurt by betrayal in close relationships in a 2026 paper. Betrayal by trusted people, in childhood or adult life, is tied to later depression and troubled personality functioning. Two hundred nine adults answered tested questionnaires about trauma, mood, spacing out under stress, and reading other minds.

Trauma in adult life linked more strongly to depression than childhood trauma did. Effects on personality problems were about equal for both periods. Much of the harm traveled through spacing out and through weaker mind-reading skill, with mind-reading the stronger path. The results point to those two processes as promising targets for therapy after betrayal.
plos-pone-0353762:
Maduko and colleagues, in a 2026 study, listen to communities in Enugu, Nigeria, about how they use antibiotics. Drug resistance grows fastest where antibiotics are sold loosely and clinics are hard to reach. The team combined a large survey with interviews and group talks to hear the grassroots view.

More than half of the survey respondents had used antibiotics in the past six months, often without a prescription and for illnesses that are not bacterial, including malaria. Nearly half of users dosed themselves, mostly buying from chemist shops. Very few people had heard of resistance, and many confused it with fake drugs or allergy. Some reported stark new uses, such as taking antibiotics to end a pregnancy or as a preventive cleanse. Poverty, weak access, and loose selling rules fed the habits. Participants themselves suggested radio jingles, teaching through religious leaders, and firmer control of drug sales.
plos-pone-0353862:
Kassouha and colleagues identified the virus behind recent cattle outbreaks in Syria in a 2026 study. Foot-and-mouth disease spreads fast among farm animals and threatens milk, meat, and farm income. Samples from blister fluid and mouth swabs were taken at six cattle farms in two regions during January 2026, despite an ongoing vaccine program.

All six farms tested positive for a virus type not confirmed in Syria before by gene testing. Two samples were read in full and matched each other closely, and both grouped with recent strains reported in nearby countries. Naming the exact type matters because vaccines must match the strain in the field to protect herds well.
plos-pone-0354162:
Tang and colleagues, in a 2026 study, look inside a desert plant that survives as a parasite on other roots in northwestern China. Cynomorium songaricum stores nutrients in a fleshy stem wrapped in a thin outer skin. The team asked whether its building blocks, amino acids, are shared evenly between the two tissues or split by job.

The split was clear. The outer skin held more of several key amino acids tied to daily function, while the fleshy stem stockpiled two others known to help plants endure stress. Each tissue also answered to different surroundings: the skin's mix tracked water features in the soil, while the stem's mix tracked soil salts. Even though the plant feeds from a host, its tissues tune their chemistry to local conditions. The authors say treating a plant as one uniform body misses this teamwork.
plos-pone-0354262:
Gonçalves and colleagues, in a 2026 study, examine whether political ideology in Brazil shapes what Indigenous schools teach. By law, these schools must weave Indigenous culture and languages into lessons. More than three thousand such schools serve Indigenous communities nationwide. The team analyzed school census data from 2009 to 2022 to see whether practice matched the law, and how it shifted with the government in power.

Non-compliance was widespread: many schools fell short of the legal duty to teach culture and native languages. The shortfall was not random. Periods under far-right administrations lined up with stronger suppression of cultural materials and languages in the data. Statistical checks, from simple tests to layered models, pointed the same way. The authors argue that cultural erosion in these schools is partly a political product, and that protecting Indigenous education requires shielding curricula from swings in ruling ideology.
plos-pone-0354362:
Uma Maheswari S and Jagatheswari S published this 2026 methods paper on fixing dark, low-contrast color photos. Dim images often lose detail and true color, and simple brightening can wash them out. Their approach first converts a photo into a special fuzzy form that handles pixel uncertainty more flexibly, then applies a local contrast technique.

On benchmark image sets, the combined method scored well on measures of detail, brightness error, and similarity to the original scene. It held its own against existing enhancement tools. Better low-light cleanup matters for phone cameras, security footage, and medical scans taken under poor lighting.
plos-pone-0354462: Workplace interventions — for work-related and mental health outcomes — needed systematic mapping. This scoping review protocol outlines it. The planned synthesis will reveal which occupational interventions genuinely protect workers’ bodies and minds.
plos-pone-0355162:
Juan Suárez and co-authors evaluate in 2026 the nutritional worth of common bean lines bred by crossing five related bean species, grown under acid soil and heat stress in Colombia's Amazon region. More than a hundred lines were tested for protein, fibre parts, and minerals such as iron and zinc, then grouped by their strengths. A new index combined helpful and harmful traits into one selection score.

Lines rich in iron and zinc scored highest on average, and two named lines stood out overall. A tepary type species supplied most high fibre lines. The index correlated well with protein and key minerals, helping breeders pick parents for more nutritious beans.
plos-pone-0355362:
Marius P Ngouanom Kuate led a team of eight authors studying a toxin-making fungus in Yaoundé, Cameroon, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The fungus, Aspergillus flavus, spoils food with toxins and also infects people. The team sampled it from different ecological niches around the city and tested how it responds to antifungal drugs.

Kuate's group compared the strains' genes and their drug responses side by side. Local data like this tell doctors which drugs are likely to work on local infections. They also tell food safety staff which strain types dominate in local settings. Both uses depend on local evidence, since fungus populations differ a great deal from place to place.
plos-pone-0355462:
Tanvir Turin and colleagues surveyed foreign-trained doctors in Canada about considering work outside clinical medicine. Many international medical graduates face long odds in matching to residency posts, so some weigh alternative careers that still use their training. Their 2026 analysis drew on more than twelve hundred complete survey responses.

Well over half of respondents were considering alternative pathways. Consideration was highest among doctors aged fifty and over, where three quarters were looking beyond clinical roles. Doctors many years past graduation were also more likely to consider alternatives. Sex and length of stay in Canada showed no clear link. Turin and colleagues say tailored career support could help these doctors contribute sooner.
plos-pone-0355562:
Joanne Hall and colleagues ask which balanced number arrays can be grown by simple local rules called cellular automata. The arrays, named F-squares, hold each symbol equally often in every row and column, a property prized in experiment design. Their 2026 paper works over the two-symbol case and studies row and column totals.

Careful attention goes to column and row pairs whose codes differ in just one position. Two families of local rules turn out to guarantee the equal totals: rules that shuffle symbols bijectively and rules that stay constant. The punchline is restrictive. Every F-square an automaton can generate this way is either a Latin square, where each symbol appears once per line, or a trivial case.
plos-pone-0355862:
Dhinakaran Veeman and colleagues asked whether machine learning can predict the hardness of 3D-printed medical plastic parts. The plastic, known as PMMA, is favoured for prosthetics and dental work because the body tolerates it well. Testing each printed part by hand is slow and costly, and print settings strongly affect strength.

Their 2026 study varied layer height, fill density, fill pattern, and line direction, then trained models on the measured hardness. The analysis shows how each setting pushes hardness up or down. Veeman and colleagues conclude that learned models can stand in for many physical tests. That shift could let clinics tune print settings on screen before committing to a final part.
plos-pone-0355962:
Chishun Zhou led a team of eight authors tracing how a plant compound reaches cancer cell nuclei, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Kaempferol, found in many vegetables, can fight colon cancer, but only if it gets inside the cell nucleus where genes are controlled. The team studied the enzymes and transporters that move it there.

Zhou's group showed that metabolic enzymes and efflux transporters together orchestrate kaempferol's nuclear entry, and that this entry suppresses colorectal cancer growth. Knowing the transport route reveals how to make the compound work harder, perhaps by blocking its removal. Natural compounds often fail as drugs for delivery reasons, not potency. This study attacks the delivery problem directly.
plos-pone-0356062:
Chunye Yang, Xuedong Yu, and Hongshun Li model how motivation, study tactics, and word stock hang together for Chinese university English learners, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Two hundred thirty students who were not English majors answered surveys on motivation and on memory, mental, and planning tactics, and took a standard word stock test. The authors fitted a model to see which arrows between the three truly carry weight.

Students reported motivation a touch below the scale's middle and favored mental tactics, such as using words in sentences, over the other kinds. Motivation strongly drove tactic use. It also lifted word stock directly, by a fair amount. Tactics themselves, surprisingly, did not predict word stock. No side path through tactics appeared either. The practical moral is unfashionable: wanting to learn English grows word knowledge more reliably than the memory tricks students adopt along the way.
plos-pone-0356262:
Maria Betânia Niehues and seven colleagues test alternatives to a common antibiotic feed additive in feedlot cattle, in this 2026 trial from Brazil. Monensin helps control rumen acidity on grain-heavy diets, but rules and consumer pressure favor natural options. Twenty-four crossbred bulls were assigned to monensin, a blend of essential oils with an enzyme, or that blend plus a vitamin D compound, and followed through finishing.

Both natural blends raised feed intake and carcass weight compared with monensin, with no loss of feed efficiency and no harm to meat quality. Cattle on the blends kept a healthier rumen acidity, spending less time at dangerously low pH, and had cooler rumens. The vitamin D addition brought little extra benefit. The authors conclude the essential oil blend is a credible replacement for monensin in feedlot diets.
plos-pone-0356362:
A. T. M. Ahsanul Kyum Siam and two colleagues hunt for the drivers of childbirth at risky ages in Bangladesh, in this 2026 analysis of a national health survey. Giving birth at eighteen or younger, or at forty or older, raises dangers for mother and child. The team applied machine learning to records of more than fifteen thousand ever-married women, trying several ways of picking the most useful predictors.

A gradient boosting model fed with statistically selected features performed best overall. The strongest predictors included early marriage, the mother's own age, contraceptive use, the number of children, and the husband's age, job, and schooling. Regional gaps mattered too. The authors use these results to argue for practical steps: delaying first births, expanding girls' education, and focusing help on the districts where risky-age births cluster.
plos-pone-0356462:
Shixiu Liu and colleagues assessed how well nurses who care for elderly patients cope with death itself. They surveyed 203 geriatric nurses at a hospital in Kunming, China. They also interviewed them about end-of-life care, in a culture where death is often taboo. Their 2026 mixed-methods study used a validated coping scale. It covered six abilities, from reviewing life to discussing one's own death.

Overall coping landed at a moderate level. Nurses scored highest on life review. They scored lowest, by a wide margin, on discussing other people's deaths. The study's second half develops death education strategies shaped to the local culture rather than imported wholesale. As China's population ages, the authors argue, nurses' own relationship with death becomes a quality-of-care issue.
plos-pone-0356562:
Jia Liu and three colleagues look inside the kneecap tendons of elite volleyball players in this 2026 study. Repeated jump-landings remodel these tendons, and the far end of the tendon is rarely examined. Ultrasound scans of more than one hundred thirty athletes measured tendon thickness and how orderly the collagen fibers were, at both the near and far ends. The team also recorded body measurements and joint flexibility tests, plus a single-leg squat.

About half the athletes had tendon pain, and their near-end collagen was measurably less organized. Near-end organization also declined with more years of play. At the far end, disorganization tracked with stiffer ankles and hips and with greater body weight, height, and waist-to-hip ratio, though effects were modest. The authors say tendon health in jumping athletes reflects a whole-body profile, and they urge broader biomechanical follow-up.
plos-pone-0356762:
Daniel Alzate and colleagues validated a whole-exome sequencing pipeline that can diagnose inherited cancer risk in triple-negative breast cancer patients straight from the same test used on their tumors. Their 2026 study built a curated panel of cancer susceptibility genes, proved the pipeline on twenty-five patients with already-confirmed hereditary diagnoses, then applied it to twenty-four triple-negative patients.

One patient in eight in the discovery group carried a harmful inherited variant, landing in three genes that all serve the cell's main DNA repair pathway. The result matters clinically: such diagnoses change a patient's own treatment and trigger testing for relatives. The authors show a single exome test can carry both jobs, tumor profiling and germline answers.
plos-pone-0357262:
Qimeng Chen and co-authors study how the shape of a laser pulse changes the way it blasts metal away, pairing computer simulation with bench tests. They fired single pulses at a common aluminum alloy and compared a standard bell-shaped pulse with a flatter, more even one. Simulations tracked heat spread, plasma growth, and how much metal each pulse removed across energy levels and spot sizes.

The flatter pulse coupled energy into the metal more efficiently and removed more material under the same settings, thanks to its even spread. Test results from their lab laser matched a commercial laser closely, which supports the model. Chen and colleagues argue that shaping pulses is a direct lever for cleaner, steadier laser cutting and drilling in factories.
plos-pone-0357462:
Admire Hlupeni and co-authors pool results from randomized trials to ask how long patients should take two blood-thinning drugs after a stent opens a heart artery. Long courses prevent clots but raise bleeding risk, and modern stents may need shorter cover. Their network analysis compares one, three, six, and twelve month courses across many trials with tens of thousands of patients.

Shorter courses matched the year-long course on major heart events, with no clear penalty at any shorter length. Bleeding, however, fell clearly with one and three month courses, and the three month option ranked best at balancing both risks. Hlupeni and colleagues say the evidence supports shorter therapy for many patients with current stents, chosen with their doctors.
plos-pone-0357562:
Tamara O Gordeeva and two colleagues studied family life and school outcomes in teenagers, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. They asked how family structure and how satisfied teens feel with family life relate to self-driven motivation, cheating, and achievement at school. The three outcomes rarely get studied together.

Gordeeva's team traced what home life contributes to each outcome. Their findings help separate what families can influence from what schools must handle themselves. The cheating link is of special interest: pressure and satisfaction at home may shape honesty under strain. For counselors and parents, the study offers a grounded view of how the climate at home reaches into the classroom, for better and for worse.
plos-pone-0357662:
Jiawei Wang led a team of five authors evaluating a Chinese rural education program, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The program, nicknamed One Village, One University Student, trains local people to degree level so they return skills to their home villages. The team asked whether that training strengthens farmers' social capital, their networks of trust and help.

Wang's group weighed evidence on whether villages gain stronger community ties from the program. Social capital decides much in rural life, from getting loans to organizing shared work. If trained returnees weave stronger networks, the program's value goes beyond one person's career. The study helps officials judge a long-running scheme on community effects, not just graduation counts.
plos-pone-0357762:
Sophie Orchard and colleagues published in 2026 the protocol for a worldwide review of brain injury acquired during childhood and youth. Acquired brain injury covers damage from falls, road crashes, infections, and strokes, and it is a major cause of lasting disability in the young. Surprisingly, no one has pinned down solid global figures for how often it occurs and how many live with it.

Their systematic review and meta-analysis protocol fixes in advance how studies will be found, judged, and combined to produce those figures. Publishing the plan first keeps the review transparent and repeatable. Reliable global numbers would help governments argue for prevention, from safer roads to helmets, and for the rehabilitation services injured children need.
plos-pone-0357962:
Erika Gazzetta and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for evaluating a pilot that brings artificial intelligence ultrasound to pregnancy care in Zambia. Knowing a baby's age in the womb accurately guides care, but scanners, infrastructure, and trained staff are scarce in low-income settings. The PIKABU program will place portable, AI-enabled ultrasound devices in six antenatal clinics across three districts of Lusaka Province, and this protocol sets out how its rollout will be judged.

The evaluation mixes methods: focus groups, interviews, register reviews, time-and-motion observation, strategy checks, and patient exit surveys, repeated at baseline and every four months. Patients, community members, and health workers all take part, and the study asks three questions throughout: do people accept the service, can clinics deliver it, and is it delivered as designed? The authors expect lessons for other resource-limited health systems weighing similar technology.
plos-pone-0358362:
Nanako Yamada leads a team of eight identifying an unexpected killer of the brain's insulation cells, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Oligodendrocytes wrap nerve fibers in myelin, and their death drives diseases such as multiple sclerosis. Most known attackers are secretions of immune and support cells. This team suspected neurons themselves, focusing on chromogranin B, a protein neurons package and release, better known from hormone secreting tissue.

Adding the purified protein, mouse or human versions alike, to cultured oligodendrocytes and their precursor cells drove many of them into programmed death. An antibody against the protein blocked the effect. In mixed cultures, the protein naturally secreted by neurons did the same damage, and the antibody rescued the cells again. The finding adds neurons to the list of suspects in myelin loss and names a possible drug target that no one had aimed at.
plos-pone-0358562:
Weijian Liu leads a team of eight building software to pick tremor events out of very noisy seismic recordings, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Microseismic monitoring listens for tiny rock fractures in mines and reservoirs, but under heavy noise the start and end of each event blur. Their model reshapes a standard segmentation network with an attention module that reweights signal channels toward event boundaries, and stretches one dimensional waveforms into a form two dimensional networks can read.

Validated on acoustic emission data from rock compression tests, the system segmented events with accuracy near ninety-nine percent, about a point above its parent network. Under strong noise, four fifths of start picks and nine tenths of end picks landed within a tight tolerance. It also outscored a recognized rival method on both detection quality measures reported. Reliable boundaries are what turn raw rumble into usable warnings about rock under stress.
plos-pone-0358762:
V D Meena leads a team of eight tuning nitrogen fertilizer for mustard with a handheld crop sensor, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Over fertilizing wastes money and leaks a potent greenhouse gas, yet blanket dose advice ignores how each field is actually growing. Across four winter seasons, the team compared nine nitrogen strategies plus an unfertilized control, including sensor guided dosing built on a rate chart they developed for target yields.

The sensor treatment reads leaf greenness to judge plant nitrogen status in real time. It raised seed yield by more than a fifth. It also used about a fifth less nitrogen than the standard recommended dose. Farm profits and nitrogen efficiency measures improved alongside. The authors argue that reading the crop, rather than the calendar, lets mustard growers cut emissions and input costs without surrendering harvest, a pattern worth testing on other oilseed farms.
plos-pone-0358862:
Liangming Jia, Qisen Zhang, Weimin Zhai, Zhongzhen Lin, and Shasha Li wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It concerns smart homes and the control screens older adults use to run them. The authors study how these adults judge different screen designs.

The work runs in several stages and looks at appearance dimensions, the visual qualities of a screen, alongside behavioral intentions, what users say they would do with it. A design that looks confusing can stop an older person from using helpful home technology at all. Designers of age-friendly devices are the audience for evidence linking looks to willingness to use.
plos-pone-0359862:
Lucía Martínez-Salvador and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on foot mechanics. The condition is bilateral pes cavus, high arches in both feet. In a case-control study, the authors examine dynamic gait phase alterations, changes in the stages of walking, plus spatiotemporal stance characteristics, the timing and spacing of each stance.

Comparing walkers with high arches against controls shows where their gait departs from the usual pattern. Such departures explain pain and instability that a static foot exam cannot. Podiatrists and gait laboratories deciding on orthotics or therapy are the readers for stance-level detail like this.
plos-pone-0359962:
Syed Shaukat Ali Muttaqi Shah and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on child health in Baghdad, Iraq.
