pmc-3218662:
Anders and Huber present methods for differential expression analysis of sequence count data. Assays such as RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq give quantitative readouts as counts of reads per gene or region. To spot real differences in such data with good statistical power, variability must be estimated well across the full range of values.

Weak handling of noisy low counts can fake effects or bury real ones. Their approach models count variation carefully, forming the basis of the widely used DESeq package. Sound count statistics underpin thousands of gene activity studies in medicine and biology.
pmc-3507962:
Norman, Byambaa, De, and co-authors systematically review the long-term health consequences of child physical abuse, emotional abuse, and neglect. Child maltreatment was often treated as a childhood problem alone. The authors ask how it relates to mental and physical health in later life.

They pool evidence across studies on outcomes such as depression, anxiety, and chronic disease. Their meta-analysis strengthens the case that abuse and neglect cast long shadows over adult health. Such numbers help policymakers justify early protection and support as long-term health investments.  Effects persisted decades after childhood, underlining the value of intervening as early as possible.
pmc-3818162:
Ferrari, Charlson, Norman, and co-authors report the burden of depressive disorders from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2010. They analysed burden by country, sex, age, and year. Their analysis identifies depressive disorders among the leading causes of burden worldwide.

The paper presents how severity is distributed and how burden differs between regions and groups over time. Such breakdowns show where treatment gaps hurt most and which age groups carry the heaviest load. The findings strengthened calls to treat depression as a major public health priority, not a private trouble.
pmc-4248462:
Korneliussen, Albrechtsen, and Nielsen presented ANGSD in 2014, a program suite for next generation sequencing data. High-throughput machines were producing vast amounts of DNA data. Labs needed fast, flexible tools that used memory well enough to handle thousands of samples at once.

ANGSD runs several tasks in parallel threads to keep speed up on large jobs. It works with the uncertainty in low-depth reads instead of pretending each call is sure. That matters for population genetics, where many samples are read only lightly. The suite lets researchers study variation across whole populations without first forcing the data into hard genotype calls.
pmc-4676162:
Finak, McDavid, Yajima, and their co-authors presented MAST in 2015 for single-cell RNA data. Reading gene expression one cell at a time reveals variety that bulk samples hide. The data are tricky, though, with random dropout and a split pattern where a gene reads as strong or not at all.

MAST is a flexible statistical framework built for that two-part pattern. It models whether a gene is detected and how strongly, in one system. That lets researchers test for real transcriptional changes and describe heterogeneity between cells. Sound handling of single-cell quirks is vital as the method spreads into immunology, cancer, and development studies.
pmc-5447962:
Wee and Wang reviewed EGFR signaling in 2017. EGFR is a receptor on the cell surface that passes growth signals inward. It is switched on too strongly in many cancers, among them lung, bowel, brain, head and neck, pancreatic, and breast tumors.

The review maps the paths by which EGFR drives cell growth and division. Tumors raise its activity in many ways, from gene copies to changes in the gene itself. Those paths explain why EGFR is a prime drug target, with drugs that block it in wide use. They also explain how tumors learn to resist those drugs, which shapes the design of the next drugs in line.
pmc-5697162:
Igor Puzanov and many colleagues wrote these shared recommendations in 2017 for the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer. Immune checkpoint drugs have changed cancer care by freeing the immune system to attack tumors. Their growing use also brought a distinct set of immune side effects.

The guidance explains how to spot and grade these side effects in organs such as the gut, lungs, liver, and skin. It gives steps for holding treatment, using steroids, and calling in specialists. Because the side effects can look like other illnesses, clear rules help teams act fast. Clinicians use this document as a bedside reference.
randolph-dealings-with-the-dead-1862:
Paschal Beverly Randolph launched his strange career with Dealings with the Dead, his book of 1862. Randolph was a Black sage, healer, and seer in the United States. He claimed gifts of sight and a rank in the Rosy Cross. Here he tells of talks with the dead and what they taught him.

Grief, hope, and the fate of the soul fill the pages. His voice is bold, warm, and sure of its path. The book is the first stone of the Rosy Cross in his land. It shows a rare, brave mind at work. Randolph sailed, wed, and built bands in a life of bold turns. He wrote as he lived: fast, warm, and sure of his strange path.
rousseau-social-contract-1762: Rousseau's 1762 Social Contract argues legitimate rule rests on the general will. It fueled revolutions. The Tower library holds the full text. It crowned the people. Kings trembled. Citizens ruled. Will reigned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
sendschreiben-an-einen-durchlauchtigsten: Sendschreiben an einen durchlauchtigsten Prinz, 1762. The princely letter. This book preserves that epistle. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
spencer-first-principles-1862:
Herbert Spencer published First Principles in 1862, the opening volume of his System of Synthetic Philosophy. Spencer argues that evolution is a universal law for all things. Matter integrates and motion dissipates, from nebulae to societies and minds. His phrase survival of the fittest, coined here, became famous worldwide.

The first part treats the unknowable, the realm beyond science and religion alike. The second part states the laws of the knowable in abstract form. Spencer aimed to unify all science under one principle. Later science outgrew much of the system. The book remains a bold monument of Victorian system-building.
stowe-agnes-of-sorrento-1862:
Agnes of Sorrento appeared in 1862 and stands here as volume seven of Stowe's Riverside writings. The setting is Italy in the 1400s, in the seaside town of Sorrento. Young Agnes grows up in a devout home while the fierce preacher Savonarola shakes the cities near her.

Love, faith, and harsh church power cross in her story as she is pulled toward a convent. A young cavalier pulls her heart the other way, toward life and marriage. Stowe wrote the novel while grieving a son lost in the Civil War, by the v1 account. Its thoughts on suffering and faith run deeper than most of her tales.
stowe-pearl-orrs-island-1862:
Stowe set The Pearl of Orr's Island on the coast of Maine, where she spent her summers. Copyright dates of 1862 and 1890 appear in this Riverside Press printing of 1896. The tale centers on young Mara Lincoln, raised among fishermen and sailors on the island.

Her quiet love story unfolds against storms, wrecks, and the steady rhythms of seafaring life. Stowe writes with deep fondness for New England's maritime people and their hard, plain ways. Reform takes a back seat here to place, character, and the sea that shapes both. Many readers judge it her most purely lovely novel.
targum-onkelos-etheridge-1862:
J. W. Etheridge translated the Targum of Onkelos into English in 1862. Onkelos is the official Aramaic rendering of the Torah, the five books of Moses. Synagogues read it beside the Hebrew text for many centuries.

Aramaic had replaced Hebrew in daily speech for many ancient Jews. The Targum let congregations follow scripture in their own tongue. Onkelos stays close to the Hebrew while softening hard expressions about God. Etheridge's translation opened this ancient paraphrase to English readers in two volumes. The work is the oldest bridge between the Hebrew Bible and its first audience. Students of biblical interpretation still consult it regularly.
the-great-american-crisis-or-cause-and-c: The Great American Crisis, 1862. The rebellion's cause and cure. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Book twelve of Casanova’s memoirs: new cities and new loves for the rover. The Venetian adventure rolls on without pause. The endless tale, ever fresh. The endless tale, ever fresh and lively, ever fresh and lively to the end.
timon-of-athens-pg2262: The gold speech curses in this edition: Timon, ruined by flatterers, digs roots and rails at Athens over yellow, glittering, precious gold. The misanthrope’s fury is bitter and magnificent, and Apemantus the cynic stands as his dark mirror.
tob-14462:
The Mahatma Letters are letters said to come from hidden masters, Koot Hoomi and Morya, to A. P. Sinnett and A. O. Hume in the 1880s. They arrived by odd means in India, through Helena Blavatsky's circle. No set of papers in theosophy has stirred more debate.

The letters teach theosophical cosmology: rounds of worlds, root races, karma, and the hidden brotherhood guiding mankind. They also give sharp personal advice and scolding to the two Englishmen. Believers treat them as scripture of the movement; critics call them fakes. Either way, they shaped the Theosophical Society from its early years.
tob-4162:
Max Muller delivered four lectures at the Royal Institution in London to introduce a new field: the science of religion. Published in book form in 1882, the lectures argue that faiths can be studied side by side, with the same calm methods used on language or nature. Contempt and blind belief both bar the way.

Muller sorts religions, traces their growth, and pleads for fairness toward creeds not one's own. His own field, the tongues of India, supplies much of the evidence. Verified from the 1919 edition, the lectures state the great orientalist's method plainly. Comparative religion as a discipline starts, in public, here.
turgenev-fathers-and-sons-1862:
Ivan Turgenev published Fathers and Sons in 1862, the novel that named an age's philosophy in one word, nihilism. The nihilist Bazarov clashes with the older generation in a book that angered young and old alike on publication. Turgenev claimed to love Bazarov most, though critics of both camps accused him of betrayal.

Arkady brings his friend Bazarov, a medical student, home to his father Nikolai and uncle Pavel. Bazarov scorns art, authority, and romance, dissects frogs, and duels Pavel over a morning's insult at Marino. He loves the cool widow Odintsova, is refused, and dies of typhus caught at a peasant's autopsy, asking her blessing at home. His parents' grief at the village grave closes a book far tenderer than its famous label suggests to most readers. The novel remains the classic account of a generation gap.
un-ga-res-1962:
Space had just opened to mankind when the General Assembly set its first rules of law in Resolution 1962, adopted on 13 December 1963. The text is a declaration of legal principles for the work of states in space. It hails the vast prospects that man's entry into space has opened, and the shared stake of all mankind in its peaceful study and use.

Space work, the principles hold, must serve the good of all states, rich or poor in science and wealth. Joint work in space, both in science and in law, will build trust and warm ties between peoples. These nine principles became the seed of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, still the base law of space.
un-ga-res-68-262:
Crimea's seizure by Russia in 2014 met a wall of votes in Resolution 68/262, adopted by the General Assembly that March. The text puts the Charter first: no state may threaten or use force against the land or freedom of another, and rows must be settled by peaceful means. It recalls the 1970 pledge that land taken by force is no lawful gain.

Ukraine's unity and land, within its known borders, are backed in full. The hasty vote staged in Crimea under Russian guns is held to have no force, and states are urged not to accept the change it claimed to make. One hundred states backed the text, with eleven against. The stand still frames the UN map of Ukraine.
un-ga-res-a-69-62:
Arms deals struck in the shadows are the target of Resolution A/69/62, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Illicit brokering, the fixing of arms sales off the books, can slip past the world's arms and spread controls. Left unchecked, the text warns, it will harm peace, drag out wars, and block fair growth. Worse, it can feed arms to terror groups and put mass-kill goods in their hands.

States are called to bar and fight such brokering in all its forms. The ban must cover not just standard arms, but goods and know-how that could feed mass-kill weapons and the missiles that carry them. Lawful arms trade, and lawful joint work on such goods, must not be hurt by the fight.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1761 (XVII) was adopted on 6 November 1962. It condemned the apartheid policies of the Government of the Republic of South Africa. The Assembly noted that South Africa had ignored repeated calls to drop racial segregation. The calls came from both the Assembly and the Security Council. The Assembly said those policies put world peace and security at risk.

To press for change, members were asked to break off diplomatic ties. They were asked to close ports to South African ships and boycott South African goods. They were also asked to stop arms exports there. The resolution created a Special Committee on apartheid. It was to watch South African racial policy between sessions and report back. The resolution also asked the Security Council to weigh sanctions.

General Assembly Resolution 1962 (XVIII), adopted on 13 December 1963, is the Declaration of Legal Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space. With human flight into space newly begun, the Assembly set out shared rules meant to keep that work peaceful and open to all.

The principles state that space work must serve all mankind. They state that space and the Moon and planets are free for all states to use, and cannot be claimed by any country. They state that states answer for their own space acts. Launching states are liable for harm their objects cause. Astronauts are to be treated as envoys of mankind and helped in distress.

UN General Assembly Resolution 68/262 — the landmark 2014 resolution affirming Ukraine’s territorial integrity after Russia’s annexation of Crimea. It declared the referendum invalid. The 2014 Crimea affirmation is the landmark declaration: the Russian annexation’s referendum formally declared invalid here.

Adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, Resolution 69/62 addresses the prevention of illicit brokering in arms and sensitive materials. It calls on states to put national laws and measures in place covering brokering in conventional arms. The laws must also cover goods and technology that could feed weapons of mass destruction. It draws on the recommendations of a group of governmental experts. It points to article 10 of the Arms Trade Treaty as a model for regulating brokers.
un-sc-res-1162: For Sierra Leone, the Council's answer came in Resolution 1162, adopted on 17 April 1998. The elected president had returned on 10 March after West African troops drove out the junta. The Council authorizes up to ten United Nations military liaison and security advisers to deploy at once for ninety days. They will work with the government and the West African force, report on the military picture, and help plan disarmament of former fighters. The text also urges urgent aid for civilians and funds for the peace effort.
un-sc-res-1362:
Prevlaka's observer mission was renewed in the summer of 2001. On 11 July 2001 the Security Council authorized UNMOP to keep monitoring the peninsula. The zone between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia stayed demilitarized. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission that month. Talks between the two governments on the disputed ground had resumed. The Council welcomed that step warmly.

Both parties had to stop breaking the demilitarized regime. They had to work with the observers and guard their safety and free movement. The Council urged them to settle the Prevlaka question by negotiation, fast and in good faith. Trust-building steps between the sides earned encouragement. The mission was small, but it kept a border quarrel cold.
un-sc-res-1462:
Georgia's observer mission was renewed with sharper words on status on 30 January 2003. The Secretary-General's report of 13 January lay before the Council. A UNOMIG helicopter had been shot down on 8 October 2001, killing nine people, and the killers were still unknown. The lack of progress on a settlement was called unacceptable. UNOMIG and the CIS force kept the zone steady between them.

The Council extended UNOMIG's mandate for a further six months. It restated that Abkhazia's status had to be defined inside the state of Georgia. The paper on basic principles for dividing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi won strong backing again. The Abkhaz side's repeated refusal to discuss the paper's substance drew deep regret. Status talks had to begin, and both sides would need to give ground. The Council stressed that no settlement could stand on the population changes the war had forced.
un-sc-res-1562: Resolution 1562, from 2004, is a Security Council decision kept here in its official-record wording. English Wikisource is the source of the transcription. The Council's format holds steady across subjects: a preamble weighing the facts, then operative paragraphs that decide. Reading the voted text itself is the surest way to know what the members actually agreed.
un-sc-res-162: Jordan's complaint against Israel was taken up by the Security Council on 11 April 1961. Jordan had filed its complaint on 1 April. The Israel-Jordan Mixed Armistice Commission had ruled on the matter on 20 March 1961. The Council endorsed that decision. It urged Israel to comply with the ruling. It also asked the commission's members to cooperate so the General Armistice Agreement between Israel and Jordan would be obeyed. The short text only backs the armistice body's verdict and presses the parties to work through it.
un-sc-res-1662:
Afghanistan's assistance mission was renewed under the Compact on 23 March 2006. The London Conference of January and February had launched the Afghanistan Compact. Parliamentary and provincial elections had been held on 18 September 2005, closing the Bonn process. The Secretary-General's report of 7 March set out the mission's next mandate. Security, governance, development, and counter-narcotics were judged to stand or fall together.

The Council welcomed the United Nations' long-term pledge to work beside the Afghan people. It extended UNAMA's mandate as laid out in the Secretary-General's report, for twelve months. Kabul and the international partners were called to carry out the Compact in full and on time. The Compact's benchmarks and timelines had to be met. All Afghan parties were called to join the political process in a constructive spirit and shun violence. Progress in disarming and reintegrating fighters was welcomed.
un-sc-res-1762:
Iraq's weapons inspectors are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1762, adopted on 29 June 2007. The vote passed with fourteen in favor and one abstention. Inspectors had not set foot in Iraq since the 2003 invasion. The United States and United Kingdom stated that Iraq's known banned weapons had been destroyed.

The Council ends the mandates of UNMOVIC and the atomic energy agency in Iraq at once. The agency's nuclear verification office in Iraq also closes. Leftover inspection funds move to the Development Fund for Iraq within three months. UNMOVIC's archives must stay under strict control, above all its sensitive proliferation files. Iraq should report within one year on joining the main disarmament treaties.
un-sc-res-1862:
Djibouti and Eritrea's border clash brought a deadline for Asmara on 14 January 2009. Eritrea had attacked at Ras Doumeira in June 2008 and kept its forces on Djibouti's side of the line. A fact-finding mission had reported in September 2008. Djibouti had pulled its troops back and cooperated fully. Eritrea refused dialogue, mediation, and every offer of good offices.

The Council urged both states to settle the border dispute in peace and welcomed the Secretary-General's offer to help. It demanded that Eritrea pull its forces back to the positions held before the clash. Eritrea also had to admit the dispute existed, restore dialogue, and free or account for Djibouti's missing soldiers. It had to comply within five weeks of the text's adoption at the latest. The Secretary-General owed the Council a report on the parties' conduct within six weeks.
un-sc-res-262:
Lebanon brought a grave complaint to the Council at the end of 1968. Israeli forces had attacked the civil international airport at Beirut. On 31 December 1968 the Council condemned that attack. It called the raid premeditated, large in scale, and carefully planned. Truce supervision officials had supplied extra detail on what took place.

The Council warned Israel in solemn terms. If such acts were repeated, it would weigh further steps. It also held that Lebanon had suffered damage in the raid. Israel, it noted, had acknowledged responsibility for that harm. The text closes with concern for free international air traffic.
un-sc-res-362: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 362, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 1974. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-562:
Nicaragua's sovereignty and the Contadora peace effort were backed on 10 May 1985. Nicaragua's envoy addressed the Council, and many states joined the debate. The General Assembly had urged full cooperation with the Contadora Group, the regional mediation effort. Talks between Washington and Managua at Manzanillo had stalled.

The Council restated the sovereign right of Nicaragua and other states to choose their own political, economic, and social systems free of outside pressure. It voiced firm support for the Contadora Group and urged it to press its work harder. All states were called to carry out no political, economic, or military action against any state in the region meant to coerce it. The United States and Nicaragua were called to resume their Manzanillo dialogue, in a climate good for frank and constructive talks. The Secretary-General would keep the Council informed.
un-sc-res-62:
Truce must grow into armistice in Palestine, ruled Security Council Resolution 62, passed on 16 November 1948. The text recalls the chain of past calls for a truce in the land. It recalls above all the vote of 15 July, which held the state of Palestine to be a threat to the peace under Article 39 of the Charter. The Assembly was still at work on the land's future rule.

An armistice must now be set in all parts of Palestine, the Council rules. That step will clear the threat to the peace and ease the path from truce to a lasting peace. The sides in the fight are called to seek such armistice deals at once, through the Acting Mediator's work. The deals struck in 1949 close the first Arab-Israeli war on this base.
un-sc-res-662:
Iraq had declared a complete and eternal merger with occupied Kuwait. On 9 August 1990 the Security Council answered that claim. It recalled its demand that Iraq pull all forces out of Kuwait. It restated its goal of restoring Kuwait's sovereignty and its lawful government. The vote was unanimous.

The Council decided that the annexation has no legal validity at all. It is null and void under any form or pretext. All states and organizations must refuse to recognize it. They must also avoid any act that hints at recognition. Iraq had to cancel its annexation moves. The item stayed on the Council's agenda.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A small UN military team is sent to Sierra Leone in Resolution 1162, adopted on 17 April 1998. The democratically elected president had returned on 10 March 1998. ECOMOG forces were restoring security. The Secretary-General's 18 March report proposed strengthening his Special Envoy's office in Freetown with civilian and military staff.

The Council authorizes up to ten United Nations military liaison and security advisory personnel to deploy immediately for up to ninety days, under the Special Envoy's authority. Working closely with the government and ECOMOG, they must report on the military situation and check conditions. They must help finalize ECOMOG's planning, including identifying former combatants to be disarmed and designing a disarmament plan. The Council welcomes talks on ECOMOG's concept of operations. It urges urgent humanitarian aid under the March inter-agency appeal. It asks states to fund the peacekeeping trust fund and give ECOMOG technical and logistical support.

Oil did not drive this text, whatever some lists may say. Its stage is the Prevlaka cape in Croatia. UN men had watched the cape's bare-of-arms state since 1992. Trade posts in the zone hummed with calm use. The two states' chiefs met in Italy in June 2001 and swore to heal ties. Resolution 1362 passed with no dissent on 11 July 2001.

The watch ran to 15 January 2002. Breaches of the bare zone had to end. The UN men needed free range and safe work. Talks on the cape's fate had just restarted. Both sides were urged to push them to a swift, fair end. News of the talks was due each two months. The NATO-led force near by and the UN men had to work as one. A chief's report of 3 July had paved the way.

Resolution 1462, adopted on 30 January 2003, deals with the conflict over Abkhazia in Georgia. The UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, worked beside a CIS peacekeeping force to keep the area steady. Talks on Abkhazia's status inside Georgia had stalled, and the Council recalled the 2001 shooting down of a UNOMIG helicopter, which killed nine people and was still unsolved.

The Council extends UNOMIG's mandate to 31 July 2003. It backs a paper on sharing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi as a basis for real talks, and it deplores the Abkhaz side's refusal to discuss it. It presses both sides to revive the peace process, guard patrols in the Kodori Valley, and focus on letting refugees and displaced people return home safely.

Sierra Leone's mission enters its final phase in this text of 17 September 2004. UNAMSIL is extended until 30 June 2005. Drawdown benchmarks had been met further, and a smaller residual presence would stay from 1 January 2005 for an initial six months. Building Sierra Leone's own police and army remained the key gap.

The residual force is given a set list of tasks, including watching the security situation, supporting elections, and backing the police and military as they take over. It may use all necessary means, within its means and areas, to carry out that mandate. The government is again urged to build lasting security institutions so it can assume full responsibility as soon as possible.

One armistice row in Jerusalem fills Resolution 162. It passed on 11 April 1961, with eight votes in favor and three members not voting either way. Jordan had laid a complaint on 1 April. A joint Israel-Jordan armistice board had ruled on the case on 20 March.

The Council backed the board's ruling. It urged Israel to obey it. It asked the board's members to work as one, so the 1949 truce pact held firm. The text shows the Council's early method in the Middle East. Back the local truce team. Name the side that must act. Keep the thin 1949 lines from snapping into war once more.

Afghanistan's rebuilding after the Bonn Process is the subject of Resolution 1662, adopted on 23 March 2006. Parliamentary and provincial votes had been held in September 2005, and the London Conference had just backed the Afghanistan Compact, a shared plan for safety, government, and growth. Attacks by the Taliban, Al-Qaida, and other armed groups were still rising.

The Council extends the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, for twelve more months. It calls on the Afghan government and its partners to carry out the Compact in full and hit its targets on time. It welcomes gains in disarming fighters and building the Afghan army and police. It also presses for fair courts, respect for human rights, and strong action against the opium trade.

Iraq's weapons inspectors are stood down by Resolution 1762, adopted on 29 June 2007. A democratically elected Iraqi government was in place, its constitution barred nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons, and a National Monitoring Directorate controlled dual-use imports. Letters from the US and UK and from Iraq's government reported that the disarmament steps had been taken and asked for the mandates to end.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminates immediately the mandates of UNMOVIC, the UN inspection commission, and of the IAEA under the Iraq resolutions. It reaffirms Iraq's disarmament duties. It invites Baghdad to report within one year on joining the Chemical Weapons Convention and an Additional Protocol to its safeguards agreement. It also invites a report on export-control progress. UNMOVIC's archives must be disposed of under strict control of sensitive information, and leftover inspection funds are transferred to the Development Fund for Iraq.

Resolution 1862, adopted on 14 January 2009, orders Eritrea to unwind its border clash with Djibouti. Eritrean forces had seized ground at Ras Doumeira in June 2008 and, as a UN fact-finding mission confirmed, had still not pulled back despite a presidential statement demanding it. Djibouti, by contrast, had withdrawn to the previous positions and cooperated with every mission sent.

The Council demanded that Eritrea pull its forces back to the status quo ante within five weeks at the latest. It also demanded that Eritrea acknowledge the border dispute, engage in dialogue, and stop refusing every offer of mediation, whether from the Secretary-General, regional bodies, or others. Djibouti's cooperation was explicitly welcomed, making the one-sidedness of the rebuke unmistakable.

Resolution 1962, adopted on 20 December 2010, answers a stolen election in Côte d'Ivoire. Two rounds of presidential voting that autumn had drawn massive, peaceful turnout after a decade of division. The electoral commission and UN certification pointed to Alassane Ouattara's victory, but the incumbent, Laurent Gbagbo, refused to leave, raising fears of renewed violence.

The Council condemned in the strongest terms the attempts to override the people's will and damage the election's integrity. It aligned itself with the African Union and West African states, which had suspended Côte d'Ivoire until the elected president took power. It also kept the UN operation, UNOCI, in place, renewing its mandate into 2011 while demanding restraint and protection of civilians.

Civil airliners blown up on the tarmac at Beirut drew this rebuke of 1968. On 31 December, the Council adopted Resolution 262 without dissent. Two days before, Israeli commandos had wrecked more than a dozen planes at Lebanon's airport. The raid answered an attack on an Israeli plane in Athens. Lebanon brought the case to New York.

The Council finds the raid planned in advance and run on a large scale. It condemns Israel for breaching the Charter and the truce texts. A grave warning follows. If such acts recur, the Council will weigh further steps. Lebanon is owed redress for its losses, the text adds. Israel had owned up to the raid.

Quiet held between the Egyptian and Israeli armies in the autumn of 1974, but the peace was thin. The Secretary-General warned that the Middle East as a whole would stay unstable while its underlying problems went unsolved. He judged that the United Nations Emergency Force was still required. Resolution 362 was adopted on 23 October 1974.

The Council extended the force's mandate for six more months, until 24 April 1975. The extension would support further work toward a just and lasting peace. The force and the governments that supplied its troops were praised. The Council said the force had to be run with maximum efficiency and economy. It also had to work as one united military unit across the whole sector. No contingent was to be treated differently from the others.

On 10 May 1985 the Council passed Resolution 562 by a full vote. It shields Nicaragua from force and squeeze from abroad. Nicaragua's envoy spoke, and many states joined the debate. Past texts had backed the right of Nicaragua and its neighbors to live in peace, free of outside meddling. Each land may pick its own way of rule and its own path for trade and growth. A bloc of Latin states, the Contadora Group, was then chasing a peace pact for the region.

The Council restated a key rule of world law. No state may use trade bans, cash pressure, or other force to bend a weaker state to its will. The words were broad, but the aim was plain. Days before, the United States had slapped a trade ban on Nicaragua and backed armed foes of its regime.

Palestine stood under a fragile truce in November 1948, and the Council wanted something firmer. The General Assembly was still debating the future government of Palestine. The Acting Mediator was working to carry out the Council's truce order on the ground. Resolution 62 was adopted on 16 November 1948.

The Council decided that an armistice should be established in all sectors of Palestine. An armistice would remove the threat to the peace. It would also ease the passage from a truce to a permanent peace. Acting as a provisional measure under Article 40 of the Charter, the Council called on the parties to negotiate at once. They could talk directly or through the Acting Mediator. They had to agree on permanent armistice lines that their forces could not cross. Forces also had to be pulled back and reduced, so the armistice would hold.

Resolution 662 is the UN Security Council's legal annulment of Iraq's annexation of Kuwait, adopted unanimously on 9 August 1990, a week after the invasion. Baghdad had just declared a comprehensive and eternal merger with Kuwait, claiming the emirate as Iraqi territory.

The resolution decides that the annexation, in any form and on any excuse, carries no legal weight at all and is null and void. It calls on all states, international organizations, and agencies not to recognize the annexation or do anything that might imply recognition, and demands Iraq rescind it. The doctrine that conquest creates no title, stated here in its bluntest form, underpinned the coalition case for liberating Kuwait.
van-helmont-oriatrike-1662:
Jean Baptiste van Helmont was a Flemish physician whose Ortus Medicinae reshaped seventeenth-century medicine. Chandler's 1662 English translation, Oriatrike, or Physick Refined, carried his Paracelsian chemical medicine to English readers. Van Helmont trusted the furnace and the balance as much as the ancient authors.

He teaches that life runs by ferments and by the archeus, an inner governor seated in the stomach's region. Fevers, stones, and plagues get new explanations in chemical terms, with cures drawn from mineral and plant preparations. His system broke Galen's long rule and taught doctors to think of the body as a chemical workshop.
wilson-prehistoric-man-1862:
Daniel Wilson, a Scottish scholar who became a Toronto professor, published Prehistoric Man in 1862. Wilson had coined the word 'prehistoric' in English a decade earlier. His book researches the origin of civilization in both the Old World and the New, the first systematic account of North American archaeology beside the European evidence.

He treats the mounds, earthworks, and copper tools of North America as seriously as Europe's barrows and flints. Against the fashion of his day, he argues the continent's ancient works were built by ancestors of its native peoples. The book is generous, learned, and early. It helped found archaeology in Canada and the United States.
